title: 3. β-OXIDATION OF FATTY ACIDS IN MITOCHONDRIA
section: 3. β-OXIDATION OF FATTY ACIDS IN MITOCHONDRIA › (untitled panel)
text: Mitochondrial β-oxidation is the principal pathway for fatty acid catabolism, producing acetyl-CoA, NADH and FADH2 for energy. It is especially important during fasting and in energy-tissues such as liver, heart and skeletal muscle. The liver can convert acetyl-CoA to ketone bodies to fuel extrahepatic tissues, including the brain.

source: ACar/beta oxidation of fatty acids in mitochondria.png
title: 3. β-OXIDATION OF FATTY ACIDS IN MITOCHONDRIA
section: 3. β-OXIDATION OF FATTY ACIDS IN MITOCHONDRIA › OVERVIEW
text:
- Main pathway for degradation of fatty acids.

- Occurs in mitochondrial matrix (after transport via carnitine shuttle).

- Repeats cycles of four reactions → progressive removal of two-carbon units as acetyl-CoA.

- Present in all eukaryotes and most prokaryotes.

- Many isoenzymes adapt to different chain lengths and substrates.

- Long-chain fatty acids (>C8) use carnitine-dependent transport; short/medium chains can cross membrane without carnitine.

title: 3. β-OXIDATION OF FATTY ACIDS IN MITOCHONDRIA
section: 3. β-OXIDATION OF FATTY ACIDS IN MITOCHONDRIA › KEY POINTS
text:
- Each cycle shortens the acyl chain by 2 carbons.

- FADH2 and NADH feed the electron transport chain → ATP.

- Final products (even-chain): multiple acetyl-CoA.

- Odd-chain fatty acids yield propionyl-CoA in final cycle → converted to succinyl-CoA.

- Enzymes 2–4 are assembled in a trifunctional enzyme complex on the inner mitochondrial membrane.

source: ACar/beta oxidation of fatty acids in mitochondria.png
title: 3. β-OXIDATION OF FATTY ACIDS IN MITOCHONDRIA
section: 3. β-OXIDATION OF FATTY ACIDS IN MITOCHONDRIA › ENERGY YIELD (example: palmitate, C16:0)
text:
- 7 cycles → 7 FADH2 + 7 NADH + 8 Acetyl-CoA

- TCA yield per acetyl-CoA: 3 NADH + 1 FADH2 + 1 GTP (≈10 ATP equivalents)

- Total ≈ 129–131 ATP per palmitate

- Fatty acids yield ~2× more energy than glucose (39 kJ g−1 vs 15 kJ g−1).

title: 3. β-OXIDATION OF FATTY ACIDS IN MITOCHONDRIA
section: 3. β-OXIDATION OF FATTY ACIDS IN MITOCHONDRIA › REGULATION
text:
- Product inhibition: each enzyme inhibited by its own acyl-CoA product.

- High NADH/NAD+ or acetyl-CoA/CoA inhibits β-oxidation.

- Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT I → blocks entry of fatty acyl-CoA into mitochondria.

- Transcriptional control: PPARs + coactivator PGC-1α (with RXR) ↑ expression of genes for β-oxidation enzymes.

title: 3. β-OXIDATION OF FATTY ACIDS IN MITOCHONDRIA
section: 3. β-OXIDATION OF FATTY ACIDS IN MITOCHONDRIA › PHYSIOLOGICAL AND CLINICAL NOTES
text:
- Carnitine maintains acyl-CoA/CoA balance and removes excess acyl groups.

- Defects in carnitine transport or β-oxidation enzymes cause hypoketotic hypoglycemia, cardiomyopathy, muscle weakness, rhabdomyolysis, exercise intolerance.

- Acylcarnitine profiling in plasma/tissues is a key diagnostic tool for inborn errors of metabolism.

- Carnitine and acylcarnitines also export products from peroxisomes (e.g., short-chain acyl groups).

title: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH
text: Carnitine shuttles acyl groups for β-oxidation and removes excess acyl-CoAs. Defects in this system cause toxic acyl-CoA accumulation and disease. Acylcarnitine profiling in blood/urine is a powerful diagnostic tool and has implications for many disorders and therapeutic strategies.

title: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH
section: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH › 6.1 ROLE OF CARNITINE AND ACYLCARNITINES
text:
- Carnitine transports fatty acyl groups into mitochondria for β-oxidation and removes surplus acyl groups from mitochondria and peroxisomes.

- Maintains balance of acyl-CoA/CoA ratio and prevents accumulation of toxic acyl-CoAs.

- Acylcarnitines with highly polyunsaturated acyl chains are less cardiotoxic than saturated/monounsaturated analogues.

- Plasma acylation state of carnitine reflects cytosolic acylcarnitine pool → marker of acyl-CoA/acylcarnitine equilibrium.

- Alterations in acylcarnitine profiles can affect the tissue lipidome.

title: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH
section: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH › ACYLCARNITINES AS BIOMARKERS
text:
- Accumulation of unusual acylcarnitines indicates specific defects in β-oxidation.

- Chain length and degree of unsaturation help identify the enzymic block.

- Used in newborn screening and diagnosis of metabolic diseases.

title: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH
section: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH › 6.2 SELECTED INHERITED DISORDERS OF β-OXIDATION AND CARNITINE METABOLISM
text:
- Disorder (defective step): Primary Carnitine Deficiency (OCTN2 transporter defect); Accumulated acylcarnitines: Free carnitine ↓; Typical features: Hypoketotic hypoglycemia, cardiomyopathy, muscle weakness, infertility; Inheritance: Autosomal recessive

- Disorder (defective step): Medium-Chain Acyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency (MCAD); Accumulated acylcarnitines: C6, C8, C10:1 medium-chain; Typical features: Hypoketotic hypoglycemia, vomiting, lethargy, seizures; triggered by fasting/illness; Inheritance: Autosomal recessive

- Disorder (defective step): Very-Long-Chain Acyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency (VLCAD); Accumulated acylcarnitines: C14:1, C14, C16:1 long-chain; Typical features: Cardiomyopathy, muscle weakness, rhabdomyolysis, hypoketotic hypoglycemia; Inheritance: Autosomal recessive

title: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH
section: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH › 6.2 SELECTED INHERITED DISORDERS OF β-OXIDATION AND CARNITINE METABOLISM
text:
- Disorder (defective step): Carnitine Palmitoyltransferase II Deficiency (CPT II); Accumulated acylcarnitines: C16, C18, OH-C16, OH-C18; Typical features: Muscle cramps, myoglobinuria, exercise intolerance, cardiomyopathy; Inheritance: Autosomal recessive

- Disorder (defective step): Multiple Acyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency (MADD/GA II); Accumulated acylcarnitines: Multiple acylcarnitines (broad profile); Typical features: Hypoketotic hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, neurodevelopmental defects; Inheritance: Autosomal recessive

- Disorder (defective step): Peroxisomal Biogenesis Disorders (e.g., Zellweger, X-linked ALD); Accumulated acylcarnitines: VLC acylcarnitines, pristanic, phytanic; Typical features: Hypotonia, seizures, organomegaly, neurologic degeneration; Inheritance: Autosomal recessive or X-linked

title: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH
section: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH › 6.2 SELECTED INHERITED DISORDERS OF β-OXIDATION AND CARNITINE METABOLISM
text: >30 inherited metabolic diseases detectable by acylcarnitine profiling in newborns. Overall incidence ~1 in 10,000 live births.

title: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH
section: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH › 6.3 CLINICAL AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGICAL IMPACT
text:
- Brain uses ketone bodies as major energy source during fasting. Acylcarnitine abnormalities associated with encephalopathy and neurodevelopmental issues.

- Cardiac and skeletal muscle rely on fatty acid oxidation; defects cause cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, exercise intolerance.

- Liver: impaired β-oxidation → hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, fatty liver; contributes to MAFLD and metabolic syndrome.

- Acylcarnitines detected in obesity, type 2 diabetes, CVD, diseases of the eye.

- Lipotoxicity from accumulated acyl species → inflammation, insulin resistance, organ dysfunction.

- Gut microbiota converts carnitine → TMA → TMAO, associated with atherosclerosis, MI and stroke risk.

Dysregulation of CPT1 and carnitine cycle implicated in cancer, ferroptosis, and many cardiometabolic disorders.

title: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH
section: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH › 6.4 HEALTH BENEFITS AND NEUROPROTECTION
text:
- L-Acetyl-carnitine crosses the BBB. Modulates acetylcholine, serotonin, dopamine and neurotrophic factors.

- Marketed for neuropathic pain.

- Evidence for benefit in cognitive and mood disorders; may help in early Alzheimer's disease.

- Supports lipid metabolism in brain (membrane synthesis, signalling).

- May protect against traumatic brain injury and neurodegeneration.

- Elevated palmitoyl-carnitine in aging mice → mitochondrial dysfunction.

title: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH
section: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH › POTENTIAL MECHANISMS
text:
- Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions

- Epigenetic effects (histone acetylation)

- Mitochondrial biogenesis and function

- Regulation of membrane lipid composition

title: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH
section: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH › 6.5 CARNITINE AND ACYLCARNITINE SUPPLEMENTATION
text:
Common Supplements and Functions

- Compound: L-Carnitine (levocarnitine); Key functions: Supports fatty acid oxidation, energy production, removes excess acyl groups; Notes: Essential in rare deficiencies; may help in angina, arrhythmias, dialysis patients, liver and heart disease

- Compound: Acetyl-L-carnitine; Key functions: Energy metabolism, neurotransmitter modulation, acetate donor; Notes: Better absorbed; crosses BBB readily; may support cognition, mood, neuropathic pain

- Compound: Propionyl-L-carnitine; Key functions: Anaplerotic (propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA); supports energy; Notes: Potential benefit in vascular disease, peripheral neuropathy

- Compound: Octanoyl-L-carnitine; Key functions: Shuttles medium-chain acyl groups; energy; Notes: Shown beneficial in models of long-chain FAO disorders

title: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH
section: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH › 6.5 CARNITINE AND ACYLCARNITINE SUPPLEMENTATION
text:
- Useful as adjunct therapy in selected patients (cardiac, metabolic liver disease, dialysis, some neuropathies).

- Important and lifesaving in genetic carnitine or FAO disorders.

- Potential benefits for exercise performance and recovery (evidence mixed).

- High doses may cause GI discomfort, fishy body odour, or seizures in predisposed individuals.

title: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH
section: 6. CARNITINE, β-OXIDATION AND HEALTH › 6.6 KEY TAKE-HOME MESSAGES
text:
- Carnitine is essential for mitochondrial and peroxisomal β-oxidation and removal of excess acyl groups.

- Acylcarnitine profiling is a sensitive diagnostic tool for inherited metabolic diseases and other disorders.

- Defects in carnitine transport or β-oxidation lead to toxic metabolite accumulation and organ dysfunction.

- Ketone bodies are vital alternative fuels during fasting and in disease, with signalling roles beyond energy.

- Peroxisomal β-oxidation handles VLC, branched and dicarboxylic fatty acids and protects against lipid accumulation.

- Carnitine and acylcarnitine supplementation may benefit certain clinical conditions and support brain and heart health, but therapy should be individualized.

title: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA
section: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA › (untitled panel)
text: Carnitine transports long-chain fatty acyl groups (>C8) into the mitochondrial matrix for β-oxidation and helps remove surplus acyl groups. It maintains the balance between acyl-CoA and free CoA and is essential for energy production and metabolic homeostasis.

title: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA
section: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA › 2.1 SOURCES AND ACTIVATION OF FATTY ACIDS
text:
Sources of fatty acids

- Exogenous: diet and mobilization from other tissues.

- De novo synthesis from acetyl-CoA.

- Hydrolysis of triacylglycerols and phospholipids.

Activation to acyl-CoA

Fatty acid + CoA + ATP → Acyl-S-CoA + AMP + PPi

Diagram labels: Acyl-CoA synthetase

Cost: equivalent of 2 ATP.

- Acyl-CoAs bind to proteins (acyl-CoA binding domains).

- Directed to pathways: storage, oxidation, or other metabolism depending on cellular energy status.

- Long-chain acyl-CoAs cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Carnitine enables transport into mitochondria and removal of excess acyl groups; prevents accumulation of acyl-CoAs, which is potentially toxic.

title: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA
section: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA › 2.2 CARNITINE AND ACYLCARNITINES: ROLES
text:
- Carnitine (3-hydroxyl) esterifies with acyl-CoA → acylcarnitines.

- Acylcarnitines are more lipophilic than carnitine.

- Functions:

- Transport long-chain fatty acyl groups into mitochondria.

- Export surplus acyl groups from mitochondria and peroxisomes.

- Export acetyl- and other short-chain acyl groups.

- Regulate acyl-CoA/CoA ratio and CoA homeostasis.

- Aid excretion of acyl residues from amino acid metabolism (especially branched-chain amino acids).

- Homocarnitine can be esterified similarly.

Carnitine acetyltransferase (CrAT)

Found in mitochondrial matrix, peroxisomal matrix, ER and nucleus.

- Regulates acetyl-CoA / CoA ratio.

- During high workload (e.g., exercise): exports excess acetyl groups as acetylcarnitine → preserves free CoA.

- When workload ends: reconnects acetylcarnitine → acetyl-CoA for Krebs cycle.

- In peroxisomes: exports products of β-oxidation.

title: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA
section: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA › Step 1: CPT I (outer membrane)
text:
- Transfers acyl group from acyl-CoA to carnitine → acylcarnitine.

- Inhibited by malonyl-CoA.

title: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA
section: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA › Step 2: Translocation (inner membrane)
text:
- CACT exchanges acylcarnitine (in) for carnitine (out).

- Maintains mitochondrial carnitine level.

title: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA
section: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA › Step 3: CPT II (matrix side)
text:
- Transfers acyl group from acylcarnitine back to CoA → acyl-CoA.

- Carnitine is released and recycled.

title: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA
section: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA › Key features of the carnitine transport system
text:
- Long-chain fatty acids (>C8) require this shuttle; they cannot cross the inner membrane as CoA-thioesters.

- Rate-controlling step for mitochondrial β-oxidation.

- Three proteins: CPT I, CACT, CPT II.

- Requires intact membrane potential for efficient exchange.

title: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA
section: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA › CPT I isoforms and regulation
text:
- CPT IA – liver, kidney

- CPT IB – heart, skeletal muscle

- CPT IC – brain (may act as sensor of lipid metabolism in neurons)

- Malonyl-CoA (from ACC2) binds with high affinity to CPT I isoforms → inhibits acyl transfer → decreases fatty acid oxidation.

- High energy demand: ↓ ACC2 inhibition → ↑ β-oxidation. Inhibition of ACC1 → ↓ fatty acid synthesis.

title: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA
section: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA › 2.3 SHORT- AND MEDIUM-CHAIN FATTY ACIDS
text:
- Short-chain fatty acids (≤C8, e.g., octanoate) can cross the inner mitochondrial membrane in non-esterified form.

- Activated to acyl-CoA in the matrix for oxidation.

- Peroxisomes oxidize very long-chain fatty acids.

title: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA
section: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA › 2.4 CLINICAL AND PHYSIOLOGICAL SIGNIFICANCE
text:
- Carnitine deficiencies or defects in transport (CPT I, CACT, CPT II) → impaired fatty acid oxidation → hypoketotic hypoglycemia, cardiomyopathy, muscle weakness, exercise intolerance.

- Acylcarnitine profiles in plasma/tissues are diagnostic markers for inborn errors of metabolism.

- Supports energy homeostasis, insulin sensitivity and regulation of lipid and carbohydrate metabolism.

- Neuroprotective, anti-inflammatory, and involved in gene regulation and cell signalling.

title: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA
section: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA › 2.5 SUMMARY
text:
- Carnitine is essential for mitochondrial uptake of long-chain fatty acyl groups.

- Forms acylcarnitines to transport acyl groups into mitochondria and remove excess.

- Maintains acyl-CoA/CoA balance and CoA homeostasis.

- Works with three key proteins: CPT I, CACT, CPT II.

- Regulated by malonyl-CoA and the cell's energy status.

- Short- and medium-chain fatty acids use different transport routes.

- Carnitine is vital for energy production and metabolic health.

title: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA
section: 2. CARNITINE, ACYLCARNITINES AND FATTY ACID TRANSPORT INTO MITOCHONDRIA › Abbreviations
text: ACC1/2, acetyl-CoA carboxylase isoforms 1 and 2; CACT, carnitine:acylcarnitine translocase; CoA, coenzyme A; CPT I/II, carnitine palmitoyltransferases I and II; ER, endoplasmic reticulum; PPi, inorganic pyrophosphate.

title: 4. KETONE BODIES
text: During fasting, prolonged exercise, low-carbohydrate intake and uncontrolled type 1 diabetes, the liver converts acetyl-CoA (from fatty acid β-oxidation) into ketone bodies. These water-soluble molecules are exported to extrahepatic tissues where they are reconverted to acetyl-CoA for energy production and other biosynthetic processes.

title: 4. KETONE BODIES
text:
Diagram labels: Acetoacetate (3-oxobutanoate); β-Hydroxybutyrate (3-hydroxybutyrate); Acetone (propanone)

Acetone is produced spontaneously from acetoacetate (decarboxylation).

title: 4. KETONE BODIES
section: 4. KETONE BODIES › SOURCES AND PHYSIOLOGICAL ROLES
text:
- Produced in liver mitochondria from acetyl-CoA during fasting, starvation, prolonged exercise, low-carbohydrate diet, or uncontrolled diabetes mellitus (ketosis).

- Major fuel for brain, heart, skeletal muscle and kidney during low glucose availability.

- Provide acetyl-CoA for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis in extrahepatic tissues.

- Transported in blood as water-soluble anions (acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate).

- Excessive production → ketoacidosis (low blood pH, dangerous).

title: 4. KETONE BODIES
text: Diagram labels: 2 Acetyl-CoA; Thiolase; Acetoacetyl-CoA; HMG-CoA synthase; HMG-CoA; HMG-CoA lyase; Acetoacetate; β-Hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase; NADH + H+; NAD+; Acetone + CO2 (spontaneous); β-Hydroxybutyrate

title: 4. KETONE BODIES
section: 4. KETONE BODIES › UTILIZATION OF KETONE BODIES (extrahepatic tissues)
text:
Diagram labels: Acetoacetate; Acetoacetyl-CoA synthetase; CoA-SH + ATP; AMP + PPi; Acetoacetyl-CoA; Thiolase; Acetyl-CoA + Acetyl-CoA

- Acetyl-CoA enters tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle → ATP.

- Acetyl-CoA can also be used for fatty acid or cholesterol synthesis.

title: 4. KETONE BODIES
text:
- Ketone bodies are produced only in liver mitochondria.

- Extrahepatic tissues lack HMG-CoA lyase → cannot synthesise ketone bodies but can use them.

- Transport form: acetoacetate (anion) and β-hydroxybutyrate (anion); acetone is volatile and excreted in breath.

- Ketogenic diets ↑ ketone production; therapeutic uses in epilepsy and some metabolic disorders.

- Signalling roles: ligands for GPCRs; regulate gene expression (epigenetic modifications); influence inflammation and immunity.

title: 4. KETONE BODIES
text:
- Elevated ketones (ketosis) in fasting, diabetes, alcoholism, pregnancy.

- Excess → ketoacidosis: high ketones, low bicarbonate, metabolic acidosis.

- Urine/blood ketone tests used clinically.

- Defects in ketone body utilisation: e.g., SCOT deficiency → ketosis with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia.

title: 4. KETONE BODIES
section: 4. KETONE BODIES › 5. PEROXISOMAL β-OXIDATION IN ANIMALS
text: Peroxisomes oxidize very-long-chain (≥C24), methyl-branched and dicarboxylic fatty acids and perform the first steps of α-oxidation. They also carry out an essential step in ether lipid biosynthesis and detoxify reactive oxygen species.

title: 4. KETONE BODIES
text:
- Occurs in peroxisome matrix; not coupled to ATP synthesis.

- Uses acyl-CoA oxidase (ACOX1/2/3) which transfers electrons directly to O2 → H2O2.

- Two bifunctional proteins (DBP, LBP) catalyse hydration and dehydrogenation steps.

- β-Ketothiolase (with CoA-acyltransferase activity) performs thiolysis.

- Shortens acyl chains to ~C8 (octanoate) → exported to mitochondria for further β-oxidation.

- Generates acetyl-CoA, which cannot enter TCA cycle in peroxisome; exported as acetylcarnitine or acetate.

- Major roles in lipid metabolism, ROS detoxification and plasmalogen (ether lipid) synthesis.

title: 4. KETONE BODIES
section: 4. KETONE BODIES › Figure 4. Peroxisomal β-oxidation of fatty acyl-CoA (general pathway)
text: Diagram labels: Fatty acyl-CoA (very-long-chain, methyl-branched, dicarboxylic); 1 Acyl-CoA oxidase (ACOX1/2/3); FAD; FADH2; O2; H2O2; trans-2-Enoyl-CoA; 2 Bifunctional protein (DBP or LBP); H2O; Hydratase; L-3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA; 3 Dehydrogenase; NAD+; NADH + H+; 3-Ketoacyl-CoA; 4 β-Ketothiolase (CoA-acyltransferase); CoA-SH; Acetyl-CoA; Acyl-CoA (n~2 carbons); Cycle repeats until ~C8 (octanoate)

title: 4. KETONE BODIES
text:
- Acetyl-CoA → converted to acetylcarnitine (by CrAT) or acetate → to mitochondria for oxidation.

- H2O2 → detoxified by catalase in peroxisome.

title: 4. KETONE BODIES
text:
- Preferred substrates: ≥C24 fatty acids, pristanic acid, phytanic acid precursors, dicarboxylic acids.

- Monomethyl branched fatty acids → rapid turnover in brown adipose tissue (thermogenesis).

- Essential for α-oxidation of phytanic acid (Refsum disease if impaired).

title: 4. KETONE BODIES
section: 4. KETONE BODIES › CLINICAL AND DIAGNOSTIC ASPECTS
text:
- Peroxisomal β-oxidation disorders → accumulation of VLCFAs.

- Biomarkers: ↑ plasma 24:0- and 26:0-lysophosphatidylcholines.

- Associated diseases: Zellweger spectrum disorders, X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.

- Peroxisome biogenesis disorders → ↑ dicarboxylic acid carnitine esters in plasma.

- Protects against lipid accumulation in neurological diseases.

title: 4. KETONE BODIES
section: 4. KETONE BODIES › ADDITIONAL PATHWAYS IN PEROXISOMES
text:
- α-Oxidation: removes methyl group at α-carbon → shortens methyl-branched fatty acids (e.g., phytanic acid).

- ω-Oxidation (minor): fatty acids → ω-hydroxy fatty acids → dicarboxylic acids can be esterified with carnitine.

- Ether lipid biosynthesis: dihydroxyacetone phosphate acyltransferase step occurs in peroxisomes.

- ROS metabolism: catalase converts H2O2 → H2O + O2.

text: ACC, acetyl-CoA carboxylase; ATP, adenosine triphosphate; CoA, coenzyme A; CrAT, carnitine acetyltransferase; CPTI/II, carnitine palmitoyltransferases I and II; DBP, D-bifunctional protein; FAD, flavin adenine dinucleotide; FADH2, reduced FAD; GPCR, G protein-coupled receptor; NAD+/NADH, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (oxidized/reduced); ROS, reactive oxygen species.

title: CARNITINE
text: CARNITINE: The quaternary ammonium compound and amino acid carnitine (L-3-hydroxy-4-aminobutyrobetaine) and its acyl esters (acylcarnitines) are essential for the mitochondrial transport of long-chain fatty acids for β-oxidation and energy production. They also bind acyl groups from amino acid metabolism (especially branched-chain amino acids) to aid their elimination and help regulate the acyl-CoA/CoA ratio and mitochondrial enzyme activities.

title: CARNITINE
section: CARNITINE › STRUCTURAL FORMULAE FOR CARNITINE AND ACYLCARNITINES
text:
Diagram labels: L-Carnitine (L-3-hydroxy-4-N-trimethylaminobutanoic acid) (3-hydroxy-4-aminobutyrobetaine); Acylcarnitines (general structure); Homocarnitine (γ-butyrobetaine or 4-trimethylammonio-1-hydroxybutyrate)

L-Carnitine

- Quaternary ammonium betaine (positively charged).

- Exists naturally in the L-configuration.

- Highly water-soluble, zwitterionic at physiological pH.

Acylcarnitines (general structure)

- Formed by esterification of carnitine with acyl-CoA.

- R = acyl group (fatty acyl or other acyl residues).

- Acylcarnitines are more lipophilic than carnitine.

Homocarnitine

- One methylene longer than carnitine.

- Synthesised in mammals by hydroxylation of δ-valerobetaine derived from the microbiome.

title: CARNITINE
section: CARNITINE › 1A. DE NOVO BIOSYNTHESIS IN ANIMALS
text:
Occurs in liver, kidney and brain using N-trimethyl-lysine from protein degradation as the primary precursor.

Diagram labels: Protein degradation; Lysine; Trimethyllysine dioxygenase; N6-Trimethyl-lysine; Trimethyllysine hydroxylase; 3-Hydroxy-N6-trimethyl-lysine; Aldehyde dehydrogenase; γ-Butyrobetaine aldehyde; Aldehyde dehydrogenase; γ-Butyrobetaine (butyrobetaine); γ-Butyrobetaine hydroxylase; L-Carnitine

Total endogenous synthesis ≈ 1.2 μmol/day/kg body weight (insufficient for most individuals).

title: CARNITINE
text:
- Carnitine concentrations in tissues: 0.2–6 mmol/kg.

- Highest levels in heart and skeletal muscle.

- Essential for transport of long-chain fatty acyl groups into mitochondria for β-oxidation.

- Binds acyl groups from amino acid metabolism (particularly branched-chain amino acids) → facilitates excretion.

- Regulates the acyl-CoA/CoA ratio and activity of several mitochondrial enzymes.

title: CARNITINE
text:
- High-affinity reabsorption of carnitine and butyrobetaine by OCTN2 transporter.

- Minimizes urinary loss; excess amounts are eliminated when necessary.

title: CARNITINE
text: D-Carnitine does not occur naturally. It does not participate in key biological processes and can interfere with them.

title: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND METABOLISM OF CARDIOLIPIN
section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND METABOLISM OF CARDIOLIPIN › A. BIOSYNTHESIS IN EUKARYOTES (mitochondrial inner membrane)
text:
Two different precursors are required: (i) phosphatidylglycerol (PG) and (ii) CDP-diacylglycerol (CDP-DG). All enzymes face the matrix side.

Diagram labels: Phosphatidic acid (PA); Phosphatidylglycerol phosphate (PGP); Phosphatidylglycerol (PG); CDP-diacylglycerol (CDP-DG); Cardiolipin (CL); PGP synthase (PgsA); PGP phosphatase (Pgp1); CDP-DG synthase (TAM41/TAMM41); Cardiolipin synthase (CLS, Tafazzin); CTP; PPi; Pi; CMP

PA is synthesized on the ER and imported to mitochondria by protein complexes (e.g., [illegible] ASSOCIATED MEMBRANES, MAMs).

CDP-DG synthase in mitochondria (TAM41/TAMM41) is structurally distinct from the ER CDP-DG synthases. Cardiolipin synthase is a phosphatidyltransferase belonging to the CDP-alcohol phosphatidyltransferase superfamily (in animals and plants).

title: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND METABOLISM OF CARDIOLIPIN
section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND METABOLISM OF CARDIOLIPIN › B. BIOSYNTHESIS IN PROKARYOTES (bacterial inner membrane)
text:
(i) Main pathway – transphosphatidylation (energy independent)

Diagram labels: 2 Phosphatidylglycerol (PG); Cardiolipin (CL); Cardiolipin synthase (ClsA or ClsB); – Glycerol; PG + Phosphatidylethanolamine (PE); ClsB or ClsC; – Ethanolamine; Cardiolipin (CL)

- ClsA is the major synthase in E. coli during exponential growth (ClsB/C are minor).

- Cls enzymes belong to the phospholipase D superfamily.

- Some bacteria (e.g., Acinetobacter baumannii) have ClsO on the outer membrane that decorates LPS with cardiolipin.

section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND METABOLISM OF CARDIOLIPIN › C. REMODELLING OF CARDIOLIPIN IN EUKARYOTES – UNIQUE TAFAzzin PATHWAY

- Tafazzin catalyzes a CoA-independent transacylation between MLCL and other phospholipids.

- The process yields the characteristic symmetrical molecular species (e.g., tetra-linolooyl CL). It is essential for optimal function.

title: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND METABOLISM OF CARDIOLIPIN
section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND METABOLISM OF CARDIOLIPIN › A. KEY FUNCTIONS OF CARDIOLIPIN
text:
Mitochondrial bioenergetics

- Essential for assembly, stability and activity of respiratory chain complexes (esp. III and IV) and ATP synthase (V).

- Optimizes electron transport and ATP production.

- Modulates membrane curvature and supercomplex formation.

Membrane structure

- Promotes negative curvature and tight packing.

- Stabilizes mitochondrial inner membrane and cristae architecture.

- Contributes to membrane fluidity and domain formation.

Protein binding and signalling scaffold

- Binds cytochrome c, tBid, kinases, and other proteins.

- Acts as a scaffold for signalling platforms.

- Interacts with proteins via electrostatic and hydrophobic contacts.

Apoptosis regulation

- Peroxidized or oxidized CL releases cytochrome c.

- Facilitates apoptosome formation and caspase activation.

- Central in intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptotic pathway.

Oxidative stress defence

title: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND METABOLISM OF CARDIOLIPIN
section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND METABOLISM OF CARDIOLIPIN › A. KEY FUNCTIONS OF CARDIOLIPIN
text:
- Scavenges ROS and limits lipid peroxidation.

- Contributes to mitochondrial redox homeostasis.

- Protects against oxidative damage.

title: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND METABOLISM OF CARDIOLIPIN
section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND METABOLISM OF CARDIOLIPIN › B. CONSEQUENCES OF CARDIOLIPIN DYSFUNCTION
text:
Cardiolipin depletion or remodelling defects

- Impaired respiratory chain activity and lower ATP.

- Mitochondrial fragmentation and structural defects.

- Increased ROS production.

Peroxidized cardiolipin

- Promotes cytochrome c release.

- Triggers apoptosis.

- Associated with aging and degenerative conditions.

Clinical and disease associations

- Barth syndrome (tafazzin deficiency).

- Cardiomyopathies and heart failure.

- Neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Huntington's).

- Metabolic disorders.

Cancer

- Altered CL metabolism supports tumour growth and survival.

- Affects mitochondrial fusion, bioenergetics and apoptosis resistance.

Other

- Ischemia-reperfusion injury.

- Diabetes and obesity.

- Sepsis.

- Liver disease.

title: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND METABOLISM OF CARDIOLIPIN
section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND METABOLISM OF CARDIOLIPIN › 4. KEY POINTS
text:
- Cardiolipin is a dimeric phospholipid unique to mitochondria and some bacteria.

- Eukaryotes use PA → PG → CDP-DG → cardiolipin (energy-dependent) pathway.

- Bacteria use transphosphatidylation of PG (energy-independent) via Cls enzymes.

- Final composition is achieved by tafazzin-dependent remodelling.

- Cardiolipin is vital for mitochondrial structure, respiration, apoptosis regulation and stress defence.

- Dysfunction or oxidation of cardiolipin is linked to many human diseases.

- Cardiolipin is indispensable for cellular energy production and integrity.

title: 3. FUNCTION OF CARDIOLIPIN
text:
Cardiolipin (CL) is the signature lipid of mitochondria (and some bacteria), located almost exclusively in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM). Its unique dimeric structure with two phosphate groups and four acyl chains enables diverse interactions that are essential for mitochondrial structure, bioenergetics, metabolism and quality control.

Diagram labels: Outer membrane; Intermembrane space; Inner membrane (cardiolipin rich); Matrix; Cristae

title: 3. FUNCTION OF CARDIOLIPIN
section: 3. FUNCTION OF CARDIOLIPIN › A. CARDIOLIPIN–PROTEIN INTERACTIONS
text:
- CL binds hundreds of unrelated proteins.

- No universal sequence motif; three key interaction regions in proteins:

1. Phosphate binding patches (basic residues: Arg, Lys, His)

2. Hydroxyl binding patches (aromatic/polar residues: Trp, Tyr)

3. Acyl chain (hydrophobic) patches (Ile, Leu, Val, Phe)

- Head groups interact via electrostatic and H-bonds; acyl chains via van der Waals contacts.

- CL adapts its conformation to different protein surfaces; promotes membrane curvature and domain formation.

Diagram labels: Cardiolipin interacting with a protein; Protein surface; Electrostatic / H-bond; Hydrogen bond; Hydrophobic interaction

Examples of CL-binding proteins

- Cytochrome c (haemoprotein)

- Elamipretide (cell-permeable peptide)

- Snake venom cardiotoxins

- α-Synuclein

- ABC transporter ABCB10

- Plasma protein β2-glycoprotein I

title: 3. FUNCTION OF CARDIOLIPIN
section: 3. FUNCTION OF CARDIOLIPIN › A. CARDIOLIPIN–PROTEIN INTERACTIONS
text:
- Many respiratory chain proteins and enzymes

CL promotes non-bilayer structures and lateral organization of the IMM.

title: 3. FUNCTION OF CARDIOLIPIN
section: 3. FUNCTION OF CARDIOLIPIN › B. ROLE IN OXIDATIVE PHOSPHORYLATION (OXPHOS)
text:
Diagram labels: Electron transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane; Matrix (side); 4 H+; 4 H+; 2 H+; H+; I; II; Q; III; Cyt c; IV; NADH dehydrogenase; Succinate dehydrogenase; Cytochrome bc1 complex; Cytochrome c oxidase; Intermembrane space; NADH; NAD+; Succinate; Fumarate; 1/2 O2; H2O; ADP + Pi; ATP; Cardiolipin

One respirasome (example): I + (III2) + (IV) – can contain up to ~200 CL molecules.

1 Respiratory chain complexes

- CL is required for assembly, stability and optimal activity of OXPHOS complexes.

- Integral component in structures of complexes III (bc1), IV (cytochrome c oxidase), I, and probably II, and the ADP/ATP carrier.

- "Glue" that organizes components into supercomplexes (respirasomes).

- Displacement of linoleate by DHA in CL reduces respiratory complex activities.

2 Enzymes and metabolic pathway components

title: 3. FUNCTION OF CARDIOLIPIN
section: 3. FUNCTION OF CARDIOLIPIN › B. ROLE IN OXIDATIVE PHOSPHORYLATION (OXPHOS)
text:
- Required for optimal activity of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) – links glycolysis to TCA cycle.

- Stabilizes mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU) – couples Ca2+ signalling to bioenergetics.

- Essential for assembly and activity of many matrix and membrane enzymes.

3 Uncoupling and energy metabolism

- Three CL molecules bind tightly to uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1) in brown adipose tissue – crucial for thermogenesis.

- Supports proper function of ATP synthase – degree of oligomerization and order of assemblies.

4 Mitochondrial dynamics and quality control

- Regulates fusion–fission balance (interacts with Drp1, OPA1, Mfn2).

- CL externalization to outer membrane is a signal for mitophagy.

- Maintains cristae structure and IMM integrity.

title: 3. FUNCTION OF CARDIOLIPIN
text:
- Bioenergetics and ATP production

- Maintains membrane structure and cristae morphology

- Regulates proteins and enzymes

- Couples metabolism and signalling

- Protects against stress and oxidative damage

- Controls mitochondrial dynamics and quality

title: 3. FUNCTION OF CARDIOLIPIN
section: 3. FUNCTION OF CARDIOLIPIN › C. OTHER IMPORTANT FUNCTIONS
text:
Cristae biogenesis and membrane morphology

- High CL content favors negative curvature.

- Essential for cristae junctions and stability.

Endoplasmic reticulum–mitochondria contact sites (MAMs)

- CL regulates MAM formation and function.

- Important for Ca2+ transfer, lipid exchange and signalling.

Antioxidant and stress protection

- Scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS).

- Protects proteins, lipids and mtDNA from oxidative damage.

Apoptosis signalling

- Diagram labels: tBid; CL externalization (outer membrane); ROS; Cytochrome c release

- Externalization of CL promotes cytochrome c release.

- Key step in intrinsic apoptotic pathway.

Lipid raft / domain formation

- CL forms microdomains.

- Recruits and concentrates proteins and lipids for efficient function.

title: 3. FUNCTION OF CARDIOLIPIN
section: 3. FUNCTION OF CARDIOLIPIN › D. CONSEQUENCES OF CARDIOLIPIN DYSFUNCTION
text:
Energy failure

- Reduced OXPHOS efficiency

- Low ATP production

- Exercise intolerance

Oxidative stress

- Increased ROS

- Lipid peroxidation

- mtDNA damage

Mitochondrial dysfunction

- Disrupted cristae

- Impaired dynamics

- Mitophagy defects

Cellular outcomes

- Apoptosis

- Necrosis

- Inflammation

Diseases linked

- Barth syndrome (tafazzin defect)

- Cardiomyopathies

- Neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Huntington's)

- Ischemia–reperfusion injury

- Diabetes and obesity

- Cancer

- Aging

title: 3. FUNCTION OF CARDIOLIPIN
section: 3. FUNCTION OF CARDIOLIPIN › E. KEY POINTS
text:
- Unique dimeric phospholipid of mitochondria and some bacteria.

- Four acyl chains and two phosphates enable diverse functions.

- Essential for OXPHOS, membrane structure and mitochondrial dynamics.

- Interacts with many proteins and forms supercomplexes.

- Protects against oxidative stress and regulates signalling.

- Remodelling to symmetrical linoleoyl-species is crucial for function.

- Dysfunction is strongly associated with many human diseases.

title: 3. FUNCTION OF CARDIOLIPIN
text: Cardiolipin is an irreplaceable mitochondrial phospholipid whose unique dimeric structure enables it to act as a structural scaffold, a molecular glue for protein complexes, and a dynamic regulator of mitochondrial bioenergetics, metabolism, signalling and quality control. Its dysfunction is linked to a wide range of human diseases.

title: 4. CARDIOLIPIN IN DISEASE
section: 4. CARDIOLIPIN IN DISEASE › A. BARTH SYNDROME (X-LINKED INFANTILE CARDIOMYOPATHY)
text:
Normal vs. Barth syndrome cardiolipin profile in blood

Diagram labels: Normal; Barth syndrome; High tetra-linoleoyl cardiolipin (CLtetra-18:2); ↓ CLtetra-18:2; ↑ Monolysocardiolipin (MLCL)

- Caused by mutations in the tafazzin (TAZ) gene → defective remodeling of cardiolipin.

- ↓ Tetra-linoleoyl CL, ↑ monolysocardiolipin (MLCL).

- MLCL binds OXPHOS proteins with much lower affinity → impaired assembly and function of Complex I.

- ↓ Oxidative phosphorylation, ↑ membrane permeability.

- Consequences: ↓ TCA cycle enzyme activities, abnormal cristae morphology → skeletal muscle weakness, dilated cardiomyopathy.

- Yeast tafazzin mutants show similar biochemical defects.

title: 4. CARDIOLIPIN IN DISEASE
section: 4. CARDIOLIPIN IN DISEASE › Pathogenic mechanism (leading hypothesis)
text: Diagram labels: MLCL + cytochrome c complex; acts as peroxidase; ROS; Oxidizes PUFA in phospholipids; Lipid peroxidation & mitochondrial dysfunction; Energy failure & cellular damage

title: 4. CARDIOLIPIN IN DISEASE
text:
- Mitochondria-targeted anti-peroxidants (in Drosophila model: improved respiration).

- Restore plasmenylcholine (plasmalogen) with linoleate (in vitro model) → improves CL levels.

- Elamipretide (SS-31), a mitochondria-targeted tetrapeptide that binds cardiolipin → clinical trials show improvement in some symptoms.

- Stabilizing mitochondrial calcium uniporter may also be beneficial.

Diagram labels: SS-31 (elamipretide)

title: 4. CARDIOLIPIN IN DISEASE
section: 4. CARDIOLIPIN IN DISEASE › B. OTHER DISEASES AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGICAL CONSEQUENCES
text:
Cardiovascular diseases

- Reduced CL or altered composition linked to heart failure, ischemia–reperfusion injury.

- Excessive peroxidation of CL in ischemic heart & skeleton muscle → oxidative stress.

Diabetes

- Early diabetes: marked decline in myocardial CL.

- Remodelling to DHA-rich species (very oxidizable).

- Enzyme ALCAT1 (acyl-CoA:lysoCL acyltransferase 1) upregulated by oxidative stress → CL remodelling → lipid hydroperoxides → vicious cycle of oxidative stress, CL depletion and mitochondrial dysfunction in age-related diseases.

Neurodegenerative diseases

- Altered CL metabolism in brain mitochondria in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.

- α-Synuclein oligomers bind to CL → disrupt membrane integrity and mitochondrial function.

- Brain-type CLs (PUFA-rich) appear in plasma after cardiac arrest or traumatic brain injury → biomarkers of mitochondrial/tissue injury.

title: 4. CARDIOLIPIN IN DISEASE
section: 4. CARDIOLIPIN IN DISEASE › B. OTHER DISEASES AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGICAL CONSEQUENCES
text:
Autoimmune & inflammatory conditions

- Anti-cardiolipin antibodies in diseases with tissue damage → danger signals.

- Used in diagnosis of unexplained thrombosis or recurrent miscarriages.

- Unsaturated CLs can compete with LPS for TLR4 binding → anti-inflammatory; saturated CLs activate TLR4 → pro-inflammatory.

Infectious diseases

- Treponema pallidum (syphilis) releases host mitochondrial CL → major stimulus for anti-cardiolipin antibodies.

- Cardiolipin isolation in 1942 by M. Pangborn and structure elucidation in 1964 by LeCocq & Ballou were driven by this serologic property.

title: 4. CARDIOLIPIN IN DISEASE
text: Cardiolipin deficiency, oxidation, or abnormal remodelling impairs mitochondrial bioenergetics, increases ROS, and contributes to a wide range of human diseases.

title: 4. CARDIOLIPIN IN DISEASE
section: 4. CARDIOLIPIN IN DISEASE › 5. RELATED LIPIDS (CARDIOLIPIN ANALOGUES)
text: Animals and higher plants contain only cardiolipin (CL). Many bacteria and some Archaea contain cardiolipin analogues.

- Synthesised by analogous enzymes to cardiolipin.

- Participate in membrane organization, bioenergetics, stress response and pathogenesis.

- Structural diversity allows adaptation to different organisms and environments.

title: CARDIOLIPIN (DIPHOSPHATIDYLGLYCEROL)
text: Cardiolipin is a unique phospholipid with a dimeric structure containing four acyl chains, five chiral centres and up to two negative charges. It is essential for the function of mitochondria and certain bacterial membranes.

title: CARDIOLIPIN (DIPHOSPHATIDYLGLYCEROL)
text:
Structure of cardiolipin (tetralinoleoyl species)

Diagram labels: sn-1 (1A); sn-2 (2A); sn-2' (2B); sn-1' (1B)

R = R' = linoleoyl (18:2Δ9,12)

Cardiolipin = 1,3-bis(sn-3'-phosphatidyl)-sn-glycerol (trivial name for diphosphatidylglycerol)

title: CARDIOLIPIN (DIPHOSPHATIDYLGLYCEROL)
text:
- Found almost exclusively in mitochondrial inner membrane of eukaryotes (20% of mitochondrial phospholipids).

- Also in bacterial plasma membranes and hydrogenosomes; in some Archaea (halocarchaea).

- Significant in peroxisomes; occasionally in other organelles and body fluids.

title: CARDIOLIPIN (DIPHOSPHATIDYLGLYCEROL)
text:
- Four acyl chains → potential for great complexity, but compositions are remarkably simple and symmetric.

- Most mammals: ~80% linoleic acid (18:2) in total; 18-carbon fatty acids predominate.

- Relatively resistant to dietary manipulation.

title: CARDIOLIPIN (DIPHOSPHATIDYLGLYCEROL)
section: CARDIOLIPIN (DIPHOSPHATIDYLGLYCEROL) › Fatty acid composition in selected organisms (major features)
text:
- Mammals (general): Mostly 18-carbon; ~80% linoleic acid (18:2).

- Bovine heart: Enriched in α-linolenic acid (18:3 n-3).

- Testis: Mainly palmitic acid (16:0).

- Central nervous system: Many fatty acids: 16:0, 18:0, 18:1, 18:2, 20:4, 22:6 (DHA); >100 molecular species.

- Marine animals: Contain DHA (22:6 n-3) or 24:6; e.g., zebrafish ~45% DHA; some molluscs ~80% DHA.

- Fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster): 16:1 and 18:2 are major fatty acids.

- Higher plants: Linolenic (18:3) and linoleic (18:2) predominate; Arabidopsis leaf/seed ~61/58% 18:3; 35/37% 18:2 (major species with 10–11 double bonds).

- Yeast (S. cerevisiae): Mainly 16:1 and 18:1.

- Fungus (A. fumigatus): Mainly 18:2, 16:0 and 18:1.

- Bacteria (e.g., E. coli, B. drentensis): Saturated and monoenoic (14:0–18:1); some have plasmalogen (alk-1-enyl) forms.

title: CARDIOLIPIN (DIPHOSPHATIDYLGLYCEROL)
section: CARDIOLIPIN (DIPHOSPHATIDYLGLYCEROL) › Fatty acid composition in selected organisms (major features)
text: - Sulfate-reducing bacterium (D. alkenivorans): Contains mono- to tetraether forms with saturated straight or methyl-branched chains.

title: CARDIOLIPIN (DIPHOSPHATIDYLGLYCEROL)
text:
- Stabilizes mitochondrial structure and curvature.

- Essential for oxidative phosphorylation.

- Binds and organizes respiratory supercomplexes.

- Involved in apoptosis signalling.

- Required for mitochondrial dynamics (fusion/fission) and mitophagy.

title: CARDIOLIPIN (DIPHOSPHATIDYLGLYCEROL)
section: CARDIOLIPIN (DIPHOSPHATIDYLGLYCEROL) › 2. BIOSYNTHESIS IN EUKARYOTES (MITOCHONDRIAL INNER MEMBRANE)
text:
Diagram labels: Phosphatidic acid (PA); CDP-diacylglycerol (CDP-DAG); Phosphatidylglycerol phosphate (PGP); CDP-diacylglycerol synthase (CDS2); Phosphatidylglycerol phosphate synthase (PGPS); Cardiolipin synthase (CLS, Tafazzin); Cardiolipin (CL); PPi (→ 2 Pi); Pi

Key notes

- All enzymes are on the inner mitochondrial membrane (matrix side).

- Tafazzin remodels newly made CL to mature, symmetrical species.

- Bacteria use related pathways (PGP → CL via PgsA/Cls).

title: CARDIOLIPIN (DIPHOSPHATIDYLGLYCEROL)
text:
Stabilizes mitochondrial structure

- Forms non-bilayer structure in cristae; promotes membrane curvature and fusion.

Organizes respiratory supercomplexes

- Binds and stabilizes complexes I, III, IV and ATP synthase → efficient electron transport and ATP production.

Required for oxidative phosphorylation

- Essential for proton gradient maintenance and ATP synthesis.

Role in apoptosis

- Peroxidized CL releases cytochrome c → apoptotic signalling.

Mitochondrial quality control

- Important for fusion/fission balance and mitophagy.

title: CARDIOLIPIN (DIPHOSPHATIDYLGLYCEROL)
section: CARDIOLIPIN (DIPHOSPHATIDYLGLYCEROL) › 5. DISEASES ASSOCIATED WITH CARDIOLIPIN DYSFUNCTION
text:
Cardiolipin depletion

- Barth syndrome (tafazzin mutation): reduced CL remodelling → cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, neutropenia.

- Mitochondrial diseases and developmental disorders.

Peroxidized cardiolipin

- Oxidative damage to CL promotes apoptosis and mitochondrial dysfunction.

- Linked to neurodegenerative diseases (e.g., Alzheimer's, Parkinson's), ischemia-reperfusion injury and aging.

Cancer

- Altered CL levels and remodelling enzymes (tafazzin, ALCAT1) implicated in tumour metabolism and therapy resistance.

Other

- Heart failure

- Diabetes

- Liver disease

- Sepsis

title: CARDIOLIPIN (DIPHOSPHATIDYLGLYCEROL)
text:
Remodelling (acyl chain editing)

- Phospholipase A2 removes sn-2 fatty acid → monolysocardiolipin (MLCL).

- Lysocardiolipin acyltransferases (ALCAT1, tafazzin) re-acylate → mature CL.

- Lands' cycle maintains fatty acid composition and symmetry.

Diagram labels: PLA2; Monolysocardiolipin (MLCL); ALCAT1/Tafazzin

Catabolism

- Phospholipase A2/PLD → lysocardiolipin or phosphatidic acid (PA).

- Phospholipase A1 + PLA2 → glycerol + phosphatidic acid.

- Hydrolysis products are recycled or used for signalling.

title: CARDIOLIPIN (DIPHOSPHATIDYLGLYCEROL)
text:
- Cardiolipin is a dimeric phospholipid unique to mitochondria and some bacteria.

- Has a simple, highly conserved fatty acid composition (mostly 18:2).

- Essential for mitochondrial structure, respiratory supercomplex function and bioenergetics.

- Synthesized in mitochondria from PA via CDP-DAG and PGP.

- Continuously remodelled and degraded; its turnover links to signalling and quality control.

- Dysregulation is implicated in many human diseases.

title: CARDIOLIPIN (DIPHOSPHATIDYLGLYCEROL)
text: Cardiolipin is indispensable for mitochondrial energy production and integrity. Its unique structure, tightly controlled metabolism and multifunctional roles make it central to cellular homeostasis and a target in many diseases.

title: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE
section: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE › (untitled panel)
text: Ceramides are bioactive lipid second messengers. Their effects depend on fatty acyl chain length, long-chain base composition, site of generation and duration. Long-chain ceramides are often harmful, while very-long-chain ceramides are frequently relatively benign or protective.

title: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE
section: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE › A. MAJOR SOURCES AND MECHANISMS OF GENERATION
text:
Rapid generation (seconds–minutes)

- Sphingomyelinases (SMases) activated by stress, cytokines, UV, drugs, etc.

- Acid SMase (lysosomes / PM)

- Neutral SMase (PM, Golgi, ER, mito.)

- Alkaline SMase (PM, ER, Golgi)

- Ceramide synthases (de novo) (minutes–hours)

Diagram labels: Plasma membrane / ER / Golgi / Mitochondria; Sphingomyelinase (SMase); Ceramide; De novo synthesis (ER); Salvage / recycling (lysosomes); Complex sphingolipids (SM, GSLs); Degradation (ceramidases)

All stresses can activate ceramide production

- Oxidative stress

- DNA damage

- Cytokines (TNF-α, FasL)

- Chemotherapy drugs

- UV / ionizing radiation

- Growth factor deprivation

- Inflammation

Ceramide levels are controlled by synthesis, degradation and conversion to complex lipids.

title: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE
section: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE › B. MANY CERAMIDES – DISTINCT FUNCTIONS
text:
- Fatty acyl chain length: Typical roles; Medium (≤ C14): Membrane structure; Signalling (context-dependent); Long (C16–C18): Pro-apoptotic; Growth arrest; Metabolic dysfunction; Very-long (≥ C20): Barrier / structural roles; Often protective; Less inflammatory

- Fatty acyl chain length: Examples; Medium (≤ C14): C8, C12, C14; Long (C16–C18): C16 (CerS6), C18; Very-long (≥ C20): C20, C22, C24, C24:1, C26

- Fatty acyl chain length: Disease associations; Medium (≤ C14): Lysosomal storage (Farber); Some neuropathies; Long (C16–C18): Cancer, diabetes, obesity, insulin resistance, atherosclerosis; Very-long (≥ C20): Skin barrier, myelin integrity, neuroprotection

title: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE
section: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE › C. CERAMIDES AS SIGNAL MOLECULES
text:
- Activate / inhibit protein kinases (e.g., PKCζ, JNK, p38 MAPK, PP2A).

- Alter phosphatase activities (PP2A, PP1) – affect glycogen synthesis, insulin signalling.

- Inhibit phospholipase D (PLD) in plasma membrane → ↓ phosphatidic acid signalling.

- Promote cell cycle arrest (G0/G1, G2/M) and senescence.

- Regulate gene expression via transcription factors (e.g., NF-κB, p53, FOXO).

- Modulate inflammation and immune responses.

- Act locally in ceramide-rich membrane microdomains (rafts/platforms).

title: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE
section: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE › D. CERAMIDES AND APOPTOSIS
text:
Extrinsic pathway (plasma membrane)

Death ligands (TNF-α, FasL, TRAIL) bind to receptors → activates acid SMase → ceramide clusters in rafts → receptor aggregation → DISC formation → caspase-8 activation → apoptosis.

Diagram labels: Death ligand; Ceramide-rich domain (raft); DISC; Caspase-8

Intrinsic pathway (mitochondria)

Stress (ER → MAMs → mitochondria) → ↑ acid SMase → ↑ ceramide in mitochondrial outer membrane → mitochondrial permeability → cytochrome c release → Apaf-1 / caspase-9 activation → caspase-3 / -7 → apoptosis.

Other ceramide actions in apoptosis

- Promote Bax translocation and inhibit Bcl-2.

- Induce ER stress and Ca2+ release.

- Facilitate autophagy or necroptosis (context-dependent).

title: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE
section: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE › Diet [illegible]
text:
- High saturated fat and fructose ↑ ceramide synthesis.

- Omega-3 PUFAs can lower ceramide levels.

- Caloric restriction and exercise reduce ceramides.

- Phyto-ceramides (from plants) may support skin barrier.

- Mediterranean-style diet associated with lower ceramides.

title: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE
section: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE › E. HEALTH AND DISEASE ASSOCIATIONS
text:
- Disease / Condition: Cancer; Role of ceramides: ↑ Long-chain ceramides promote tumour suppression; Key points: Induce apoptosis, inhibit proliferation, angiogenesis; many tumours down-regulate ceramide synthesis or up-regulate degradation.

- Disease / Condition: Metabolic diseases (obesity, diabetes, insulin resistance); Role of ceramides: ↑ C16–C18 ceramides impair insulin signalling; Key points: Accumulate in muscle, liver and adipose tissue; ceramide:diacylglycerol ratio correlates with insulin resistance.

- Disease / Condition: Cardiovascular disease; Role of ceramides: Pro-atherogenic effects; Key points: Endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, foam cell formation, plaque instability.

- Disease / Condition: Neurodegenerative diseases; Role of ceramides: Altered ceramide metabolism; Key points: Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, Huntington's: increased ceramides in affected brain regions.

title: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE
section: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE › E. HEALTH AND DISEASE ASSOCIATIONS
text:
- Disease / Condition: Lysosomal storage diseases; Role of ceramides: Ceramide accumulation; Key points: Farber disease (acid ceramidase deficiency); Niemann–Pick disease (SM accumulation). Cer(d18:1/26:0) biomarker in Farber disease.

- Disease / Condition: Skin disorders; Role of ceramides: Altered ceramide levels or composition; Key points: Atopic dermatitis (↓ ceramides); psoriasis; ichthyosis (defects in synthesis / processing).

- Disease / Condition: Infectious diseases; Role of ceramides: Modulate pathogen entry; Key points: Ceramide-rich domains facilitate many viral infections (e.g., JEV, Ebola, Norovirus). High ceramide can inhibit HIV entry.

- Disease / Condition: Autoimmune / inflammatory; Role of ceramides: Regulate immune cell function; Key points: Influence T-cell activation, cytokine production, macrophage polarization.

title: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE
section: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE › E. HEALTH AND DISEASE ASSOCIATIONS
text: - Disease / Condition: Ageing; Role of ceramides: Ceramide accumulation; Key points: Associated with cellular senescence, frailty and chronic diseases.

title: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE
section: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE › F. KEY POINTS
text:
- Ceramides are versatile lipid mediators with a central role in cell signalling and metabolism.

- Different ceramide species have distinct and sometimes opposing functions.

- Generated rapidly by SMases under stress or synthesized de novo.

- Control growth arrest, senescence, apoptosis, inflammation and metabolism.

- High levels of long-chain ceramides are linked to many diseases.

- Very-long-chain ceramides usually support structural and protective functions.

- Their levels are tightly regulated by enzymes of synthesis, interconversion and degradation.

- Targeting ceramide pathways offers therapeutic potential in cancer, metabolic and inflammatory diseases.

- Lifestyle and diet can influence ceramide metabolism and disease risk.

title: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE
section: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE › G. CERAMIDE COMPOSITION IN HEALTH AND DISEASE (examples)
text:
Typical ceramide composition (mol%)

- Tissue / Cell type: Brain (grey matter); C16:0: 20; C18:0: 30; C18:1: 25; C24:0: 10; C24:1: 5; ≥ C26: 10

- Tissue / Cell type: Skin (epidermis); C16:0: 5; C18:0: 10; C18:1: 15; C24:0: 25; C24:1: 20; ≥ C26: 25

- Tissue / Cell type: Liver; C16:0: 30; C18:0: 20; C18:1: 25; C24:0: 10; C24:1: 5; ≥ C26: 10

- Tissue / Cell type: Plasma; C16:0: 45; C18:0: 25; C18:1: 15; C24:0: 5; C24:1: 5; ≥ C26: 5

- Tissue / Cell type: Diabetic muscle; C16:0: 40; C18:0: 25; C18:1: 15; C24:0: 5; C24:1: 5; ≥ C26: 10

Disease-associated changes (examples)

- Condition: Obesity / T2D; Change in ceramide profile: ↑ C16:0, ↑ C18:0 in muscle, liver; Implication: Insulin resistance

- Condition: NAFLD (fatty liver); Change in ceramide profile: ↑ C16:0, C18:0, C18:1; Implication: Inflammation, fibrosis

title: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE
section: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE › G. CERAMIDE COMPOSITION IN HEALTH AND DISEASE (examples)
text:
- Condition: Alzheimer's disease; Change in ceramide profile: ↑ Very-long-chain (C24, C24:1); Implication: Synaptic dysfunction

- Condition: Atopic dermatitis; Change in ceramide profile: ↓ Ceramides (especially EOS); Implication: Impaired skin barrier

- Condition: Psoriasis; Change in ceramide profile: Altered CER ratios; Implication: Hyperproliferation

- Condition: Farber disease; Change in ceramide profile: ↑ C26:0-ceramide; Implication: Lysosomal pathology

Values are approximate and vary with species, diet, age and analytical method. Most sphingoid bases are d18:1; phytosphingosine predominates in plants.

title: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE
section: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE › Abbreviations
text: ASM: acid sphingomyelinase nSMase: neutral sphingomyelinase aSMase: alkaline sphingomyelinase CerS: ceramide synthase MAMs: mitochondria-associated membranes ER: endoplasmic reticulum GSLs: glycosphingolipids S1P: sphingosine-1-phosphate C1P: ceramide-1-phosphate PLD: phospholipase D DISC: death-inducing signaling complex ELOVL: fatty acid elongase

title: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE
section: 4. CERAMIDES IN HEALTH AND DISEASE › Key takeaway
text: The balance between ceramide synthesis, interconversion and degradation is essential for cellular homeostasis. Dysregulation contributes to a wide spectrum of human diseases, but also offers opportunities for intervention.

title: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
text: Ceramides are hydrolysed by ceramidases to sphingoid bases and free fatty acids. This is the only route to unesterified sphingosine. Sphingoid bases can be re-used for ceramide resynthesis (salvage pathway) or converted to other signalling lipids.

title: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › A. Ceramide hydrolysis and resynthesis (salvage pathway)
text:
Diagram labels: Ceramide; CERAMIDASES (hydrolysis); CERAMIDE SYNTHASES (resynthesis); Sphingoid base (sphingosine, etc.); Free fatty acid; Fatty acyl-CoA; Other fates of sphingoid bases

Other fates of sphingoid bases

- Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P)

- Ceramide-1-phosphate (C1P)

- Sphingoid base phosphates (e.g., SphK2)

- N-Acylation (recycling)

- Export from lysosome to cytosol

title: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › B. Ceramidases in humans
text:
- Enzyme (Other name): Acid ceramidase (ASAH1); pH optimum: ~4.5; Cellular location: Lysosomes; Preferred acyl chain length (substrate preference): C6 – C18 (short to medium); Notes / Functions: Key in lysosomal ceramide degradation. Deficiency → Farber disease (↑ ceramide). Regulates epidermal ceramide levels/composition.

- Enzyme (Other name): Neutral ceramidase (ASAH2); pH optimum: ~7; Cellular location: Plasma membrane, Golgi, (Intestinal epithelial cells, colon); Preferred acyl chain length (substrate preference): C16 – C18 (long chain); Notes / Functions: Can work in reverse (synthesis) e.g., in mitochondria. Dietary ceramides (lumen) hydrolysed here. May contribute to ceramide synthesis in mitochondria.

title: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › B. Ceramidases in humans
text:
- Enzyme (Other name): Alkaline ceramidase 1 (ACER1); pH optimum: ~9; Cellular location: Endoplasmic reticulum (also plasma mem./ mitochondria); Preferred acyl chain length (substrate preference): Very-long chain (C20 – C26+); Notes / Functions: Highly expressed in skin. Prefers very-long-chain acyl ceramides.

- Enzyme (Other name): Alkaline ceramidase 2 (ACER2); pH optimum: ~9; Cellular location: Golgi apparatus (also mitochondria); Preferred acyl chain length (substrate preference): Very-long chain (C20 – C26+); Notes / Functions: Found in placenta, pancreas, heart. Prefers very-long-chain acyl ceramides.

title: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › B. Ceramidases in humans
text:
- Enzyme (Other name): Alkaline ceramidase 3 (ACER3); pH optimum: ~9; Cellular location: ER and Golgi (widespread; also nucleus); Preferred acyl chain length (substrate preference): Unsaturated long chain (18:1, 20:1, 20:4) (also dihydroceramides); Notes / Functions: Broad tissue distribution (esp, placenta). Acts on unsaturated ceramides, dihydroceramides, phytoceramides.

Sphingoid bases released from lysosomes can be exported to the cytosol and re-acylated by ceramide synthases. The salvage pathway is estimated to contribute 50-90% of sphingolipid biosynthesis.

title: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › C. Plants and lower organisms
text:
- Arabidopsis has alkaline ceramidase (AtACER) and several neutral ceramidases (AtNCERs).

- No equivalent acid ceramidase identified in plants.

- Rice enzyme prefers d18:1Δ4-ceramide; can operate in reverse to increase C26, C28 phytoceramides.

- Ceramidases occur in Pseudomonas aeruginosa and slime moulds (secreted proteins).

- Most prokaryotes have a neutral ceramidase only, including some pathogenic bacteria.

title: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › KEY POINTS (SUMMARY)
text:
- Ceramidases are the only enzymes that release free sphingoid bases from ceramides.

- Five human ceramidases differ in pH optimum, location, and acyl-chain preference.

- Salvage pathway recycles sphingoid bases and supplies the majority of sphingolipid synthesis.

- Ceramides have unique physical properties that shape membranes and enable signalling.

- Dysregulation of ceramide metabolism contributes to many human diseases.

title: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › Clinical relevance examples
text:
- Farber disease: acid ceramidase deficiency → ceramide storage (↑ C26:0).

- Metabolic syndrome, diabetes, cancer: altered ceramide species and levels.

- Skin barrier defects: abnormal ceramide composition (e.g., in atopic dermatitis).

- Neurodegeneration: ceramide accumulation and imbalanced signalling.

title: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
text: ASM: acid sphingomyelinase CerS: ceramide synthase SPT: serine palmitoyltransferase ER: endoplasmic reticulum SM: sphingomyelinase S1P: sphingosine-1-phosphate C1P: ceramide-1-phosphate LPA: lysophosphatidic acid GCS: glucosylceramide synthase GC: glucocerebrosidase

title: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › A. Molecular shape and membrane effects
text:
- Cone-shaped (small head group + bulky tails).

- Short-chain ceramides → positive curvature; long-chain ceramides → negative curvature.

- Favour non-bilayer (inverted hexagonal) phases and membrane fusion/invagination.

- Increase acyl chain order in bilayers.

- Affect ion channels → increase membrane permeability to solutes (small to protein size).

- Required for formation and secretion of exosomes.

Diagram labels: Cone shape; Negative curvature; Small hydrated head group; Hydrophobic tails; Inverted hexagonal (HII) phase

title: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › B. Ceramide-rich domains ("ceramide platforms")
text:
Diagram labels: Extracellular; Cytosol; Ceramide; Cholesterol; Sphingomyelin; Other lipids

- Ceramides concentrate in lateral liquid-ordered microdomains (ceramide platforms/rafts).

- Can displace cholesterol (C12–C18 ceramides).

- Generated by acid sphingomyelinase in rafts.

- Promote raft coalescence and clustering of receptors and signalling proteins.

- Amplify receptor- and stress-mediated signalling.

title: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › C. Signalling and physiological roles
text:
- Ceramide-rich domains recruit receptors (e.g., death receptors, cytokine receptors) and signalling complexes.

- Facilitate oligomerization of death receptors → apoptosis.

- In endothelial cells: peptide (CGSPGWVRC) binds C16-ceramide → activates ASM without apoptotic signalling.

- Sites for endocytic uptake of pathogens (concentrates receptors); enhances infection by Norovirus, JEV, Ebola, SARS-CoV-2, etc.

- Elevated ceramide inhibits HIV entry.

- Ceramide-rich domains initiate and amplify primary signals while excluding inhibitory signals.

Diagram labels: Signal amplification

title: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › D. Comparison with other lipids
text:
- Similar in structure to diacylglycerols but different in location and behaviour.

- Cross synthetic bilayers relatively quickly in vitro.

- Flip-flop in complex membranes in vivo may be restricted within ceramide-rich domains → opposite leaflets may have different ceramide pools and functions.

title: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › E. Factors influencing ceramide behaviour
text:
- Sphingoid base unsaturation → stronger intramolecular H-bonding → tight packing.

- Fatty acyl chain length → curvature, membrane order, phase behaviour.

- Chain composition → microdomain preference and protein interactions.

Diagram labels: Intramolecular hydrogen bonding stabilizes ceramide packing

title: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › A. Catabolism
text:
- Ceramidases hydrolyse ceramide → sphingoid base + fatty acid.

- Acid ceramidase active in lysosomes (C6–C18).

- Neutral/alkaline ceramidases act at plasma membrane, Golgi, ER, mitochondria, nucleus (tissue- and substrate-specific).

- Lipases and sphingomyelinases provide ceramide precursors.

- Catabolism regulated by pH, cofactors, localization, and protein partners.

title: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 2. CERAMIDE HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › B. Biological significance
text:
- Balance of ceramide synthesis (de novo vs salvage) and hydrolysis controls cellular ceramide levels.

- Regulates apoptosis, proliferation, inflammation, stress responses, and lysosomal function.

- Aberrant ceramidase activity or ceramide accumulation linked to cancer, metabolic diseases, neurodegeneration, lysosomal storage disorders, and skin diseases.

title: CERAMIDES
text: Ceramides are central sphingolipid intermediates and potent lipid mediators that regulate a wide range of biological processes in eukaryotic cells.

title: CERAMIDES
text:
Diagram labels: Sphingoid base (long-chain base); Fatty acyl chain

n = usually 12–20 (often 18) m = usually 14–24 (often 16–24)

Key features

- Amide-linked long-chain (sphingoid) base and fatty acid.

- >200 molecular species exist in mammalian cells.

- Free ceramides are present in small amounts but are important mediators.

- Precursors of all complex sphingolipids and of sphingosine-1-phosphate and ceramide-1-phosphate.

title: CERAMIDES
text:
Lipid mediators

- Regulate apoptosis, cell cycle arrest, differentiation, senescence, stress responses and inflammation.

Membrane structure

- Promote membrane rigidity, lipid raft formation and membrane domain organization.

Metabolic regulators

- Modulate insulin signalling, calcium homeostasis, autophagy and mitochondrial function.

Precursors of signalling lipids

- Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) promotes survival and proliferation.

- Ceramide-1-phosphate (C1P) is involved in cell growth and stress responses.

Skin barrier lipids

- Ceramides are major components of the stratum corneum; essential for epidermal barrier and water retention.

Disease relevance

- Dysregulation is linked to cancer, metabolic disorders, neurodegeneration, inflammatory and skin diseases.

title: CERAMIDES
section: CERAMIDES › THE CENTRAL ROLE OF CERAMIDE IN SPHINGOLIPID METABOLISM
text:
Diagram labels: Sphingolipid biosynthesis; Complex sphingolipids (sphingomyelin, glycosphingolipids, gangliosides); De novo synthesis (in ER); CERAMIDE; Polar head group removal (lysosomes) recycling; Ceramide breakdown (catabolism); Sphingoid bases (sphingosine, etc.)

Ceramide is at the hub of the ceramide (sphingomyelin) cycle.

title: CERAMIDES
section: CERAMIDES › TYPICAL FATTY ACID COMPOSITION (wt%) OF CERAMIDES from different tissues and cell types

title: CERAMIDES
text:

- Neurodegenerative diseases (e.g., Alzheimer's, Parkinson's).

- Metabolic disorders – insulin resistance, obesity, diabetes.

title: CERAMIDES
text: Ceramides are bioactive sphingolipids at the crossroads of metabolism and signalling. Their diverse molecular species, tissue-specific roles and tightly regulated metabolism underlie essential physiological functions and link their dysregulation to many human diseases.

title: CERAMIDES
text: New lipidomics tools are revealing the complexity of ceramide species and compartmentalization, opening avenues for targeted therapies that modulate ceramide pathways.

title: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES
text:
Ceramides in which the 1-O-acyl group is linked to the ε-amino group of lysine. Structural analogues of lysyl-diacylglycerols of Mycobacteria. Identified in anaerobic marine bacteria from the Black Sea.

title: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES
text:
Diagram labels: Stratum corneum (lipid lamellae + corneocytes); Granular layer; Spinous layer; Basal layer; Dermis (collagen, immune cells, blood vessels); Subcutaneous fat (thermogenic depots)

- Ceramides (up to ~50% of total lipids) with cholesterol and free fatty acids (~1:1) are the major lipids of the stratum corneum interstices.

- Lipids are arranged in two lamellar phases (crystalline) with repeat distances of ~6 nm (short) and ~13 nm (long), plus small liquid sub-domains.

- Essential for barrier function: prevent water loss and entry of harmful agents.

- Adipose tissue supplies fatty acids; sebum (waxes, squalene) forms a protective film; antimicrobial peptides/proteins add defence.

title: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES
text:
- 17 classes of free ceramides and 3 classes of protein-bound ceramides with up to ~1600 molecular species.

- Sphingoid bases: C16–C26 (C18 most abundant) with layer-specific distributions.

- Numerous glucosylceramides based on the same ceramide structures are also essential.

- Non-branched long chains and small head groups → tight packing → low permeability, high barrier efficiency.

title: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES
text:
- Distinct structures not seen in other tissues.

- Include ω-O-acyl and 1-O-acylceramides (~5% of total ceramides; up to 700 molecular species in humans/mice).

- Form highly ordered lamellae essential for the epidermal barrier.

title: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES
text:
- Prevent transepidermal water loss and block penetration of xenobiotics, allergens and pathogens.

- Maintain skin hydration, elasticity and mechanical strength.

- Defects → dry skin, atopic dermatitis, ichthyosis.

title: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES
text:
- Ceramides are produced rapidly and transiently in response to many stimuli.

- Sources: de novo synthesis, sphingomyelinase pathways, cytoplasmic droplets.

- Promote growth suppression, senescence, cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, migration/adhesion and tumour suppression.

- "Many Ceramides" hypothesis: distinct ceramides in distinct compartments → distinct functions.

title: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES
section: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES › A. Major sources and mechanisms of generation
text:
Sphingomyelinase pathways (rapid: seconds–minutes)

- Acid SMase (lysosomes/PM)

- Neutral SMase (PM, Golgi, ER, mitochondria)

- Alkaline SMase (PM, Golgi)

CELLULAR STRESS

- Oxidative stress

- DNA damage

- Cytokines (TNF-α, FasL)

- Chemotherapy drugs

- UV / ionizing radiation

- Growth factor deprivation

- Inflammation

De novo synthesis pathway (minutes–hours)

- Ceramide synthases (CerS1–6)

- Endoplasmic reticulum

Diagram labels: CERAMIDE

title: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES
section: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES › B. Enzyme activation / deactivation and signalling
text:
- Ceramides activate or inhibit many enzymes: PKCζ, JNK, p38 MAPK, PP2A, etc.

- Inhibit phospholipase D → ↓ phosphatidic acid → alters signalling.

- Alter protein phosphatases (PP2A, PP1) → affect glycogen synthesis, apoptosis.

- Regulate gene expression (NF-κB, p53, FOXO), cell cycle arrest (G0/G1, G2/M), senescence.

- Modulate inflammation, immune responses and membrane microdomains (rafts).

title: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES
text:
Extrinsic pathway (plasma membrane)

Death ligands (TNF-α, FasL, TRAIL) → bind to death receptors → activates acid SMase → ceramide-rich microdomains (rafts) → receptor clustering → DISC formation → caspase-8 activation → apoptosis

Intrinsic pathway (mitochondria)

Stress (ER → MAMs) → mitochondria → activates acid SMase → ↑ mitochondrial ceramide → outer membrane permeabilization → cytochrome c release → Apaf-1 / caspase-9 activation → caspase-3 / -7 activation → apoptosis

Diagram labels: Ceramide-rich platforms (rafts); DISC

Other ceramide actions

- Promote Bax translocation and inhibit Bcl-2.

- Induce ER stress and Ca2+ release.

- Facilitate autophagy or necroptosis (context-dependent).

title: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES
section: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES › D. Ceramide species and function (chain-length dependent)
text:
- Fatty acyl chain length: Medium (≤ C14); Typical roles: Membrane structure; Signalling (context-dependent); Examples: C8, C12, C14; Disease associations: Lysosomal storage (Farber); some neuropathies

- Fatty acyl chain length: Long (C16–C18); Typical roles: Pro-apoptotic; Growth arrest; Metabolic dysfunction; Examples: C16 (CerS6), C18; Disease associations: Cancer, diabetes, obesity, insulin resistance, atherosclerosis

- Fatty acyl chain length: Very-long (≥ C20); Typical roles: Barrier / structural; Other protective; Less inflammatory; Examples: C20, C22, C24, C26+; Disease associations: Skin barrier, myelin integrity, neuro-protection

title: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES
text:
- Disease / Condition: Cancer; Role of ceramides: ↑ Long-chain ceramides; Key points: Induce apoptosis, inhibit proliferation; tumour suppressor

- Disease / Condition: Metabolic diseases (obesity, diabetes, insulin resistance); Role of ceramides: ↑ C16–C18 ceramides; Key points: Accumulate in muscle, liver and adipose tissue; correlate with insulin resistance

- Disease / Condition: Cardiovascular disease; Role of ceramides: Pro-atherogenic; Key points: Endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, foam cell formation, plaque instability

- Disease / Condition: Neurodegenerative diseases; Role of ceramides: Altered ceramide metabolism; Key points: Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, Huntington's; ceramide accumulation in neurons

title: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES
text:
- Disease / Condition: Lysosomal storage diseases; Role of ceramides: Ceramide accumulation; Key points: Farber (acid ceramidase deficiency); Niemann–Pick (ASM deficiency); [illegible] biomarker in Farber

- Disease / Condition: Skin disorders; Role of ceramides: Altered levels or composition; Key points: Atopic dermatitis ↓ ceramides; psoriasis, ichthyosis (synthetic/processing defects)

- Disease / Condition: Infectious diseases; Role of ceramides: Modulate pathogen entry; Key points: Ceramide-rich domains facilitate many viral infections; high ceramide can inhibit HIV entry

title: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES
text: - Disease / Condition: Aging; Role of ceramides: Ceramide accumulation; Key points: Associated with cellular senescence, frailty and chronic disease

title: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES
section: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES › G. Role of very-long-chain vs long-chain ceramides
text:
- Long-chain ceramides (C16–C18): often harmful in excess (apoptosis, insulin resistance, inflammation).

- Very-long-chain ceramides (≥ C24): usually support structural functions, barrier integrity, neuroprotection and are less inflammatory.

title: 5. 1-O-ACYLCERAMIDES
text:
- Levels controlled by: enzymes of synthesis, interconversion (SMases, ceramidases, CerS) and degradation.

- Targeting ceramide pathways shows promise in cancer, metabolic and inflammatory diseases.

- Lifestyle and diet can modulate ceramide metabolism and disease risk.

title: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS
text: Many sterols other than cholesterol occur in small amounts in tissues, most of which are intermediates in the biosynthetic pathway from lanosterol, and some have distinct functions of their own. Lanosterol, the first sterol intermediate in cholesterol biosynthesis, is found in wool wax (still the main commercial source) and at low levels in animal tissues (~0.1% of the cholesterol concentration). Its biosynthesis requires oxygen, hence its absence from prokaryotes, and its appearance is thought to have been a key event in the evolution of eukaryotes. Evolutionary 'streamlining' from lanosterol to cholesterol removes protruding methyl groups to improve interaction with phospholipids in membranes.

section: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS › STRUCTURES AND ORIGINS OF IMPORTANT ANIMAL STEROLS

All sterols shown have 3β-hydroxyl group (HO) on C-3.
