title: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS
text:
Source: wool wax (free and esterified); ~0.1% of cholesterol in tissues.

Role: first sterol in biosynthesis of cholesterol and other sterols.

title: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS
text:
Last intermediate in Bloch pathway (Δ24-sterol).

Functions:

- Involved in myelination (abundant in brains of young animals).

- Present in testes and spermatozoa; essential for reproduction.

- Stimulates genes for lipid biosynthetic enzymes via LXR; anti-inflammatory.

- Desmosterolosis: genetic block in conversion to cholesterol → severe neurodevelopmental defects.

title: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS
text:
Intermediate after demethylation (7-dehydro-lanosterol → lathosterol).

Significance:

- Serum level inversely related to size of bile acid pool.

- Strongly correlates with cholesterol balance under dietary conditions.

- Biomarker of endogenous cholesterol synthesis.

title: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS
text:
Final precursor in Kandutsch-Russell pathway to cholesterol.

Functions:

- In skin, UV light converts to vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol).

- Precursor of 'spiral steroids' that regulate Na+/K+-ATPases.

- Protects plasma & mitochondrial membranes from phospholipid autoxidation.

- In insects, converted back from cholesterol in pathway to ecdysone hormones.

title: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS
text:
Major sterol in animal tissues.

Functions:

- Structural component of cell membranes.

- Precursor of steroid hormones, bile acids, vitamin D3 and oxysterols.

- Essential for development, signalling, transport, nerve function and gene regulation.

title: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS
text: Fully saturated sterol. Present in ruminant brain and adrenal glands. May influence membrane fluidity and steroid metabolism.

title: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS
text: Oxysterol formed in cells by CYP46A1 (mainly in brain). During cholesterol turnover. Involved in cholesterol transport across BBB and signalling.

title: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS
text: Formed in many tissues. Regulates cholesterol homeostasis and gene expression via LXR. Can be converted to bile acids.

title: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS
section: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS › TESTIS MEIOSIS-ACTIVATING STEROL (TMAS)
text: Related sterol present in testes and spermatozoa. Essential for meiosis and fertility in mammals.

title: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS
text: Produced in liver and brain. Regulates cholesterol synthesis and inflammatory responses. Precursor of bile acids.

title: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS
section: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS › MARINE INVERTEBRATES: NOVEL STEROLS
text:
- Many marine invertebrates contain unusual sterols with novel ring structures and/or side chains.

- At least 80 distinct sterols have been isolated from echinoderms and ~100 from sponges.

- Some are derived from cholesterol; others from plant sterols or alternative biosynthetic intermediates.

title: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS
text:
- Cholesterol can be oxidized in tissues or foods to form oxysterols with hydroperoxy, epoxy, hydroxy or keto groups.

- Enter body via diet or are formed in tissues by microsomal/mitochondrial oxidations.

- Associated with inhibition of cholesterol and bile acid synthesis and other abnormalities in lipid metabolism.

- Some oxysterols (e.g., 7-ketocholesterol, 25-hydroxycholesterol) have signalling roles; excessive levels may be toxic.

- Oxysterols in membranes, especially with conjugated diene systems (e.g., 7-dehydrocholesterol), may contribute to ferroptosis.

title: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS
section: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS › HYDROLYSIS OF CHOLESTEROL ESTERS
text:
- Cholesterol ester hydrolases (CEHs) liberate cholesterol and fatty acids on demand.

- Provide cholesterol for membrane turnover, lipoprotein remodeling and steroid hormone synthesis (e.g., adrenal cortex).

- Major CEHs in mammals:

- Neutral cholesterol ester hydrolase (nCEH) – macrophages, liver; important in preventing foam cell formation.

- Lysosomal acid lipase (LAL) – lysosomes.

- Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) – adrenal, adipose tissue.

- Hepatic cytosolic CE hydrolase (HCEH).

- Carboxyl ester hydrolase (CEH).

title: 7. OTHER ANIMAL STEROLS
text: Other animal sterols are present in small amounts but have important roles in development, reproduction, cholesterol regulation and signalling. Some (e.g., desmosterol, 7-dehydrocholesterol) are biosynthetic intermediates with distinct functions. Oxidized sterols and their esters are biologically active and implicated in disease.

title: 3. CHOLESTEROL BIOSYNTHESIS
text: At least ~30 enzymatic reactions are required for cholesterol biosynthesis (Bloch & Lynen, Nobel Prize, 1964). The pathway described below is the classical mevalonate (MVA) pathway. Synthesis occurs mainly in liver, but also in brain, nervous system, skin and all nucleated cells. First, acetyl-CoA is converted to mevalonic acid in the cytosol. Subsequent reactions occur on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). reductase is a key regulatory, rate-limiting enzyme and the target of statin drugs.

text: Diagram labels: Lanosterol; ~19 reactions; Demethylations; Desaturations; Isomerizations; Reductions; Zymosterol; TWO LATE PATHWAYS TO CHOLESTEROL; Bloch pathway (major in most tissues); Kandutsch-Russell pathway (major in brain); 3 steps; Desmosterol (Δ24-sterol); Cholesterol (cholest-5-en-3β-ol); 7-Dehydrocholesterol (Δ7-sterol)

title: 3. CHOLESTEROL BIOSYNTHESIS
text:
- Lanosterol is converted to cholesterol in ~19 enzymatic steps.

- Bloch pathway uses desmosterol (Δ24-sterol) as immediate precursor.

- Kandutsch-Russell pathway uses 7-dehydrocholesterol (Δ7-sterol).

- Brain uses Kandutsch-Russell pathway predominantly.

title: 3. CHOLESTEROL BIOSYNTHESIS
text: Overall: acetyl-CoA → MVA → IPP/DMAPP → FPP → squalene → lanosterol → cholesterol

title: 3. CHOLESTEROL BIOSYNTHESIS
section: 3. CHOLESTEROL BIOSYNTHESIS › REGULATION OF THE PATHWAY
text:
- HMG-CoA reductase is the major control point.

- Regulated by: SREBP transcription factors, feedback by sterols, insulin, glucagon, AMPK.

- Statins (e.g., atorvastatin, simvastatin) competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase.

- Squalene monooxygenase is another control point.

- Cholesterol regulates its own synthesis and cellular uptake via SREBP and SCAP.

title: 3. CHOLESTEROL BIOSYNTHESIS
text: To synthesise 1 molecule of cholesterol: 18 ATP (direct), 16 NADPH, 11 O2. acetyl-CoA → ~100 ATP equivalents.

title: 3. CHOLESTEROL BIOSYNTHESIS
text:
- Cholesterol is exported from liver in VLDL → LDL.

- Peripheral tissues obtain cholesterol from LDL receptors or by synthesis de novo.

- Dietary cholesterol (eggs, red meat) is absorbed in intestines and enters circulation.

title: 3. CHOLESTEROL BIOSYNTHESIS
text:
Under hypoxia or UV stress (skin, gonads) some cholesterol is made via the MEP pathway (2C-methyl-D-erythritol 4-phosphate) with cycloartenol as intermediate.

- Major pathway for sterols in plants.

- Only a few bacteria can synthesise cholesterol de novo.

title: 3. CHOLESTEROL BIOSYNTHESIS
section: 3. CHOLESTEROL BIOSYNTHESIS › SUMMARY OF KEY POINTS
text:
- Cholesterol is synthesised in all nucleated cells.

- MVA pathway converts acetyl-CoA → MVA → isoprenes → squalene → lanosterol → cholesterol.

- Two major late pathways: Bloch and Kandutsch-Russell.

- Highly regulated to maintain cholesterol homeostasis.

title: 6. CHOLESTEROL ESTERS
text: Cholesterol esters (CEs) with long-chain fatty acids esterified to the 3β-hydroxyl group are hydrophobic and biologically inert. They are ideal for transport in plasma lipoproteins and for intracellular storage in lipid droplets to buffer excess free cholesterol. CEs do not contribute to membrane structure, but can accumulate in atherosclerotic plaques and steroidogenic tissues such as the adrenal glands.

title: 6. CHOLESTEROL ESTERS
section: 6. CHOLESTEROL ESTERS › Biosynthesis of cholesterol esters
text:
In most tissues, ACAT (sterol O-acyltransferase) esterifies cholesterol with fatty acyl-CoA. Two isoforms exist in the ER membrane.

title: 6. CHOLESTEROL ESTERS
text:
- Isoform: ACAT1; Tissue distribution: Most tissues, especially macrophages, adrenal & sebaceous glands; Main function: Stores CEs in cytosolic lipid droplets; important in foam cells & cancer.

- Isoform: ACAT2; Tissue distribution: Liver and small intestine; Main function: Supplies CEs for nascent lipoproteins (VLDL, chylomicrons).

title: 6. CHOLESTEROL ESTERS
text:
- ACATs are ER membrane proteins with multiple transmembrane domains and a catalytic histidine.

- Prefer saturated and monoenoic fatty acyl-CoAs as substrates.

- Members of the MBOAT (O-acyltransferase) superfamily.

title: 6. CHOLESTEROL ESTERS

section: 6. CHOLESTEROL ESTERS › Esterification of cholesterol in plasma by LCAT (on HDL)

In plasma, LCAT transfers the fatty acid at sn-2 of phosphatidylcholine (PC) to cholesterol.

title: 6. CHOLESTEROL ESTERS
text:
- LCAT is a 49 kDa glycoprotein (≈60 kDa with glycans); made in liver; circulates bound to HDL.

- ApoA-I concentrates substrate and opens "lid" on LCAT to expose active site.

- Prefers C18 fatty acids (18:1, 18:2) in plasma PC.

- CE accumulation in HDL core → particle matures (discoidal → spherical).

- CEs are transferred to LDL and VLDL by CETP.

- Drives reverse cholesterol transport to liver.

title: 6. CHOLESTEROL ESTERS
text:
- Promotes efflux of cholesterol from cell membranes and macrophages.

- Essential for cholesterol homeostasis; deficiency → low HDL, corneal opacity, accelerated atherosclerosis.

- Target for therapeutic intervention.

- Bind CD14 (not CD36) → activates TLR4.

- Stimulate macrophages to release inflammatory cytokines.

- Hydrolysis releases oxidized fatty acids → incorporated into phospholipids → further bioactive lipids.

- Contribute to inflammation and atherogenesis.

title: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS
text: Cholesterol cannot be catabolized for energy. Its levels are maintained by a dynamic equilibrium of synthesis, uptake, efflux and conversion. Cholesterol in the plasma membrane (PM) regulates gene expression and enzyme activity in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to ensure an adequate but not excessive supply.

title: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS
section: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS › 4.1 CHOLESTEROL POOLS IN THE PLASMA MEMBRANE
text:
Diagram labels: Extracellular; Cytosol; 1. Accessible (active) pool; 2. Sphingomyelin-sequestered pool; 3. Structural (residual) pool

1. Accessible (active) pool: Readily available to receptors and transport proteins; moves to ER or to nascent HDL. ~16 mol% of PM lipids

2. Sphingomyelin-sequestered pool: Bound by sphingomyelin in lipid rafts; released by sphingomyelinase when needed. ~15 mol% of PM lipids

3. Structural (residual) pool: Essential for membrane integrity and barrier function; not mobilized under normal conditions. ~12 mol% of PM lipids

When cellular cholesterol is in excess

- ↑ Accessible cholesterol (after LDL uptake, diet, etc.)

- Some cholesterol → nascent HDL

- Most cholesterol → returned to ER

- Inhibits cholesterol biosynthesis and LDL receptor expression

- Cholesterol homeostasis is restored

title: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS
section: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS › 4.1 CHOLESTEROL POOLS IN THE PLASMA MEMBRANE
text:
Transport to ER via vesicular and non-vesicular pathways using carriers (e.g., ABC transporters, Aster proteins A, B, C).

Values are approximate for cholesterol-replete cells. Pools are dynamic, not fixed compartments.

title: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS
section: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS › 4.2 SREBP–SCAP REGULATORY PATHWAY
text:
LOW CHOLESTEROL IN ER

1. SCAP senses low cholesterol (binds glutamine).

2. SCAP–SREBP-2 complex moves to Golgi.

3. Sequential cleavage by Site-1 and Site-2 proteases.

4. N-terminal fragment (NTF) translocates to nucleus.

5. Activates genes: LDL receptor; HMG-CoA reductase; Other cholesterol biosynthetic genes ↑ Cholesterol uptake and synthesis

HIGH CHOLESTEROL IN ER

1. ER cholesterol binds SCAP.

2. SCAP–SREBP-2 is retained in ER.

3. No cleavage; SREBP-2 cannot enter nucleus.

4. Transcription of target genes is repressed. ↓ Cholesterol synthesis and ↓ LDL receptor expression

Diagram labels: SCAP; SREBP-2 (precursor); ER; Golgi; NTF; Feedback inhibition

title: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS
section: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS › 4.3 CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS: OVERVIEW
text:
- Synthesis occurs in ER; uptake via LDL receptor in PM.

- Plasma membrane cholesterol regulates SREBP pathway.

- Feedback control prevents both deficiency and excess.

- Multiple layers of regulation act on genes, proteins and enzymes.

- Cholesterol is also esterified (ACAT) and exported (ABCA1).

title: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS
section: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS › KEY REGULATORY PLAYERS
text:
SCAP (SREBP cleavage-activating protein) Cholesterol sensor in ER; escorts SREBP to Golgi when cholesterol is low.

SREBP-2 (sterol regulatory element-binding protein-2) Master transcription factor for cholesterol homeostasis.

Insig (insulin-induced gene 1 protein) Binds SCAP–HMGCR complex when cholesterol is high; retains in ER and targets HMGCR for degradation.

LXR (liver X receptor) Nuclear receptor activated by oxysterols; promotes cholesterol efflux and modulates SREBP transcription.

title: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS
section: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS › TRANSPORT AND EFFLUX
text:
LDL receptor (LDLR): mediates uptake of LDL-cholesterol.

HDL / ABCA1: mediates cholesterol efflux to HDL.

ABC transporters (e.g., ABCG1, ABCG5/G8): export cholesterol and sterols to HDL or bile.

Aster proteins (A, B, C): non-vesicular transport of cholesterol from PM to ER contact sites.

title: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS
section: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS › CONSEQUENCES OF DYSREGULATION
text:
Excess cholesterol

- Hypercholesterolemia

- Atherosclerosis

- Fatty liver disease

- Gallstones

- Some cancers

Low cholesterol

- Impaired membrane structure

- Defective steroid hormone and bile acid synthesis

- Neurological disorders

- Developmental defects

title: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS
section: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS › 4.4 POST-TRANSLATIONAL REGULATION OF BIOSYNTHETIC ENZYMES
text:
HMG-CoA REDUCTASE

Regulation

- Binding of sterols triggers Insig binding.

- Insig holds SCAP–HMGCR complex in ER.

- HMGCR ubiquitinated and degraded by proteasome.

- Also regulated by phosphorylation (AMPK ↑ activity; insulin ↑ activity).

Diagram labels: NH2; COOH; HMG-CoA; NADPH; Mevalonate

Rate-limiting step (statin target)

SQUALENE MONOOXYGENASE (SQM)

Regulation

- Cholesterol binds to SQM.

- 12-aa hydrophobic degron is exposed.

- Ubiquitinated and degraded by proteasome.

Diagram labels: NH2; COOH; Squalene; O2, NADPH; Squalene 2,3-epoxide

Rate-limiting step in committed pathway

OTHER BIOSYNTHETIC ENZYMES

- Many enzymes are rapidly turned over.

- Regulated by sterol intermediates: lanosterol, 24,25-dehydrolanosterol (dimethyl-sterols).

- Cholesterol sulfate and side-chain oxysterols accelerate degradation.

title: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS
section: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS › 4.4 POST-TRANSLATIONAL REGULATION OF BIOSYNTHETIC ENZYMES
text:
- Enzyme activities also controlled by phosphorylation, acetylation, and allosteric effectors.

Result: rapid tuning of flux through the pathway according to cellular need.

title: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS
section: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS › 4.5 INTEGRATION WITH CELLULAR LIPID CONTROL
text:
AMPK activation (energy stress) ↓ cholesterol synthesis (via HMGCR phosphorylation)

Insulin / mTOR activation ↑ SREBP processing → ↑ synthesis

Oxysterols activate LXR ↑ ABCA1, ABCG1 → ↑ efflux to HDL ↓ SREBP-2 transcription

PPARα activation Enhances cholesterol catabolism to bile acids in liver

section: 4. REGULATION OF CHOLESTEROL HOMEOSTASIS › ENERGY COST
text: Synthesis of 1 cholesterol molecule consumes: 18 ATP, 16 NADPH, 11 O2 and acetyl-CoA (~100 ATP equivalents).

title: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE
text: Cholesterol is essential for life, but when its homeostasis is disturbed, or when sterol metabolism is genetically or environmentally altered, disease can result. Below are key human disorders and health issues in which cholesterol and its metabolism play major roles.

title: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE
text:
- Hypercholesterolemia is a major risk factor for atherosclerosis, MI and stroke.

- Excess cholesterol in intima is taken up by macrophages → foam cells → fatty streaks → atherosclerotic plaques.

- Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase (the rate-limiting enzyme in sterol synthesis).

- Other potential drug targets: squalene monooxygenase, lanosterol synthase, ACAT1.

- Mediterranean-type diet and healthy lifestyle are preferred preventive strategies.

title: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE
text:
- Elevated LDL cholesterol and cholesterol esters promote atherosclerotic plaque formation.

- Plaque rupture can cause myocardial infarction and stroke.

- Risk increased by hypertension, diabetes, smoking, inflammation, abnormalities, genetic factors and lifestyle.

title: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE
text:
- Cholesterol supersaturation of bile → nucleation of cholesterol crystals.

- Stones may form in gallbladder or bile ducts.

- Can cause biliary colic, cholecystitis, pancreatitis and other complications.

- High prevalence and high healthcare cost in developed countries.

title: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE
text:
- Gallstones consist mainly of cholesterol (~85%) with smaller amounts of bile pigments and calcium salts.

- Primary cause: excessive hepatic secretion of cholesterol into bile.

- Genetic, hormonal and dietary factors also contribute.

title: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE
section: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE › 3. INHERITED DISORDERS OF CHOLESTEROL METABOLISM
text:
- ≥8 congenital disorders of cholesterol biosynthesis cause developmental malformations and neurologic defects.

- Limited placental transfer of cholesterol → fetus depends on endogenous synthesis.

- Impaired hedgehog signalling (cholesterol-modified proteins) in many cases.

Diagram labels: Lanosterol → Desmosterol; (7-DHCR); Cholesterol

Example: Smith–Lemli–Opitz syndrome (7-dehydrocholesterol reductase deficiency)

- Accumulation of 7-dehydrocholesterol and 27-hydroxy metabolite in brain.

- Symptoms range from mild autism to severe, often fatal, abnormalities.

- Dietary or peripheral cholesterol cannot cross the blood–brain barrier.

title: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE
section: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE › 4. LYSOSOMAL STORAGE DISEASES
text:
Niemann–Pick type C disease

- Defective intracellular cholesterol transport due to mutations in NPC1 (or NPC2).

- Accumulation of unesterified cholesterol and other lipids in late endosomal/lysosomal compartments.

- Leads to neurodegeneration and multi-organ dysfunction.

- Distinct from Niemann–Pick types A and B (sphingomyelinase deficiency), though secondary cholesterol storage can occur.

Diagram labels: Late endosome/lysosome

Other storage disorders

- Deficiencies of cholesterol ester hydrolases:

- Wolman disease (lysosomal acid lipase deficiency)

- Cholesteryl ester storage disease

- Accumulation of cholesterol esters in lysosomes.

- Causes hepatosplenomegaly, steatosis, failure to thrive.

title: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE
section: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE › 5. NEUROLOGIC AND EYE DISEASES
text:
- Cholesterol is vital for myelin, synapse function and neuronal membranes.

- Altered cholesterol metabolism implicated in:

- Neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer's, Huntington's).

- Niemann–Pick type C disease.

- Cognitive decline with aging.

- Eye disorders linked to cholesterol dysregulation:

- Age-related macular degeneration

- Diabetic retinopathy

- Cataracts, corneal disease, dry eye syndrome

- Oxysterols and cholesterol metabolites may contribute to pathology.

title: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE
section: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE › 6. IMMUNITY AND INFLAMMATION
text:
Diagram labels: Macrophage; T cell; Cholesterol; αβTCR

- Cholesterol and sterols bind immune receptors in macrophages and T cells.

- Dynamic control of cholesterol synthesis affects innate and adaptive immune responses.

- Cholesterol binds to αβ T cell receptor (αβTCR) in transmembrane region, maintaining an inert state until needed → receptor nanoclustering and antigen recognition.

- Sterol regulatory pathways (SREBP, LXR, etc.) modulate inflammatory signalling.

- Dysregulated cholesterol homeostasis can promote chronic inflammation and autoimmunity.

title: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE
text:
- Cancer cells require high cholesterol for membrane biogenesis, signalling and proliferation.

- Enhanced synthesis, increased uptake and impaired efflux drive malignant phenotype.

- Crosstalk between SREBP2 and oncogenic signalling pathways promotes tumorigenesis.

- Overexpression of squalene epoxidase and ACAT1 reported in some cancers.

- Inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase (statins) and other enzymes (e.g., squalene epoxidase, ACAT1) are under clinical investigation.

title: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE
text: Perturbation of reverse cholesterol transport and sterol metabolism supports tumor growth and resistance to therapy.

title: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE
section: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE › 8. STEROL DISORDERS AND BIOMARKERS
text:
Diagram labels: Cholestanol; Campesterol; Sitosterol

- Elevated non-cholesterol sterols in plasma are markers of metabolic disease.

- Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis: accumulation of cholestanol in tissues.

- Sitosterolemia: accumulation of dietary plant sterols (sitosterol, campesterol).

- Xanthomas and premature atherosclerosis may occur.

- Appearance of precursor sterols can reflect inhibited cholesterol synthesis.

title: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE
text:
Diagram labels: M. tuberculosis; C. trachomatis; HIV

- Many pathogens exploit host cholesterol for survival and replication.

- Mycobacterium tuberculosis uses host cholesterol as a carbon and energy source in macrophages.

- Chlamydia trachomatis requires host cholesterol for growth.

- HIV envelope protein binds cholesterol in lipid rafts to mediate viral entry and membrane fusion.

- Reducing cellular cholesterol may have antiviral potential, but effects are context-dependent.

title: 8. CHOLESTEROL AND DISEASE
text:
- Cholesterol is essential but potentially harmful in excess or when misregulated.

- Dysregulation contributes to cardiovascular disease, gallstones, genetic disorders, lysosomal storage diseases, neurodegeneration, cancer, immune dysfunction and infections.

- Many diseases involve either excess cholesterol/esters, defective metabolism, or aberrant sterol signalling.

- Management includes lifestyle, diet, and pharmacologic therapies targeting cholesterol synthesis, uptake and transport.

- Continued research on sterol biology is critical for improved treatments.

title: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES
text: Experiments with mutant cell lines and specific inhibitors of cholesterol biosynthesis suggest that an equatorial hydroxyl group at C-3 of sterols is essential for the growth of mammalian cells. The Δ5 double bond ensures that the molecule adopts a planar conformation, and the flexible iso-octyl side chain and the C-18 methyl group ensure proper orientation of the sterol. Plant sterols can substitute for cholesterol in supporting many of the bulk membrane properties in vitro, but cholesterol per se is essential for innumerable other purposes.

title: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES
section: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES › 1. STRUCTURE AND ORIENTATION IN MEMBRANES
text:
Planar structure of cholesterol

Orientation in a phospholipid bilayer

Diagram labels: A; B; C; D; HO; Extracellular (β-face up); ~15 Å; Cytoplasmic (α-face down); Hydroxyl group at C-3 near headgroup region (hydrogen bonding to phospholipid headgroup); Rigid tetracyclic nucleus; Iso-octyl side chain aligned with lipid acyl chains

- Four fused rings (A–D) are essentially planar.

- 3β-hydroxyl group is equatorial.

- Double bond between C-5 and C-6.

- Methyl groups at C-18 and C-19 are β-oriented (above plane); iso-octyl side chain at C-17 is flexible.

- The molecule spans ~half the bilayer (~15 Å).

title: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES
text:
- Intercalates between phospholipids, spanning ~half the bilayer.

- Amino/α-face (down) is smooth → contacts saturated acyl chains.

- β-face (up) is rough → methyl groups at C-10 and C-13 project.

- Interactions: van der Waals, hydrophobic, and H-bonding (3-OH).

- Side chain aligns with saturated chains; poorly with unsaturated chains.

title: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES
section: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES › 2. EFFECTS ON MEMBRANE PHYSICAL PROPERTIES
text:
Cholesterol modulates membrane fluidity across a broad range of temperatures

Membranes rich in unsaturated lipids (liquid-disordered, Lo) + Cholesterol → Becomes more ordered (liquid-ordered, Lo)

Membranes rich in saturated lipids (solid gel, So) + Cholesterol → Becomes more fluid (liquid-ordered, Lo)

title: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES
section: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES › Consequences of cholesterol in membranes
text:
- Increases order and thickness of unsaturated membranes; decreases order (increases fluidity) of saturated membranes.

- Promotes and stabilizes the liquid-ordered (Lo) phase over a wide range of sterol concentrations and temperatures.

- Decreases passive permeability to small solutes.

- Allows membranes to bend and withstand mechanical stresses.

- Enables fine-tuning of membrane composition and organization for cell metabolism.

title: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES
section: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES › Rafts and sphingolipids
text: Cholesterol forms stoichiometric complexes with saturated acyl chains of sphingomyelin and, to a lesser extent, phosphatidylcholine in lipid rafts, contributing to raft stability and signalling. It may also regulate sphingomyelin synthesis, particularly very-long-chain species.

title: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES
section: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES › Lipid raft (ordered nanodomain)
text: Diagram labels: Sphingomyelin; Cholesterol; Phosphatidylcholine; Saturated acyl chains; Unsaturated acyl chains

title: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES
section: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES › Distribution and functions in organelles
text:
- Plasma membrane: highest level (30–50% of lipid); ~60–80% of cell free cholesterol. → Barrier function, signalling, endo/exocytosis.

- Early & recycling endosomes: enriched; role in trafficking and signalling.

- Late endosomes: little or no cholesterol.

- Endoplasmic reticulum: low (~5%). → Greater membrane flexibility for protein insertion and folding.

- Golgi apparatus: intermediate amount.

- Mitochondria: low overall; concentrated in nanodomains at regions of high curvature in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

- Brain: ~25% of total body free cholesterol; 70–80% in myelin; essential for synapse function and precursor of oxysterols.

title: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES
section: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES › Cholesterol flip-flop and leaflet asymmetry
text:
- Cholesterol flips rapidly between leaflets, but its distribution is asymmetric in many cells.

- Most evidence indicates more cholesterol in the outer (exoplasmic) leaflet of the plasma membrane.

- This asymmetry promotes negative curvature and facilitates membrane fusion (exocytosis) and signalling.

- Human erythrocyte inner (cytoplasmic) leaflet has >50% excess phospholipids, possible only with asymmetric cholesterol distribution.

title: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES
section: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES › 3. INTERACTIONS WITH MEMBRANE PROTEINS
text:
Sterol-sensing domain (SSD) ~180 amino acids; 5 transmembrane helices; binds sterols. Found in many proteins involved in cholesterol homeostasis and trafficking.

G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs)

- Cholesterol binds directly or allosterically.

- Affects ligand binding, activation or oligomerization.

- Essential for β2-adrenergic, oxytocin and serotonin receptors (increases agonist affinity).

- Rhodopsin stabilized in inactive state by direct binding + membrane curvature effects.

- Serotonin1A receptor binds ~10 cholesterol molecules; senses via Lys in "CRAC" motif (TM2).

Ion pumps and transporters

- (Na+–K+)-ATPase and others have specific cholesterol binding sites.

- Cholesterol depletion in plasma membrane can inhibit ion pumps.

- These pumps consume high ATP and maintain ion gradients essential for cell metabolism.

Diagram labels: N; C; Ligand; Na+; K+; ATP; ADP + Pi

title: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES
text:
- Cholesterol in nucleus associates with chromatin.

- Ends bind deep within protein cavities or at membrane-facing surfaces; H-bonding involved.

title: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES
section: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES › 4. KEY ROLES OF CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANE FUNCTION
text:
- Barrier function: Increases membrane thickness and reduces permeability to ions and small molecules.

- Membrane mechanics: Confers flexibility yet stability; enables bending, fission and fusion.

- Lipid organization: Drives formation of ordered raft domains with sphingolipids.

- Protein function regulation: Necessary for proper structure, localization and activity of many membrane proteins.

- Signalling platforms: Organizes receptors and effectors; controls signalling pathways.

title: 2. CHOLESTEROL IN MEMBRANES
text:
- Cholesterol is an amphiphilic sterol that intercalates between phospholipids in bilayers.

- It modulates membrane fluidity: orders unsaturated membranes and fluidizes saturated membranes.

- It lowers permeability, increases thickness and provides mechanical resilience.

- It is asymmetrically distributed, mostly in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane.

- It organizes lipid rafts with sphingolipids and regulates proteins, including GPCRs and ion pumps.

- These actions are essential for membrane integrity, signalling, trafficking and overall cell function.

Diagram labels: Outer leaflet (more cholesterol); Inner leaflet (less cholesterol)

title: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE
text:
In animal tissues, cholesterol (or cholest-5-en-3β-ol) is by far the most abundant member of a family of polycyclic lipids known as sterols, which can be classified as polyisoprenoids or triterpenes from their biosynthetic origin. Cholesterol was first recognized as a component of gallstones as long ago as 1769, while the great French lipid chemist Chevreul isolated it from animal fats in 1815. However, it was well into the 20th century before the structure was fully defined by the German Chemist Heinrich Wieland, [illegible], who in 1927, received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work, the first of thirteen so honoured for research on cholesterol and its metabolism.

Cholesterol plays a vital role in animal life as a structural component of membranes, a precursor of steroid hormones and bile acids, and in signalling and transport processes.

title: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE
section: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE › 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE
text:
Structural formula for cholesterol

Diagram labels: A; B; C; D; HO; Cholesterol = cholest-5-en-3β-ol

Molecular formula: C27H46O Molecular mass: 386.7 g·mol-1

title: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE
section: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE › Key structural features
text:
- Tetracyclic cyclopenta[a]phenanthrene nucleus (rings A–D).

- Trans ring junctions.

- Hydroxyl group at C-3 (β-configuration).

- Double bond between C-5 and C-6.

- Iso-octyl side chain at C-17 (β-oriented) above the plane.

- Two angular methyl groups at C-18 and C-19 (β-oriented).

title: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE
text: Numbering system: Fieser–Fieser (1959) IUPAC-IUB system (1989) also used, but Fieser–Fieser preferred by most authors.

title: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE
section: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE › DISTRIBUTION OF CHOLESTEROL IN ANIMAL CELLS
text:
- Site (organelle): Plasma membrane; % of cellular cholesterol*: 60–80%; Features: ~30–50% of lipids in the membrane; Regulates fluidity, permeability, signalling

- Site (organelle): Mitochondria; % of cellular cholesterol*: ~10–15%; Features: Essential for membrane integrity and function

- Site (organelle): Endoplasmic reticulum; % of cellular cholesterol*: ~5%; Features: Lowest proportion

- Site (organelle): Golgi apparatus; % of cellular cholesterol*: ~10–15%; Features: Intermediate amount

- Site (organelle): Early & recycling endosomes; % of cellular cholesterol*: Enriched; Features: Important in trafficking and signalling

- Site (organelle): Late endosomes; % of cellular cholesterol*: Low; Features: Not enriched

*Approximate values; may vary with cell type and species.

title: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE
text: BRAIN: contains ~25% of total body free cholesterol. 70–80% of brain cholesterol is in myelin sheath. Major component of synaptic vesicles; controls their shape and function. Precursor of bioactive oxysterols.

title: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE
section: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE › FORMS AND OCCURRENCE
text:
Forms in animal tissues

- Free (unesterified) cholesterol

- Cholesterol esters (with long-chain fatty acids)

- In other covalent linkages (e.g., with proteins)

- In non-covalent aggregates in plasma lipoproteins

Occurrence

- Ubiquitous in all animal tissues (and some fungi).

- Present in every nucleated animal cell.

- Only glucose is present in blood at a higher molar concentration than cholesterol.

- Also occurs in plants (as phytosterols; cholesterol minor component) and some microorganisms.

title: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE
section: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE › Synthesis and dietary sources
text:
- Most animals synthesise high proportion of their cholesterol requirement (de novo synthesis essential even with dietary intake; vital in brain).

- Many invertebrates (insects, crustaceans, some molluscs, nematodes, e.g., C. elegans) cannot synthesise cholesterol and must obtain it from diet.

- Some species can convert plant sterols (e.g., β-sitosterol) to cholesterol.

- Most prokaryotes lack cholesterol; a few pathogens acquire it from hosts; one marine genus can synthesise it de novo.

title: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE
section: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE › VITAL ROLES AND FUNCTIONS OF CHOLESTEROL
text:
- Membrane structure: Regulates membrane fluidity, thickness, stability and permeability.

- Precursor of steroid hormones: Glucocorticoids, oestrogens, progestins, androgens, aldosterone.

- Precursor of bile acids: Essential for lipid digestion and absorption in intestines.

- Cell signalling & development: 'Hedgehog' proteins (cho-linkage) vital for embryonic development.

- Nervous system: Myelin sheath integrity, nerve conduction, synaptic vesicle function.

- Transport: Component of plasma lipoproteins (LDL, HDL) for cholesterol transport.

- Gene transcription: Modulates activity of transcription factors (e.g., SREBP, LXR).

- Reproduction: Essential for hormone synthesis and reproductive processes.

- Stress responses: Involved in cellular stress, inflammation and immune responses.

- Others: Sodium/water balance, Ca2+ & P metabolism, morphogenesis, etc.

title: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE
text: Excess cholesterol can be toxic and contributes to diseases such as cardiovascular disease, neurodegenerative disorders and cancer. Therefore, levels must be tightly balanced by synthesis, absorption, conversion and clearance.

title: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE
section: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE › RELATIONSHIP TO OTHER LIPID CLASSES

Metabolic pathways are tightly regulated to maintain optimal cellular and systemic cholesterol homeostasis.

title: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE
section: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE › DIVERSITY IN NATURE
text:
- Animals: Cholesterol is the predominant sterol.

- Plants: Mixture of phytosterols: β-sitosterol, campesterol, stigmasterol, etc.

- Fungi: Ergosterol and other sterols present.

- Microorganisms: Most lack sterols. Some pathogens acquire cholesterol from hosts.

title: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE
section: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE › WHY CHOLESTEROL IS ESSENTIAL
text:
- Structural integrity of membranes and lipid rafts.

- Precursor of many critical signalling molecules.

- Required for normal development and physiology.

- Supports rapid and precise cellular communication.

- Homeostasis is crucial – both deficiency and excess are harmful.

title: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE
section: 1. CHOLESTEROL – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE › CLINICAL RELEVANCE
text:
- High plasma LDL-cholesterol → atherosclerosis, heart disease.

- Altered cholesterol metabolism → neurodegenerative diseases, cancer.

- Therapeutic targets: HMG-CoA reductase (statins), cholesterol absorption (ezetimibe), PCSK9 inhibitors, bile acid sequestrants.

- Research continues to uncover new roles of cholesterol and its metabolites in health and disease.

title: Stereoisomers of diacyl-sn-glycerols
text: Diacylglycerols (or “diglycerides”) are esters of the trihydric alcohol glycerol in which two of the hydroxyl groups are esterified with long-chain fatty acids. They can exist as three stereochemical isomers (see our web document on Triacylglycerols (part 1) for a discussion of nomenclature). When the stereochemistry is unknown or when the mixture is racemic, sn-1,2- and 2,3-diacylglycerols are sometimes termed α,β-diacylglycerols while sn-1,3-diacylglycerols may be designated α,α′-diacylglycerols.

title: Stereoisomers of diacyl-sn-glycerols
text: Diacylglycerols are formed in animal and plant tissues as intermediates in the biosynthesis of triacylglycerols and other glycerolipids and during the hydrolysis of these by lipases. While their presence is of technological relevance in commercial seed oils as small amounts can have a profound influence on the physical properties, the function of sn-1,2-diacylglycerols derived from phospholipids as signalling mediators in animal tissues is of special importance for human health and wellbeing and is a focus of this web page.

title: Stereoisomers of diacyl-sn-glycerols
section: Stereoisomers of diacyl-sn-glycerols › 1. METABOLISM OF sn-1,2-DIACYLGLYCEROLS IN ANIMALS
text:
sn-1,2-Diacylglycerols tend to be minor components of most tissues and membranes, but in animal cells, they are required as:

- intermediates in the biosynthesis of many glycerolipids

- signalling molecules (second messengers) that respond to external stimuli to modulate vital biochemical mechanisms.

They are the only one of the three stereoisomers that act in this way. They are synthesized and metabolized by numerous enzymes at spatially different cellular locations, each with distinct enzymatic properties and selectivities.

title: 2.4. BROWN ADIPOSE TISSUE
section: 2.4. BROWN ADIPOSE TISSUE › 2.4. BROWN ADIPOSE TISSUE
text:
Brown adipose tissue (BAT) is multilocular, highly vascularized and rich in mitochondria with iron-containing pigments that give the tissue its colour. It is located in characteristic regions (around the heart, kidney, pancreas, liver, neck) where it can deliver warm venous blood to the spinal cord and brain. BAT arises from progenitors closer to skeletal muscle than white adipocytes and generates heat by rapid oxidation of fat (“non-shivering thermogenesis”), a feature critical in young animals and those recovering from hibernation.

- In cold exposure, noradrenaline release and β-adrenergic stimulation initiate lipolysis of stored TAGs, releasing free fatty acids (FFAs) and transiently activating PPARγ.

source: DAG and TAG/tag biosynthesis in BAT.png
title: 2.4. BROWN ADIPOSE TISSUE
section: 2.4. BROWN ADIPOSE TISSUE › 2.4. BROWN ADIPOSE TISSUE
text:
- FFAs activate uncoupling protein-1 (UCP1) in the inner mitochondrial membrane, which uncouples electron transport from ATP synthesis. Protons re-enter the matrix via UCP1, and energy is released as heat instead of ATP.

- Free long-chain FFAs drive UCP1 activity and act as self-regulating second messengers; purine nucleotides inhibit UCP1. Dense vasculature delivers substrates (FFAs, glucose) and warms blood.

- BAT metabolism is indispensable in hibernating mammals and can account for ~50% of dietary lipids and glucose in cold-exposed mice. BAT activity is acutely induced by cold via the sympathetic nervous system.

- BAT is increasingly recognized as an endocrine organ secreting “batokines” that may influence cardiovascular and metabolic health.

title: 2.3. TRIACYLGLYCEROL METABOLISM IN ADIPOCYTES AND LIPID DROPLETS
section: 2.3. TRIACYLGLYCEROL METABOLISM IN ADIPOCYTES AND LIPID DROPLETS › (untitled panel)
text: Adipose tissue and the adipocytes are characterized by accumulations of triacylglycerols, which act as the main energy store for animals while cushioning and insulating the body. Triacylglycerols stored when there is a surplus of nutrients are mobilized for energy production during starvation, but adipose tissue serves also as a reservoir of bioactive lipids and when required provides structural components, including fatty acids, cholesterol and retinol, for membrane synthesis and repair. By buffering against fatty acid accumulation that might exceed their capacity, non-adipose cells defend themselves against lipotoxicity while providing a rapid source of energy and essential metabolites by sensing and responding rapidly to changes in the systemic energy balance. Dysfunction contributes to numerous diseases, including hepatic steatosis, lipodystrophy, and cardiovascular, intestinal and infectious diseases. Cytosolic lipid droplets and their associated metabolic processes are found in most eukaryotic cells, including those of Drosophila melanogaster, in the plastids of plants and in the cytoplasm of some prokaryotes.

section: 2.3. TRIACYLGLYCEROL METABOLISM IN ADIPOCYTES AND LIPID DROPLETS › KEY TAKE-HOME MESSAGES
text:
- Lipid droplets are dynamic organelles, not inert fat blobs.

- They store energy as TAGs and sequester potentially harmful lipids.

- Assembly occurs in ER subdomains via coordinated enzymes, seipin and protein machinery.

- Lipolysis is tightly regulated by hormones and occurs mainly at the droplet surface.

- Adipose tissue communicates with multiple organs via adipokines and lipid mediators.

- Dysregulation of storage or lipolysis contributes to metabolic diseases (obesity, diabetes, fatty liver, CVD).

- Brown and beige fat provide thermogenic capacity.

- Lipid droplets exist in most eukaryotic cells, plants and some prokaryotes.

title: 2.2. TRIACYLGLYCEROL METABOLISM IN THE INTESTINES, LIVER AND MAMMARY GLAND
section: 2.2. TRIACYLGLYCEROL METABOLISM IN THE INTESTINES, LIVER AND MAMMARY GLAND › (untitled panel)
text: Fat comprises up to 40% of the energy intake in the human diet in Western countries, and a high proportion of this is composed of triacylglycerols. The process of fat digestion is begun in the stomach by acid-stable gastric or lingual lipases, the extent of which is variable but in general is insignificant in quantitative terms in comparison to subsequent steps, although it may be required for efficient emulsification as an aid to digestion. Entry of triacylglycerol degradation products into the duodenum stimulates synthesis of the hormone cholecystokinin and causes the gall bladder to release bile acids, which are strong detergents and act to emulsify the hydrophobic triacylglycerols so increasing the available surface area. In turn, cholecystokinin stimulates the release of the hydrolytic enzyme pancreatic lipase and a co-lipase, and these together with bile salts and calcium ions act in a complex at the surface of the emulsified fat droplets to hydrolyse the triacylglycerols. The process is regiospecific and results in the release of the fatty acids from the 1 and 3 positions and formation of 2-monoacyl-sn-glycerols, some of which can isomerize spontaneously to 1(3)-monoacyl-sn-glycerols for complete hydrolysis by the enzyme to glycerol and free fatty acids. Other lipases hydrolyse the phospholipids and other lipid esters in foods at the same time.

section: Table 2. Positional distributions of fatty acids (mol %) in triacyl-sn-glycerols of animal depot fats › KEY POINTS
text:
- Triacylglycerols are triesters of glycerol.

- Positions sn-1 and sn-3 are primary (α and α′); sn-2 is secondary (β).

- Positional distribution of fatty acids differs among species and is influenced by diet and biosynthesis.

- sn-2 fatty acid is released as 2-monoacylglycerol during digestion.

- Triacylglycerols are essential for energy storage but can cause disease when in excess.

title: 1.3. TRIACYLGLYCEROLS FROM ANIMAL FATS – ADIPOSE TISSUE
section: 1.3. TRIACYLGLYCEROLS FROM ANIMAL FATS – ADIPOSE TISSUE › (untitled panel)
text: Much of the triacylglycerols in animal tissues, including some of the commercially important fats such as lard or tallow, are contained within various adipose tissue sites in cells known as adipocytes (or in lipid droplets within cells), where they serve mainly as an energy store, but also cushion tissues such as liver. The subcutaneous fats help to insulate animals, while fat stores in fish and marine animals help to maintain buoyancy. While some fatty acids are synthesised de novo in tissues (saturated and monoenoic acids), the composition of the triacylglycerols reflects that of the diet to an appreciable extent. In terrestrial animals, the composition tends to be quite simple, with C16 (mainly 16:0) and C18 fatty acids predominating. All the essential fatty acids, such as linoleic and α-linolenic acids, must come from the diet of course, although polyunsaturated fatty acids tend to be relatively minor components of triacylglycerols in comparison to the complex lipids. Ruminant animals have relatively saturated fats because the dietary unsaturated fatty acids are subjected to biohydrogenation in the rumen, a process that generates trans fatty acids as by-products and odd- and branched-chain fatty acids.

title: 1.1 INTRODUCTION
text: Nearly all the commercially important fats and oils of animal and plant origin contain mainly (>95%) the simple lipid class – triacylglycerols (‘triglycerides’), which are chemically inert, highly hydrophobic high energy density. This includes all the vegetable oils, such as those from corn (maize), olive, palm and sunflower, and animal fats, such as tallow, lard and butter, as well as manufactured products such as margarines. The more abundant animal triacylglycerols are depots fats from adipose tissue or milk fats, where their main function in vivo is as a store of energy and perhaps of bioactive lipids, but it is increasingly being recognized that triacylglycerols in most tissues, but especially those in plasma or liver, have a more dynamic role in cellular metabolism. Similarly, seed oils serve as a source of energy and structural fatty acids for the developing plant embryo. In this web page, the fatty acid compositions of triacylglycerols together with their organization within molecules in various organisms are described. Two companion documents on this website are Triacylglycerols: Part 2. Biosynthesis and metabolism and Triacylglycerols: Part 3 – Regio- and stereospecific analysis procedures.

title: 1.1 INTRODUCTION
text:
Triacylglycerols (TAGs) consist of the trihydric alcohol glycerol esterified mainly with long-chain fatty acids (C14 to C22). When the two primary hydroxyl groups are esterified with different fatty acids, the resulting triacylglycerol can display chiral asymmetry and thus be optically active, although this is usually too low to be measured.

The stereochemistry of TAGs and other glycerolipids is described by the “stereospecific numbering” (sn) system recommended by the IUPAC–IUB Commission.

title: 1.1 INTRODUCTION
text:
- Natural glycerol is of L-configuration.

- The secondary (middle) carbon is C-2 (β-position).

- The ends are C-1 (α-position) and C-3 (α′-position).

- Triacyl-sn-glycerol is the recommended term.

- “Triglyceride” is still used industrially and clinically, but not recommended for scientific studies.

title: 3. REGIO- AND STEREOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS PROCEDURES FOR TRIACYLGLYCEROLS
section: 3. REGIO- AND STEREOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS PROCEDURES FOR TRIACYLGLYCEROLS › (untitled panel)
text: The compositions of the fatty acids linked to the different positions of the glycerol moiety of triacylglycerols (TAGs) of animals, plants and microorganinans can be very different. Natural TAGs invariably exist as enantiomers because the glycerol backbone is chiral. Positions are [illegible] numbering (sn) system as sn-1, sn-2 and sn-3 from a Fischer projection (Figure 1). Analytical determination of these positional distributions is essential for studies of physical properties, biosynthesis, metabolism and function of TAGs in tissues.

title: 3. REGIO- AND STEREOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS PROCEDURES FOR TRIACYLGLYCEROLS
section: 3. REGIO- AND STEREOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS PROCEDURES FOR TRIACYLGLYCEROLS › Key points
text:
- Position sn-2 is secondary (β); sn-1 and sn-3 are primary (α and α′).

- Each position can have a distinctive fatty acid composition.

- TAGs are enantiomers due to the chiral glycerol backbone.

- Regiospecific analysis (e.g., pancreatic lipase) determines sn-2 composition.

- Stereospecific analysis is required for sn-1 and sn-3 compositions.

- Analytical data are vital for understanding biosynthesis, metabolism and function.

title: 3. REGIO- AND STEREOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS PROCEDURES FOR TRIACYLGLYCEROLS
section: 3. REGIO- AND STEREOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS PROCEDURES FOR TRIACYLGLYCEROLS › General approaches
text:
- Regiospecific analysis (simpler): determines composition of sn-2 only (e.g., pancreatic lipase, chemical or MS/NMR methods).

- Stereospecific analysis (more complex): determines compositions of sn-1 and sn-3 by degradative + synthetic steps followed by enzymatic hydrolysis and chromatographic separations (including chiral methods).

- Reference reviews: Kuksis & Itabashi [1,2].

title: 3. REGIO- AND STEREOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS PROCEDURES FOR TRIACYLGLYCEROLS
section: 3. REGIO- AND STEREOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS PROCEDURES FOR TRIACYLGLYCEROLS › Surprising natural examples from stereospecific analyses
text:
Milk fat shows extreme asymmetry: all short-chain fatty acids (butyric, 4:0 and hexanoic, 6:0) are concentrated in position sn-3 with none in sn-1 or sn-2.

See our web page on Triacylglycerol compositions for data on representative natural samples.

title: 3. REGIO- AND STEREOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS PROCEDURES FOR TRIACYLGLYCEROLS
section: 3. REGIO- AND STEREOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS PROCEDURES FOR TRIACYLGLYCEROLS › 3.1. REGIOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS OF TRIACYL-sn-GLYCEROLS BY PANCREATIC LIPASE HYDROLYSIS
text: Porcine pancreatic lipase (with colipase, bile salts and Ca2+) hydrolyses the ester bonds at the primary positions (sn-1 and sn-3) of triacylglycerols to release free fatty acids (FFAs) and leave a 2-monoacyl-sn-glycerol (2-MAG). The fatty acid of the 2-MAG represents the composition of position sn-2 in the native TAGs.

text: Diagram labels: Triacyl-sn-glycerol (TAG); Pancreatic lipase (+ colipase, bile salts, Ca2+, buffer, 40 °C); ~50% hydrolysis; R1 → COO−; 2-Monoacyl-sn-glycerol (2-MAG)

title: 3. REGIO- AND STEREOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS PROCEDURES FOR TRIACYLGLYCEROLS
section: 3. REGIO- AND STEREOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS PROCEDURES FOR TRIACYLGLYCEROLS › Important features of the reaction
text:
- Requires micellar substrate: vigorous shaking essential.

- Bile salts (e.g., taurodeoxycholate) and Ca2+ ions are essential.

- pH optimum ~8; temperature ~40 °C.

- No preference for sn-1 vs sn-3 (hydrolysed at same rate).

- Most straight-chain saturated and mono-, di-, trienoic acids hydrolysed at similar rates.

- Some polyunsaturated or hindered acids hydrolysed more slowly (e.g., 22:6n-3, trans-3-16:1, γ-linolenic acid).

- TAGs with short-chain acyl groups are hydrolysed faster than those with only long-chain acyls.

- Stop reaction at ~50–60% hydrolysis to minimize acyl migration and side reactions.

title: 3. REGIO- AND STEREOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS PROCEDURES FOR TRIACYLGLYCEROLS
section: 3. REGIO- AND STEREOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS PROCEDURES FOR TRIACYLGLYCEROLS › Semi-micro procedure (Luddy et al. [3])
text:
1. Mix TAG sample with buffer (pH 8) containing bile salt and CaCl2 at 40 °C; pre-incubate 5 min.

2. Add pancreatin (lipase + colipase); shake vigorously 1–2 min (~50% hydrolysis).

3. Stop reaction: extract with diethyl ether–isopropanol (3:1, v/v) containing antioxidant (e.g., BHT).

4. Separate ether-soluble (FFAs) and insoluble (2-MAG + residual TAG) by partition or TLC.

5. Isolate 2-MAG band by TLC or HPLC; trans-esterify to FAMEs.

6. Analyse FAMEs by gas chromatography → composition of sn-2.

title: 3. REGIO- AND STEREOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS PROCEDURES FOR TRIACYLGLYCEROLS
section: 3. REGIO- AND STEREOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS PROCEDURES FOR TRIACYLGLYCEROLS › Advantages and limitations › Advantages
text:
- Simple, rapid and widely used.

- Good reproducibility with appropriate conditions.

- Representative of sn-2 composition for most natural TAGs (normal chain lengths).

- Small sample amounts (mg) sufficient.

title: 3. REGIO- AND STEREOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS PROCEDURES FOR TRIACYLGLYCEROLS
section: 3. REGIO- AND STEREOSPECIFIC ANALYSIS PROCEDURES FOR TRIACYLGLYCEROLS › Advantages and limitations › Limitations
text:
- Cannot determine sn-1 and sn-3 compositions.

- Reduced rates for some PUFA and hindered acyls.

- Requires micelles; unsuitable for highly polar TAGs without carriers or pre-incubation.

- Acyl migration if incubation is prolonged or conditions not optimal.

title: Biosynthesis of Monoglycosylceramides
text: Ceramides are synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) de novo or by sphingomyelin catabolism. Monoglycosylceramides are formed by transfer of a sugar from a UDP-sugar to ceramide by specific glycosyltransferases with inversion of configuration (α → β).

title: Biosynthesis of Monoglycosylceramides
section: Biosynthesis of Monoglycosylceramides › A. GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE BIOSYNTHESIS
text:
Diagram labels: UDP-galactose; Ceramide; Endoplasmic reticulum (luminal surface); UDP-galactose:ceramide galactosyltransferase (GalCer synthase); β-D-Galactosylceramide (GalCer); Lumen; Cytosol; Flip-flop (energy-independent); Transport to trans-Golgi; Golgi

GalCer synthase is expressed in oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells, kidneys and testes.

Further modification

- Sulfatide

- GM4 ganglioside

- Gal2Cer and other gala-series

title: Biosynthesis of Monoglycosylceramides
section: Biosynthesis of Monoglycosylceramides › B. GLUCOSYLCERAMIDE BIOSYNTHESIS
text:
Diagram labels: Endoplasmic reticulum (luminal surface); Ceramide; CERT; Transfer of ceramide to cytosolic leaflet of early Golgi (CERT protein); Early Golgi (cytosolic leaflet); UDP-glucose; Glucosylceramide synthase (GlcCer synthase); β-D-Glucosylceramide (GlcCer); Cytosol; Translocation to luminal leaflet of trans-Golgi; GLTP; FAPP2; ATP10A/ATP10D; ATP; ADP + Pi; Transport to plasma membrane; Trans-Golgi (luminal leaflet); Plasma membrane (outer leaflet)

GlcCer synthase is present in early Golgi membranes (except possibly neuronal tissues).

Distinct enzymes and pathways

- GalCer and GlcCer synthases have no sequence homology.

- Human flippases ATP10A/D are specific for GlcCer, not GalCer.

Non-vesicular transport by P4-ATPases (ATP10A, ATP10D) with FAPP2 and GLTP conserves energy from ATP to flip GlcCer to luminal leaflet.

title: Biosynthesis of Monoglycosylceramides
section: Biosynthesis of Monoglycosylceramides › C. BIOSYNTHESIS IN PLANTS AND FUNGI › PLANTS
text:
Diagram labels: ER; Golgi; Plasma membrane (outer leaflet)

- GlcCer is synthesized in the ER by an evolutionarily conserved glucosylceramide synthase (GCS1) using UDP-glucose and ceramide.

- Alternative pathway: sterol glucoside can donate glucose to ceramide.

- After transport through the Golgi, GlcCer is delivered to the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane.

- Expression of GCS1 increases during phosphate deficiency.

- Ceramides with Δ4 trans-double bonds are preferred for GlcCer synthesis in some species.

title: Biosynthesis of Monoglycosylceramides
section: Biosynthesis of Monoglycosylceramides › C. BIOSYNTHESIS IN PLANTS AND FUNGI › FUNGI (e.g., yeast)
text:
Diagram labels: ER; Golgi; Vesicles; Plasma membrane and cell wall; Secretion (extracellular vesicles)

- In yeast (Pichia pastoris):

- Ceramide synthase 1 produces ceramides specifically for GlcCer.

- Ceramide synthase 2 produces ceramides for ceramide phosphorylinositol (contains phytosphingosine).

- GlcCer synthases (e.g., Hsx11 in Candida albicans) synthesize GlcCer, which is exported by vesicular trafficking to plasma membrane and cell wall, or secreted in vesicles.

- A galactosylceramide synthase has not yet been identified.

title: Biosynthesis of Monoglycosylceramides
text:
- Monoglycosylceramides are synthesized by direct transfer of a sugar from UDP-sugars to ceramide with inversion of configuration (α → β).

- Galactosylceramide is made in the ER (luminal side) by GalCer synthase and trafficked to the trans-Golgi for further modification.

- Glucosylceramide is made on the cytosolic side of early Golgi by GlcCer synthase after ceramide transfer via CERT; it must be flipped to the luminal side of trans-Golgi by ATP10A/D–FAPP2–GLTP.

- Both GalCer and GlcCer are transported to and across the plasma membrane for function and signaling; some GlcCer circulates on lipoproteins (VLDL, LDL, HDL).

- In plants and fungi, GlcCer is synthesized in the ER and delivered to the plasma membrane (and cell wall in fungi); no GalCer synthase has been identified.

title: Biosynthesis of Monoglycosylceramides
text: - Specific enzymes and transport systems ensure the distinct localization and handling of GalCer and GlcCer in cells.

title: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES
section: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES › A. GALACTOSYLCERAMIDES (GalCer) › High melting point and ordered structure
text: GalCer has a transition temperature well above physiological temperature. Each molecule can form up to eight inter- or intramolecular hydrogen bonds with neighbouring molecules, creating a dense network that produces a compact, para-crystalline arrangement in membranes.

title: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES
section: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES › A. GALACTOSYLCERAMIDES (GalCer) › Localization in membrane rafts
text: GalCer is concentrated in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane together with cholesterol and sphingomyelin in lipid rafts. The combination of hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions promotes tight packing and allows binding of a wide range of raft-associated proteins, including enzymes and receptors.

title: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES
section: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES › A. GALACTOSYLCERAMIDES (GalCer) › Essential for myelin structure and function
text: GalCer is vital for oligodendrocyte differentiation, proper axo-glial interactions and normal myelin formation.

title: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES
section: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES › A. GALACTOSYLCERAMIDES (GalCer) › 2′-Hydroxy fatty acids for stability
text: Species containing 2′-hydroxy fatty acids are not required for myelin assembly, but are critical for long-term stability by strengthening hydrogen bonding and stabilizing membrane phase structure.

title: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES
section: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES › A. GALACTOSYLCERAMIDES (GalCer) › Galactosylceramide (GalCer)
text: Diagram labels: Galactosylceramide (GalCer)

section: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES › A. GALACTOSYLCERAMIDES (GalCer) › Lipid raft in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane (eukaryotic cell)
text: Diagram labels: Enzyme; Receptor; GalCer; Cholesterol; Sphingomyelin; Protein

title: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES
section: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES › A. GALACTOSYLCERAMIDES (GalCer) › Precursor of sulfatide (3′-sulfo-GalCer)
text:
GalCer is the precursor of 3′-sulfo-galactosylceramide (sulfatide), essential for brain development and many functions in other tissues.

Diagram labels: GalCer; Sulfatide

title: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES
section: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES › A. GALACTOSYLCERAMIDES (GalCer) › Role in glycosynapse and myelin stability
text: GalCer and sulfatide on opposing myelin membranes interact via carbohydrate–carbohydrate binding to form a “glycosynapse”, which contributes to the long-term stability of the myelin sheath.

title: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES
section: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES › A. GALACTOSYLCERAMIDES (GalCer) › Glycosynapse between opposing myelin layers
text: Diagram labels: Cytoplasmic face; GalCer; Extracellular space; Sulfatide (3′-sulfo-GalCer); Cytoplasmic face; Key: GalCer; Sulfatide

title: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES
section: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES › B. GLUCOSYLCERAMIDES (GlcCer) › Similar physical properties and raft localization
text: GlcCer has similar high melting point and ordered packing to GalCer and is enriched in lipid rafts in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane.

title: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES
section: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES › B. GLUCOSYLCERAMIDES (GlcCer) › Precursor of complex glycosphingolipids
text: GlcCer is the primary precursor for most complex oligoglycosphingolipids in animals, especially in brain, where they are essential for the production of neuronal glycolipids. GlcCer itself is required for axonal growth.

title: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES
section: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES › B. GLUCOSYLCERAMIDES (GlcCer) › Essential in skin
text: Major component of epidermal lipids; necessary for lamellar body formation in the stratum corneum and for the water permeability barrier.

title: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES
section: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES › B. GLUCOSYLCERAMIDES (GlcCer) › Source of epidermal ceramides
text: Epidermal GlcCer (with sphingomyelin) is the source of unique complex ceramides found in the stratum corneum, including those with terminal hydroxyl groups and estolide-linked fatty acids. Some GlcCer is covalently linked to proteins via fatty acid hydroxyls, helping to strengthen the barrier.

title: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES
section: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES › B. GLUCOSYLCERAMIDES (GlcCer) › Glucosylceramide (GlcCer)
text: Diagram labels: Glucosylceramide (GlcCer)

title: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES
section: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES › B. GLUCOSYLCERAMIDES (GlcCer) › Role in skin barrier
text:
Diagram labels: Stratum corneum; Granular layer; Lamellar body

GlcCer is essential for lamellar body secretion and maintenance of the water permeability barrier.

title: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES
section: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES › B. GLUCOSYLCERAMIDES (GlcCer) › Functions beyond structure
text:
- Required for intracellular membrane transport, cell proliferation and survival, and for immune function.

- Disruption of global GlcCer synthase gene in mice is embryonic lethal. Crucial for survival of cancer cells; over-expression promotes tumor progression and drug resistance.

- In C. elegans, GlcCer with 22:0 fatty acid and iso-methyl-branched base mediates glucose response and acts as a longevity metabolite via clathrin localization.

- In plants, GlcCer is critical for cell differentiation, organogenesis, cellulose synthesis, and stress tolerance (cold, drought).

- In fungi, GlcCer is essential for cell wall assembly, cell division, differentiation and signaling; methyl branch in long-chain base is required for division and alkali-tolerance and influences virulence.

title: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES
section: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES › C. GLUCOSYLCERAMIDES IN PLANTS
text:
Scottish thistle (Onopordum acanthium)

- Synthesized in the ER by conserved GCS1 using UDP-glucose and ceramide.

- Localized in lipid rafts with sterols in the plasma membrane and associated with specific proteins.

- Necessary for cellulose synthesis and cell differentiation.

- Help plasma membrane withstand cold and drought stresses. Species with 2-hydroxy monounsaturated very-long-chain fatty acids and 4-cis double bonds in bases are enriched in tolerant plants.

- Only small amounts are used as precursors of oligoglycosylceramides.

- Some plant GlcCer (e.g., with Δ9 double bond in LCB) induce fruiting in the fungus Schizophyllum commune.

Diagram labels: Plasma membrane; Cell wall; Raft domain; GlcCer; GalCer; Cholesterol; Sphingomyelin; Protein

title: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES
section: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES › D. GLUCOSYLCERAMIDES IN FUNGI
text:
- Major components of plasma membrane and cell wall.

- Involved in cell wall assembly, cell division, differentiation and signaling.

- Methyl branch in long-chain base is required for cell division, alkali-tolerance and is recognized by host immune system; exported in extracellular vesicles, influencing virulence.

- Not precursors for oligoglycosylceramides in fungi.

- Some fungal GlcCer (with Δ9-methyl in the base or double bonds at Δ4 and/or Δ8) trigger plant defence responses.

Schizophyllum commune

title: 3. FUNCTION OF MONOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES
text: In summary: Galactosylceramides are essential for myelin structure and stability through ordered raft domains and glycosynapse formation with sulfatide. Glucosylceramides are versatile lipids required for membrane organization, barrier function, glycosphingolipid biosynthesis, development, stress responses and signaling in animals, plants and fungi.

title: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer)
text: α-Galactosylceramides linked through an α-D-galactosyl unit are potent activators of invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells by binding to CD1d on antigen-presenting cells.

title: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer)
text:
Diagram labels: α-D-Galactosylceramide (α-GalCer)

R1 = fatty acyl chain (e.g., 16:0, 24:1, etc.)

title: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer)
text: Diagram labels: Antigen-presenting cell (e.g., dendritic cell); α-GalCer loads onto CD1d; CD1d; Recognized by iNKT cell TCR; iNKT cell; Activation, proliferation and cytokine release (e.g., IL-10, IFN-γ)

title: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer)
text:
- Natural endogenous ligand: α-GalCer with a 24:1 fatty acid (in very small amounts) is presented by CD1d as an endogenous ligand for NKT cells in the thymus and periphery.

- Activated NKT cells produce cytokines (e.g., IL-10, IFN-γ) that modulate innate and adaptive immune responses.

- Synthetic α-GalCer analogues with straight-chain fatty acids are more efficient than branched forms (e.g., from B. fragilis).

- α-Glucosylceramide and α-psychosine analogues are also active in iNKT cell activation.

title: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer)
section: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer) › SOURCE, METABOLISM AND STRUCTURAL VARIATION › Probable Source
text:
- Not certain to be synthesized in animal tissues.

- Likely derived mainly from gut microbiota (e.g., Bacteroides fragilis and relatives); also found in marine sponge Agelas mauritianus and in cow’s milk.

- Bacterial ceramide–galactosyltransferases have been identified that synthesize α-GalCer.

title: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer)
section: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer) › SOURCE, METABOLISM AND STRUCTURAL VARIATION › Typical Molecular Forms
text:
Mouse gut (dominant form)

2-R-hydroxylated hexadecanoyl (16:0) linked to C18-sphinganine

B. fragilis (common form)

Longer-chain fatty acids (often 20–24 carbons) with iso-methyl branches in the sphingoid base

title: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer)
text:
Concentration in tissues is controlled by a two-step catabolism:

Diagram labels: α-GalCer; 1. Acid ceramidase; Lyso-α-GalCer (sphingosine + sugar); 2. α-Glycosidase; Sphingosine; Galactose

title: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer)
text: Observed in mice under stress conditions that alter the gut microbiota, including Western diet, colitis and influenza A virus infection; may impact systemic immune responses.

title: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer)
text:
- Preclinical studies: effective against lung and colorectal cancers, melanoma, leukaemia.

- Safe and efficacious as anti-tumour immunotherapeutic agents and vaccine adjuvants against viruses and intracellular bacteria.

- Phase I/II clinical trials in high-risk melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer show promising results.

- Synthetic analogues with anti-viral properties under development.

- PLS-α-GalCer (scavenger receptor-A1 targeted prodrug) shows enhanced antitumour activity in mouse models.

- In a mouse model, α-GalCer improved resolution of neuroinflammation and cognitive performance by modulating inflammatory cytokines.

title: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer)
text: α-Galactosylceramides are microbial (and dietary) lipids that act as natural ligands for CD1d, activating iNKT cells and shaping immune responses. They are under active investigation as immunotherapeutic and vaccine adjuvant agents for cancer, infections and inflammatory diseases.

title: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer)
text: Glycosphingolipids are degraded primarily in lysosomes by sequential action of exohydrolases, releasing monosaccharides and ultimately ceramide, which is further hydrolysed to sphingoid base and fatty acid for reutilization.

title: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer)
text:
Diagram labels: Limiting membrane (glycocalyx of N-glycosylated proteins + GM3); Internal lysosomal vesicles; Soluble acid hydrolases (pH ~4.5–5.0); Lysobisphosphatidic acid (bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate) in the inner membrane confers digestion resistance

- Sections of plasma membrane enter the cell by endocytosis and are transported via endosomes to lysosomes.

- The glycocalyx and GM3 form a hydrophilic barrier that protects the perimeter membrane from hydrolytic enzymes and prevents escape of lipids and their hydrolysates.

title: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer)
text: Diagram labels: Complex glycosphingolipids (oligoglycosylceramides, gangliosides); Exohydrolases (sequential removal from non-reducing end); Monoglycosylceramide; Ceramide; Monosaccharides released; Degradation of ceramide; Ceramidase; Sphingoid base (e.g., sphingosine); Fatty acid

title: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer)
section: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer) › LYSOSOMAL DEGRADATION PATHWAY › β-GLYCOSIDASES / β-GALACTOSIDASE
text:
- Enzyme: GBA1 (β-glucosidase); Localization / Notes: Lysosomal hydrolase (deficiency → Gaucher disease type 1)

- Enzyme: GBA2 (β-glucosidase); Localization / Notes: Ubiquitous non-lysosomal enzyme

- Enzyme: GBA3 (β-glucosidase); Localization / Notes: Cytosolic; found in kidney, liver, spleen and other tissues; function not fully clear

- Enzyme: Lysosomal β-galactosidase; Localization / Notes: (One isoform) removes galactose from GalCer

title: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer)
text:
Glycolipids with fewer than four carbohydrate residues are embedded in intralysosomal membranes, while the enzymes are soluble. Hence, degradation requires:

Diagram labels: Negatively charged lipids (e.g., BMP, sulfatides); Activator proteins (saposin A, B, C, D); Water-soluble glycoproteins (low molecular weight)

These factors extract the glycolipid from the membrane into mixed micelles where enzymes can access and hydrolyse the substrate.

title: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer)
text:
- Monosaccharides, sphingoid bases and fatty acids are released.

- These components are transported out of the lysosome for reuse in biosynthetic pathways or further catabolism.

- Defects in lysosomal hydrolases cause accumulation of specific glycosphingolipids, leading to lysosomal storage disorders (e.g., Gaucher, Sandhoff, GM1 gangliosidosis).

title: 4. α-D-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE (α-GalCer)
text: The lysosome is the central hub for the turnover of all glycosphingolipids, ensuring cellular homeostasis and preventing toxic accumulation.

title: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES
section: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES › (untitled panel)
text:
Non-acidic oligoglycosylceramides with from three to more than twenty monosaccharide units in the head group have been detected in many animal tissues ('megaloglycolipids' with up to 50 carbohydrate groups occur in all in erythrocytes). Tri- to pentaglycosylceramides are often the most abundant or at least the most intensively studied. More than 500 oligoglycosylceramides with variations in the structure of the carbohydrate moiety have been characterized (including those that are gangliosides and other acidic forms).

Seven major and several minor series are recognized. In most, the primary unit linked to ceramide is glucose (Glc). The same main series occur in gangliosides and sulfatides.

title: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES
section: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES › (untitled panel)
text: Name of a glycosphingolipid = (root name)(root size)osylceramide (e.g., lactotetraosylceramide or LcOse4Cer). Gb3, Gb4, Gb5 refer to tri-, tetra- and pentasaccharide glycans of the globo-series.

title: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES
section: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES › (untitled panel)
text:
- Many different non-acidic oligoglycosphingolipids are present in various organs and species; composition changes during development.

- The ceramide component (fatty acid and long-chain base) is essential for optimum function in membranes.

- Fatty acids are usually long-chain saturated or monoenoic. An exception: testicular fucolipids with polyunsaturated fatty acids essential for spermatogenesis and fertility in male mice.

title: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES
section: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES › Key functions (examples)
text:
- Participate in cell recognition, adhesion, growth, differentiation and signalling.

- Mediate carbohydrate–carbohydrate interactions with proteins, lectins and pathogens.

- Involved in embryonic development, neuronal function and immune responses.

- Often concentrated in membrane microdomains (rafts) where they modulate receptor activity and signalling.

title: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES
section: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES › Key points
text:
- Sugar residues are added on the luminal side of Golgi membranes by specific glycosyltransferases using nucleotide sugar donors.

- Order and availability of enzymes and donors determine the series and structures produced.

- Lipids are sorted in the trans–Golgi and delivered to the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane.

title: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES
section: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES › B. MAJOR FUNCTIONS
text:
- Cell recognition and adhesion (Mediated by carbohydrate moieties binding to lectins, proteins and other cells.)

- Innate immunity (Act as pattern recognition receptors for pathogens; important in phagocytes.)

- Signalling and receptor regulation (Modulate growth factor receptors, immune receptors and ion channels in lipid rafts.)

- Membrane organization (Concentrated in lipid rafts; stabilize membrane structure and microdomains.)

- Development and differentiation (Critical in embryogenesis, neural development and tissue morphogenesis.)

- Disease association (Altered expression linked to cancer, inflammation, Fabry's disease and other disorders.)

title: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES
section: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES › SUMMARY
text: Non-acidic oligoglycosphingolipids are highly diverse amphipathic lipids that play essential roles in cellular function. Lactosylceramide (LacCer) is the key intermediate for the biosynthesis of most complex glycosphingolipids in animals. These lipids are involved in cell communication, membrane organization, immunity and development, and are implicated in many diseases.

title: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES
section: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES › ESSENTIAL CONCEPTS
text:
- Built on a ceramide backbone with variable oligosaccharide chains.

- Biosynthesized in the Golgi by sequential action of glycosyltransferases.

- Organized into series (e.g., globo, lacto, ganglio, etc.) based on linkage patterns and monosaccharide composition.

- Function through carbohydrate recognition, signalling and membrane structuring.

title: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES
section: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES › CLINICAL RELEVANCE
text:
- Altered glycosphingolipid expression is associated with:

- Lysosomal storage disorders (e.g., Fabry's disease – Gb3 accumulation)

- Cancer progression and metastasis

- Inflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases

- Targeting glycosphingolipid pathways is a promising therapeutic strategy.

title: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES
section: 2. NON-ACIDIC OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS OF ANIMAL TISSUES › KEY TAKE-HOME MESSAGE
text: Non-acidic oligoglycosphingolipids are not just structural membrane components, but dynamic molecules that govern vital biological processes and whose dysregulation contributes to human disease.

title: 5. CATABOLISM OF OLIGOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES IN ANIMALS AND GENETIC DISEASE
section: 5. CATABOLISM OF OLIGOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES IN ANIMALS AND GENETIC DISEASE › (untitled panel)
text: Oligoglycosphingolipids are degraded in lysosomes within the cell by water-soluble hydrolases, aided by activator proteins (saposins) and anionic lipids such as bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate (BMP). Sections of plasma membrane containing glycosphingolipids are endocytosed and transported to lysosomes where exohydrolases cleave sugar residues sequentially from the non-reducing end. The cleaved fragments (sugars and ceramides) leave the lysosome and are either degraded further or re-enter biosynthetic pathways. In certain bacteria and leeches, a ceramide glycanase can hydrolyse the β-glucosidic bond between glucose and ceramide, yielding ceramide and an oligosaccharide.

section: 5. CATABOLISM OF OLIGOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES IN ANIMALS AND GENETIC DISEASE › KEY POINTS
text:
- Degradation occurs in lysosomes by sequential action of exohydrolases from the non-reducing end.

- Activator proteins (saposins) and anionic lipids (e.g., BMP) are required for optimal enzyme activity.

- Cleaved sugars and ceramides exit the lysosome for further metabolism or recycling.

- Alternative ceramide glycanase pathway cleaves the β-glucosidic bond to give ceramide + oligosaccharide.
