section: 5. CATABOLISM OF OLIGOGLYCOSYLCERAMIDES IN ANIMALS AND GENETIC DISEASE › C. FABRY'S DISEASE (α-GALACTOSIDASE A DEFICIENCY)
text:
Diagram labels: Normal pathway; Gb3 (globotriaosylceramide); α-Galactosidase A removes terminal Gal; In Fabry disease; α-Galactosidase A absent/deficient; Cer

Accumulation of Gb3, galabiosylceramide and lactosylceramide in lysosomes of kidney, heart, brain and other tissues

Diagnosis

- Elevated Gb3 in urine or lyso-Gb3 in serum

Treatment Enzyme replacement therapy (agalsidase α or β) improves outcomes.

Clinical features

- Renal failure (proteinuria)

- Cardiomyopathy

- Cerebrovascular disease (stroke)

- Neuropathic pain, angiokeratomas

- Corneal opacities, hearing loss

- Reduced life expectancy

title: NON-ACIDIC DI- AND OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS IN ANIMALS
section: NON-ACIDIC DI- AND OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS IN ANIMALS › (untitled panel)
text: Non-acidic di- and oligoglycosphingolipids, i.e., with two to many more carbohydrate moieties attached to a ceramide unit, are vital components of cellular membranes of most eukaryotic organisms and some bacteria. Of these, lactosylceramide (diglycosyl) has crucial functions of its own, but it is also the biosynthetic precursor of most of the non-acidic oligoglycosylceramides, and the acidic sulfatides and gangliosides, which are discussed in separate web pages for practical convenience, although the biosynthetic mechanisms and metabolism of all are inextricably linked. These lipids are amphipathic, with a variable hydrophilic carbohydrate-rich head group and a hydrophobic ceramide tail. Although usually present in low abundance, they are required for viability of cells, notably during embryogenesis and development.

title: NON-ACIDIC DI- AND OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS IN ANIMALS
section: NON-ACIDIC DI- AND OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS IN ANIMALS › 1. LACTOSYLCERAMIDE (LacCer) AND OTHER DIOSYLCERAMIDES IN ANIMALS
text: The most important and abundant diosylceramide is β-D-galactosyl-(1→4)-β-D-glucosyl-(1→1')-ceramide (Galβ1-4Glcβ1Cer), more conveniently termed lactosylceramide (LacCer), using the trivial name of the disaccharide. In the early literature, it was termed 'cytolipin H'.

title: NON-ACIDIC DI- AND OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS IN ANIMALS
section: NON-ACIDIC DI- AND OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS IN ANIMALS › 1. LACTOSYLCERAMIDE (LacCer) AND OTHER DIOSYLCERAMIDES IN ANIMALS › STRUCTURE OF LACTOSYLCERAMIDE
text: Diagram labels: Galactose (β1→4); Glucose (β1→1'); Ceramide; Lactosylceramide (Galβ1-4Glcβ1Cer; LacCer)

title: NON-ACIDIC DI- AND OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS IN ANIMALS
section: NON-ACIDIC DI- AND OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS IN ANIMALS › 1. LACTOSYLCERAMIDE (LacCer) AND OTHER DIOSYLCERAMIDES IN ANIMALS › STRUCTURE OF LACTOSYLCERAMIDE
text: In animal tissues, the precursor of LacCer is glucosylceramide, which is transported by the sphingolipid transport protein FAPP2 from the site of synthesis in the cis-Golgi to the trans-Golgi, where it must first cross from the cytosolic side of the membrane possibly via the action of a flippase. Biosynthesis of LacCer then involves addition of the second monosaccharide unit as its activated nucleotide derivative (UDP-galactose) to monoglucosylceramide on the luminal side of the Golgi apparatus in a reaction catalysed by β-1,4-galactosyltransferases (B4GALT1 and B4GALT2). The LacCer produced can be further glycosylated, or it can be transferred to the plasma membrane mainly by a non-vesicular mechanism that is poorly understood, but it cannot be translocated back to the cytosolic leaflet. Deletion of the LacCer synthase is embryonically lethal.

title: NON-ACIDIC DI- AND OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS IN ANIMALS
section: NON-ACIDIC DI- AND OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS IN ANIMALS › OTHER DIOSYLCERAMIDES (ANIMAL TISSUES)
text:
- Galabiosylceramide (Galα1→4Galβ1-1'Cer) is found in small amounts in kidney, pancreas and cerebrospinal fluid; it accumulates in Fabry's disease and is the precursor of the minor 'gala' series of oligoglycosylceramides.

- Other diosylceramides containing mannose units may be present in some primitive animals and in a few plants.

- Several insects contain mannose linked to GlcCer (βMan(1→4)Glc). A starfish contains gentiobiosyl- and cellobiosylceramide as well as LacCer; other marine invertebrates contain melibiosylceramides.

text: The deacylated (lyso) form of LacCer has been detected at low levels in brain where it may have some unspecified function.

title: NON-ACIDIC DI- AND OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS IN ANIMALS
section: NON-ACIDIC DI- AND OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS IN ANIMALS › KEY PHYSIOLOGICAL AND PATHOLOGICAL ASPECTS
text:
- Forms micro-domains on neutrophils and macrophages (recognize, engulf and eliminate pathogens).

- Interaction with growth factor receptors regulates their physiological properties.

- Activates NADPH oxidase → ROS → signalling cascades affecting proliferation, adhesion, migration and angiogenesis.

- PLA2 activation → arachidonic acid → prostaglandins and other eicosanoids.

- Disruption of pathways exacerbates cancer and cardiovascular diseases; affects neural damage states (e.g., multiple sclerosis).

- Elevated levels may contribute to cardiomyocyte dysfunction in hypoplastic left heart syndrome in infants and are a biomarker of intestinal barrier dysfunction in IBD.

title: NON-ACIDIC DI- AND OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS IN ANIMALS
section: NON-ACIDIC DI- AND OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS IN ANIMALS › FUNCTIONS OF LACTOSYLCERAMIDE
text:
Diagram labels: 1. Membrane micro-domains (rafts); Lactosylceramide; Cholesterol; Sphingomyelin; Protein; 2. Innate immunity – pattern recognition receptor; 3. Signalling and inflammation; Pro-inflammatory stimuli PDGF, VEGF, Stress, TNF-α, ox-LDL; ↑ β-1,4-Galactosyltransferase; ↑ Lactosylceramide; NADPH oxidase → ROS (oxidative stress)

Assists in stabilizing membranes and activating receptor molecules in raft micro-domains. Requires very-long chain fatty acids (e.g., 24:0, 24:1). Interacts with gangliosides (e.g., GM3).

Binds to pathogenic bacteria and fungi via carbohydrate–carbohydrate interactions (β-glucans, lipoarabinomannans). Receptor for fungal lectins (Candida, Cryptococcus sp.).

Activation of signalling pathways (proliferation, adhesion, migration, angiogenesis, prostaglandin synthesis)

title: NON-ACIDIC DI- AND OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS IN ANIMALS
section: NON-ACIDIC DI- AND OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS IN ANIMALS › Roles in health and disease
text:
- Regulates growth factor receptors.

- Participates in neutrophils (70% of GSLs) and macrophages.

- Promotes chemotaxis, phagocytosis and superoxide generation via Src family kinase (e.g., Lyn) and other enzymes.

- Dysregulation linked to cancer, cardiovascular diseases, neural damage (e.g., multiple sclerosis), atherothrombosis and other inflammatory states.

- Plasma d18:1/16:0 LacCer is a biomarker of intestinal barrier dysfunction in inflammatory bowel disease.

Diagram labels: Scottish thistle

title: NON-ACIDIC DI- AND OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS IN ANIMALS
section: NON-ACIDIC DI- AND OLIGOGLYCOSPHINGOLIPIDS IN ANIMALS › SUMMARY
text:
- LacCer is the most important diosylceramide in animals.

- Synthesised in the Golgi from GlcCer by β-1,4-galactosyltransferases.

- Central intermediate for biosynthesis of complex glycosphingolipids.

- Essential roles in membrane organization, receptor regulation, innate immunity and signalling.

- Dysregulation is linked to multiple diseases; metabolism of LacCer is a potential therapeutic target.

text:
- Inhibits DNA polymerase α

- Inhibits platelet aggregation induced by LPA (possibly by inhibiting ATX)

- High-affinity ligand for PPARγ

- Inhibits cancer cell invasion & metastasis

- Enhances cell survival & neurite extension

- Neuroprotective (against apoptosis)

- Beneficial in animal model of multiple sclerosis

- Attenuates neuropathic pain & relieves osteoarthritis

- Osmotic stress (drought, salinity)

- Pathogen attack

- Wounding / mechanical stress

section: 7. PYROPHOSPHATIDIC ACID (PPA) › D. Role as a stress signal in plants › Possible downstream effects

- Regulates stomatal closure

- Enhances stress tolerance

- May have a role in the regulation of synthesis and metabolism of phospholipids, e.g., phosphatidylserine (PS) in yeasts.

- Detected in some bacteria; function less well understood.

text:
- PPA is an unusual phospholipid with a phosphoanhydride bond.

- Formed by PA kinase; rapidly dephosphorylated to PA.

- Functions as a stress-responsive signalling lipid in plants.

- Very low levels under normal conditions.

title: LYSOPHOSPHATIDIC ACID (LPA)
section: LYSOPHOSPHATIDIC ACID (LPA) › A simple glycerophospholipid and potent lipid mediator
text: Lysophosphatidic acid (1-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphate, LPA) is one of the simplest glycerophospholipids. Although present at very low levels in tissues, it is a central regulator and pleiotropic signalling molecule that controls proliferation, survival, migration, immune modulation and tissue remodelling in health and disease.

- Acts as a growth factor–like lipid mediator via specific receptors

- Biosynthetic precursor of phosphatidic acid (PA)

- Target for therapeutic drug development

title: PHOSPHATIDIC ACID (PA)
section: PHOSPHATIDIC ACID (PA) › The central intermediate and lipid mediator
text: Phosphatidic acid (1,2-diacyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphate) is a key intermediate in the biosynthesis of glycerophospholipids and triacylglycerols, and a precursor of signalling molecules. Although present at low levels in cells (often < picomolar), it modulates membrane dynamics, protein functions and many signalling and cellular processes.

title: PHOSPHATIDIC ACID (PA)
text:
- Simplest diacyl-glycerophospholipid with a phosphomonoester head group (anionic lipid, net −1 charge at physiological pH).

- Not an abundant lipid but essential as a biosynthetic intermediate and potent lipid mediator.

Diagram labels: Endoplasmic reticulum; Mitochondrial outer membrane; LPLAT1; LPLAT2; LPLAT3; LPLAT4; LPLAT5

Key points

- LPLAT1: prefers 14:0-, 16:0-, 18:2-CoAs

- LPLAT2: prefers 20:4-CoA

- LPLAT3: yields 22:6(n-3)-containing PA (retina, testes)

- LPLAT4 & 5: prefer 18:1-CoA & PUFA-CoAs; roles in synthesis & remodelling (Lands' cycle)

Biosynthesis occurs in both ER and mitochondria. Traffic of PA between organelles enables remodelling and synthesis of other lipids.

- Signalling lipid: Precursor of lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) and other mediators

title: 4. CATABOLISM OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC)
text: Phosphatidylcholine in membranes is degraded by phospholipases that act at different bonds of the molecule. The products are recycled for re-synthesis, used in signalling pathways, or serve as precursors for other metabolites. Most of the released choline is returned to the liver (CDP-choline cycle) for reuse in PC biosynthesis.

- Donor of methyl groups for S-adenosylmethionine

- Precursor of acetylcholine in nervous tissues

section: 4. CATABOLISM OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) › Recycling and transport
text: Diagram labels: Lysosomes; Spns1 transporter; Cytosol; LPC + LPE; Re-acylation (LPCATs); Plasma HDL (PC uptake); Liver (main site); Diacylglycerol + Triacylglycerol synthesis; Excretion in bile (PC loss)

title: 4. CATABOLISM OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC)
text:
- DAG → activates PKC and other kinases

- Phosphatidic acid (PA) → mTOR, cell growth

- Lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) → inflammatory and other pathways

title: 4. CATABOLISM OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC)
text:
- Non-specific phospholipase Cs (NPCs): 6 isoforms in Arabidopsis.

- Broad substrate specificity → generate diacylglycerols from many phospholipids.

- NPC4s hydrolyse glycosylinositol phosphorylceramide and galactosyldiacylglycerols.

- Phospholipase D (PLD) is especially important in plant signalling.

Diagram labels: PC; NPCs/PLD; DAG + PCo; signalling

title: 4. CATABOLISM OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC)
section: 4. CATABOLISM OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) › Yeasts and fungi
text:
- Kennedy pathway + remodelling enzymes (Gpc1, Ale1, etc.).

- Remodelling changes fatty acid composition.

- Important for growth and survival.

title: 4. CATABOLISM OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC)
text: Some Gram-positive bacteria possess PLD and NPC-like PLCs that catabolize PC.

title: 4. CATABOLISM OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC)
section: 4. CATABOLISM OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) › Major phospholipases acting on PC in animals
text:
- Enzyme family (no. isoform families): PLA2 (≥15); Bond cleaved: sn-2 ester; Main products: LPC + free fatty acid; Roles: Lipid remodelling, eicosanoid precursors, signalling

- Enzyme family (no. isoform families): PLC (6); Bond cleaved: Phosphodiester; Main products: DAG + phosphocholine; Roles: Signalling (PKC activation)

- Enzyme family (no. isoform families): PLD (3); Bond cleaved: Phosphodiester; Main products: PA + choline; Roles: Signalling (mTOR, growth)

- Enzyme family (no. isoform families): PLB (2); Bond cleaved: Both ester bonds; Main products: Glycerophosphocholine + fatty acids; Roles: Complete degradation

title: 4. CATABOLISM OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC)
text:
- PC is rapidly hydrolysed by phospholipases A2, C, D and B.

- The products are recycled for resynthesis or act in signalling.

- Choline is reused (CDP-choline cycle) or converted to betaine or acetylcholine.

- PC from plasma lipoproteins is taken up by the liver and converted to triacylglycerols.

- In plants and microbes, non-specific PLCs and PLDs generate DAGs for membrane dynamics and stress responses.

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
text: Diagram labels: sn-1; sn-2

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
text:
- Trace in most tissues; high in plasma (150–500 µM).

- Hepatocytes secrete LPC bound to albumin.

- Formed by LCAT: transfers sn-2 fatty acid from PC to cholesterol → cholesterol esters + LPC.

- Also from endothelial lipase action on PC in HDL.

- Produced in tissues by phospholipase A2 (PLA2) as part of the de-acylation/re-acylation (Lands) cycle.

- In intestines: from dietary & biliary PC → absorbed as LPC and re-esterified before export in chylomicrons.

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
text: Diagram labels: LCAT reaction; PC; Cholesterol; LCAT; LPC; Cholesterol ester

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
text:
- High concentrations → detergent properties; can disrupt membranes.

- Low concentrations → readily inserts into bilayers and alters membrane curvature and protein function indirectly.

- In plasma, bound to albumin/lipoproteins → reduced free concentration.

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
text:
- Component of oxidized LDL in plasma and atherosclerotic lesions (generated by overexpression or enhanced PLA2 activity).

- Elevated in joint fluids of rheumatoid arthritis patients.

- Major component of platelet-derived microvesicles: activates platelet receptor → vascular inflammation and plaque instability.

- Blocks early hemifusion intermediates in cell-cell fusion, enhances parasite invasion, inhibits nitric oxide production (e.g., in Chagas disease).

- High levels in cervical cancer (potential diagnostic marker).

- Reduced in some malignancies; protective during chemotherapy.

- Stearoyl-LPC is anti-inflammatory and protective against lethal sepsis in experimental animals.

- Precursor of lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) via autotaxin in plasma; some effects attributed to LPA.

- Biomarker: elevated 26:0-LPC in Zellweger spectrum disorders (e.g., X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy).

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
text: - Maternal PC → sn-2-LPC at placenta (via endothelial lipase) facilitates transfer of PUFAs to fetus.

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
text:
Possible receptors

GPCRs: GPR119, GPR40, GPR55, G2A (GPR132)

Also: TLRs (Toll-like receptors)

Ion channels: TRPV4, others

- Activates PLC → DAG + IP3 → ↑ intracellular Ca2+ → activates PKC.

- By binding to GPR119 → regulates glucose-dependent insulin secretion.

- Stimulates MAPK in certain cells; promotes demyelination in the nervous system.

- Through TRPV4 in keratinocytes → persistent itching and chronic pain; 18:0-LPC elevated in burn pain.

- Peroxisomal PLA2γ generates 2-arachidonoyl-LPC → relevant to eicosanoid generation; enriched in carotid atheroma of type 2 diabetic patients.

- Induces COX-2 in vascular endothelial cells.

- Enhances macrophage phagocytosis in the presence of T lymphocytes (beneficial for innate immunity).

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
text:
- LPC levels are tightly regulated.

- Enzymes (cytosolic serine hydrolases): – LYPLA1 (lysophospholipase A1): removes sn-1 acyl chain. – LYPLA2 (lysophospholipase A2): removes sn-2 acyl chain.

- Alkaline sphingomyelinase removes phosphocholine → 2-monoacylglycerol (inert).

Diagram labels: Lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC); H2O; LYPLA1; H2O; LYPLA2; Glycerophosphocholine (GPC); 2-Monoacylglycerol

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
text:
- Enters Lands’ cycle (re-acylation) → LPC → PC.

- Further degradation → free choline + glycerol phosphate.

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
section: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC) › Physiological roles of LPC in digestion
text:
- Derived from hydrolysis of dietary/biliary PC.

- Absorbed and re-esterified before chylomicron secretion.

- Aids intestinal lipid handling and absorption.

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
text:
- Anti-cancer ether analogues (alkyl-LPCs) induce apoptosis; used in experimental therapy and anti-parasitic treatments.

- Some beneficial effects reported, but interpretation depends on adequate carrier protein levels in studies.

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
section: 7. OTHER PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE ANALOGUES ANDMETABOLITES › A. Phosphatidylsulfocholine (PSC)
text:
- Sulfonium analogue of PC: two methyl groups on sulfur instead of three on nitrogen.

- Discovered in the diatom Nitzschia alba; replaces PC completely as the major phospholipid.

- Now found in some other marine diatoms and algae.

- Isotopic studies: both methyl groups and sulfur derived from methionine.

- Related lipid: phosphatidyl-S,S-dimethylpropanethiol reported from several algae.

Diagram labels: Phosphatidylsulfocholine (PSC); Diatom; Nitzschia alba

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
section: 7. OTHER PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE ANALOGUES ANDMETABOLITES › B. Alkylphosphocholines / alkylphosphoethanolamines
text:
Example: 1-alkyl-2-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (alkylphosphocholine)

- Saturated/monoenoic ethers (C15–C25) accumulate in Sjögren-Larsson syndrome (deficiency of fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase).

- Proposed origin: from fatty alcohols via sphingomyelin synthases.

- Serve as diagnostic biomarkers.

- Synthetic ether analogues show strong anti-cancer activity (trigger apoptosis) and treat parasitic infections (e.g., leishmaniasis).

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
section: 7. OTHER PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE ANALOGUES ANDMETABOLITES › C. Phosphatidylarsenocholine (minor in marine organisms)
text:
- Minor component of lipids of several marine organisms.

- Discussed in the web page on arsenolipids.

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
section: 7. OTHER PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE ANALOGUES ANDMETABOLITES › D. Other important metabolites derived from PC
text: Diagram labels: Diacylglycerol (DAG); Phosphatidic acid (PA); Platelet-activating factor (PAF); Phosphatidylserine (PS); Signalling (PKC activation, etc.); Key signalling lipid; precursor of many lipids; Potent inflammatory mediator; platelet activation; Anionic phospholipid; role in cell signalling and apoptosis

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
section: 7. OTHER PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE ANALOGUES ANDMETABOLITES › Biomarkers and disease
text:
- Changes in PC or LPC species in plasma/tissues reported in liver, cardiovascular, kidney, lung, brain diseases, cancer, sepsis and diabetes.

- Altered PC biosynthesis linked to NAFLD, liver failure, poor regeneration.

- Imbalance of PC/PE ratio affects insulin sensitivity and glucose homeostasis.

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
section: 7. OTHER PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE ANALOGUES ANDMETABOLITES › Newborn screening
text: - Elevated 26:0-LPC in dried blood spots identifies Zellweger spectrum disorders (e.g., X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy) early and can prevent disease onset.

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
section: 7. OTHER PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE ANALOGUES ANDMETABOLITES › Neuro- and cognitive roles
text:
- Glycerophosphocholine (GPC) in kidney has osmoprotective properties.

- Available as a pharmaceutical in some countries.

- Claimed benefits: cognitive dysfunction, cardiometabolic disorders, anti-aging.

title: 6. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (LPC)
section: 7. OTHER PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE ANALOGUES ANDMETABOLITES › Key message
text: Lysophosphatidylcholine is a bioactive lipid with multiple sources and diverse functions. Its levels are tightly controlled, and both excess and deficiency can have important physiological and pathological consequences.

title: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE
section: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE › (untitled panel)
text:
The fatty acid and molecular species compositions of phosphatidylcholine (PC) in animal tissues are determined post-synthesis by the Lands’ cycle – orchestrated hydrolysis, acyl-CoA synthesis and re-acylation (or transacylation) reactions. Similar cycles operate with all glycerophospholipid classes and generate the selective compositions required for vital functions and health.

Diagram labels: Phosphatidylcholine (PC); sn-1; sn-2; sn-3

title: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE
section: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE › Key points
text:
- Remodelling (Lands’ cycle) determines fatty acid position and molecular species composition.

- Most active in nervous and immune systems.

- Dysregulation is linked to cancer, hepatotoxicity and other diseases.

- Intermediates (e.g., lysophospholipids) are bioactive signalling molecules.

title: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE
section: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE › 1 De-acylation by phospholipase A2 (PLA2)
text:
Hydrolyses the sn-2 ester bond specifically.

- ≥15 PLA2 families (Ca2+-dependent or independent; secreted or intracellular).

- Generates free fatty acid (FFA) and LPC.

- Products used in metabolism and signalling.

Diagram labels: Phosphatidylcholine (PC); Lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC); PLA2; H2O; Free fatty acid

title: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE
section: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE › B. LANDS’ CYCLE – MAIN MECHANISM IN ANIMALS (part 2: re-acylation)
text: Diagram labels: Lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC); Acyl-CoA; LPCAT; CoA-SH; Phosphatidylcholine (PC, remodelling product)

title: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE
section: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE › Major LPCATs involved in PC remodelling in animals
text:
- Enzyme (alias): LPCAT1 (LPLAT7); Primary location: ER, PM, mitochondria; Main features / fatty acid preference: Prefers stearate > palmitate at sn-1 position.

- Enzyme (alias): LPCAT3 (LPLAT12 or MBOAT5); Primary location: ER, PM, mitochondria; Main features / fatty acid preference: Prefers linoleoyl (18:2) and arachidonoyl (20:4) in sn-2. Maintains lipid homeostasis; intestine absorption, lipoprotein secretion, lipogenesis.

- Enzyme (alias): LPCAT2 (LPLAT9); Primary location: ER, PM; Main features / fatty acid preference: Uses 1-acyl and 1-alkyl LPC; enriched in inflammatory cells (macrophages, neutrophils); contributes to oxylipin precursor generation.

- Enzyme (alias): LPCAT4 (LPLAT10); Primary location: ER; Main features / fatty acid preference: Prefers insertion of unsaturated fatty acids at sn-1 (atypical LPCAT).

title: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE
section: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE › Major LPCATs involved in PC remodelling in animals
text: - Enzyme (alias): LPCAT1 (LPLAT8); Primary location: Lung (ER); Main features / fatty acid preference: High specificity for palmitoyl-CoA; generates dipalmitoyl PC of lung surfactant.

title: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE
section: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE › Additional aspects
text:
- PC species rich in PUFA are maintained more by de novo synthesis than by remodelling.

- Over-expression of LPCAT genes is associated with cancer and other pathologies.

Cell types: Macrophage; Neutrophil

Lysophospholipid intermediates (e.g., LPC) and free fatty acids are bioactive signalling molecules.

title: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE
section: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE › 1. Transacylation between phospholipids

section: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE › 2. Transfer of acyl chains between phospholipid classes

title: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE
section: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE › (untitled panel)
text: PLA2 group IVD (PLA2G4D) catalyses transacylase reactions using phospholipids and acylglycerols as substrates to transfer fatty acids between phospholipids and from phospholipids to acylglycerols.

title: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE
section: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE › Plants
text:
- PC is central to glycerolipid metabolism.

- Major entry point for acyl groups exported from plastid to ER.

- Supplies fatty acids for TAG synthesis in developing seeds.

- Provides DAGs for thylakoid lipids (e.g., galactosyldiacylglycerol).

- In Arabidopsis, LPCAT1 and LPCAT2 remodel, preferring sn-2 with plastid-exported fatty acids.

- Strong preference for C18-unsaturated acyl chains over 16:0 in many plants.

- Remodelling responds to abiotic stresses.

Diagram labels: Plastid; Acyl export; ER; PC; TAG (synthesis); Thylakoid lipids (DAG precursors)

title: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE
section: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE › Yeasts (e.g., Saccharomyces cerevisiae)
text:
- PC synthesized via Kennedy pathway.

- Remodelling pathway in microsomal membranes:

Diagram labels: PC; Phospholipase B (A1 + A2 activity); Glycerophosphocholine (GPC); Gpc1 (acyltransferase) + Acyl-CoA; Lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC); Ale1 (LPC acyltransferase) + Acyl-CoA; PC (remodelled species)

title: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE
section: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE › Functions / significance
text:
- Alters molecular composition without total synthesis.

- Regulated with other lipid pathways; affects growth.

- Gpc1 is specific for PC in yeasts (does not act on other phospholipids).

title: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE
section: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE › Biological roles of PC remodelling
text:
Nervous system

- Maintains membrane fluidity and curvature.

- Supplies PUFA for synaptic signalling.

Immune system

- Generates oxylipin precursors.

- Modulates inflammatory responses.

Liver and metabolism

- Regulates lipid absorption, lipoprotein secretion and de novo lipogenesis.

Membrane integrity

- Maintains optimal acyl composition.

- Supports protein function and trafficking.

title: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE
section: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE › Pathological consequences of dysregulation
text:
- Cancer progression and metastasis

- Hepatotoxicity and fatty liver

- Neurodegenerative diseases

- Inflammatory disorders

- Metabolic syndrome

title: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE
section: 3. REMODELLING OF PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE – THE LANDS’ CYCLE › Summary
text: A balance of de novo synthesis and the Lands’ cycle ensures the precise molecular architecture of PC in each tissue – essential for membrane structure, signalling and overall cellular homeostasis.

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS
section: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS › A. CHOLINE METABOLISM AND UPTAKE
text:
Dietary sources

- Animal-based foods

- Cruciferous vegetables

- Soybeans

- Degradation of choline-containing lipids

Functions of choline

- Phospholipid (PC) synthesis

- Acetylcholine (neurotransmitter)

- Methyl group donor (via betaine)

- High demand in pregnancy

Diagram labels: Choline; FLVCR1/2 Transporters

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS
text: Diagram labels: Choline; ATP; ADP; Phosphocholine

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS
text:
Diagram labels: Phosphocholine; CTP; PPi; CDP-choline; Cytidine

- Two isoforms: CCTα (nucleoplasm → cytoplasm) and CCTβ (cytoplasm).

- Activated by reversible binding to ER or nuclear membranes.

- Rate-limiting step; feedback-regulated by PC levels.

- ChoKα also has regulatory functions.

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS
section: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS › 3 CDP-choline:1,2-diacylglycerol choline/ethanolamine-phosphotransferase (CEPT1) – ER and nuclei
text:
Diagram labels: Cytidine; sn-1,2-Diacylglycerol (DAG); Phosphatidylcholine (PC)

- CEPT1: major enzyme in ER (dimer; 10 transmembrane segments per protomer); interior hydrophobic chamber binds acyl chains).

- Related CPT1 in trans-Golgi prefers 1-alkyl diacylglycerols → PC species with ether linkages.

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS
text: The Kennedy pathway is distinct from the CDP-diacylglycerol pathway used for PG, PI and cardiolipin.

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS
text: The Kennedy pathway was discovered serendipitously when ATP preparations contained CTP as an impurity. Kennedy and co-workers showed the impurity was essential for PC formation.

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS
section: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS › Source of sn-1,2-diacylglycerol (DAG) precursor
text:
(Required also for PE, PS and TAG)

Diagram labels: Phosphatidic acid (PA); Phosphatidic acid phosphatase (lipin / PAP); Pi; 1,2-Diacylglycerol (DAG)

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS
text:
Yeast: PAP1 (Mg2+-dependent), PAP2 (Mg2+-independent)

Mammals: Lipin-1, -2, -3 (Lipin-1 is most important)

- Lipin-1α (nucleus)

- Lipin-1β (cytoplasm)

- Lipin-1γ (brain)

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS
section: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS › C. N-METHYLTRANSFERASE PATHWAY (Sequential methylation of PE)
text: Diagram labels: Phosphatidylethanolamine (PE); PE N-methyltransferase (PEMT, SAM-dependent); SAM; SAH; Monomethyl-phosphatidylethanolamine (MMPE); PE N-methyltransferase (SAM-dependent); SAM; SAH; Dimethyl-phosphatidylethanolamine (DMPE); PE N-methyltransferase (SAM-dependent); SAM → SAH; Phosphatidylcholine (PC)

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS
text:
- Single enzyme (~20 kDa) in two isoforms in hepatocytes: PEMT1 (ER, major) and PEMT2 (mitochondria).

- Major pathway in liver when dietary choline is low.

- Important in yeast and many bacteria.

- Uses S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) as methyl donor.

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS
section: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS › D. CDP-DIACYLGLYCEROL PATHWAY (in some bacteria)
text: Diagram labels: Phosphatidic acid (PA); CTP; CDP-diacylglycerol; Cytidine; Phosphocholine; Phosphatidylcholine (PC)

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS
text: Utilized by several Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria; analogous to pathway for PG, PI and cardiolipin.

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS
section: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS › E. REMODELLING OF MOLECULAR SPECIES (LANDS’ CYCLE)
text: Diagram labels: PC (diacyl form); Phospholipase A2 (specific for sn-2); H2O; Lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC); Lysophosphatidylcholine acyltransferase (LPCAT) (acyl-CoA); PC (new acyl in sn-2)

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS
text:
- Maintains fatty acid composition and membrane properties.

- Multiple LPCAT isoforms with different acyl-CoA specificities and tissue distributions.

- Also participates in incorporation of polyunsaturated fatty acids into PC.

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS
section: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS › F. REGULATION AND TRANSPORT
text:
- CCTα is the key regulatory point (feedback inhibited by PC).

- Lipins are regulated by phosphorylation and interact with membranes dynamically.

- PC is transported from ER to other membranes by vesicular and non-vesicular (lipid transfer proteins) routes.

Diagram labels: ER; PC; Golgi; Plasma membrane

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – BIOSYNTHESIS
text:
- Two major routes in eukaryotes: Kennedy (primary) and N-methyltransferase.

- CDP-diacylglycerol pathway in certain bacteria.

- DAG precursor from PA via lipin phosphatases.

- Remodelling (Lands’ cycle) finalizes PC molecular species.

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
text: Phosphatidylcholine is the most abundant phospholipid in animals and plants and a key structural component of membranes and lipoproteins. It also serves as a precursor of many bioactive lipids and is essential for numerous physiological processes.

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
section: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES › A. STRUCTURAL ROLES IN MEMBRANES
text:
Bilayer formation

- Cylindrical shape → forms stable bilayers.

- Makes up 80–90% of the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane of nucleated cells.

- Unsaturated acyl chains (kinked) confer fluidity.

Diagram labels: Outer leaflet (PC-rich); Inner leaflet (PE, PS-rich)

Specialized roles

- Does not induce curvature but can be metabolically converted to lipids that do.

- Microdomain (raft) organization is influenced by PC.

Lung surfactant

- Dipalmitoyl-PC (DPPC) is the main surface-active component in humans.

- Lowers surface tension during inspiration and prevents alveolar collapse at expiration.

Diagram labels: Alveolar air; Alveolar lining fluid

Nuclear membranes

- Internal nuclear membranes are enriched in disaturated PC.

- Synthesised entirely in nucleus and composition is resistant to dietary manipulation.

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
section: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES › A. STRUCTURAL ROLES IN MEMBRANES
text:
- May stabilize/regulate chromatin structure and provide DAG for signalling.

Diagram labels: Nucleus

Unique molecular species

- 1-Oleoyl-2-palmitoyl-PC: at tips of neuronal protrusions.

- 1-Palmitoyl-2-arachidonoyl-PC: required for cell cycle progression and proliferation.

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
section: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES › B. INTERACTIONS WITH PROTEINS
text:
- PC is bound non-covalently in many membrane protein structures (e.g., cytochrome c oxidase, yeast cytochrome bc1).

- Both headgroup and acyl chains can participate in binding.

- 3-Hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase requires PC binding for optimal activity.

- ADP/ATP carrier has two PC binding sites (one on each side).

Diagram labels: Cytochrome c oxidase; Cytochrome bc1 (yeast); ADP/ATP carrier (two PC sites)

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
section: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES › Lipoprotein assembly and secretion
text:
- PC (especially with PUFA in sn-2) is indispensable for assembly and secretion of VLDL and chylomicrons in liver and intestine.

- Stabilizes surface of lipid droplets.

- Inhibits endocytosis when abundant in outer membrane.

Diagram labels: VLDL

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
section: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES › Bile and lipid digestion
text:
- PC is secreted into bile with bile acids.

- Emulsifies dietary TAGs in intestinal lumen.

- After hydrolysis to LPC, it is absorbed and contributes to chylomicron formation.

- PC in mucus layer protects intestinal surface from gut microbiota.

Diagram labels: Bile (PC + bile acids)

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
section: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES › Lipid droplet metabolism
text: - PC is required to stabilize lipid droplets that store triacylglycerols.

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
section: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES › Signalling functions
text:
- PLD → phosphatidic acid (PA): regulates PI4P 5-kinase → PIP2 (second messenger).

- PLC → diacylglycerols (DAGs): act in signal transduction.

- Plasmenyl PC can release arachidonic acid (PLA2) for eicosanoid synthesis.

Diagram labels: PC; PLC; PLD; PLA2; DAG; PA; Arachidonic acid; Signalling

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
section: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES › Biosynthetic precursor
text:
PC is the precursor of many important lipids.

- Sphingomyelin

- Phosphatidic acid

- Lysophosphatidylcholine

- Platelet-activating factor (PAF)

- Phosphatidylserine

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
section: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES › Other physiological roles
text:
- PC in plasma strongly influences levels of all lipoprotein classes.

- Necessary for proper function of mitochondria and many enzymes.

- Contributes to membrane integrity, fluidity and protein function.

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
section: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES › Disease relevance
text:
- Altered PC levels or species are biomarkers for liver, cardiovascular, kidney, lung, brain diseases, cancer, sepsis and diabetes.

- Impaired PC biosynthesis in liver is linked to NAFLD, liver failure and poor regeneration.

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
section: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES › Role in cancer
text:
- PC, DAG and LPC promote tumour growth by enhancing membrane biogenesis, activating signalling, suppressing apoptosis and aiding immune evasion.

- ChoK and LPCAT3 are potential therapeutic targets.

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
section: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES › Plasma and lipoproteins
text:
Major phospholipid in all lipoproteins; highest in HDL.

Diagram labels: HDL

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
text:
- Both Kennedy and methylation pathways are required for normal lipoprotein secretion.

- Some PC → TAGs via DAG intermediates.

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
text: Choline can be oxidized to betaine in kidney.

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
section: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES › Nervous tissue
text: Essential for membrane function, synaptic signalling and myelin.

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
text: PC is almost exclusively in outer leaflet.

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
text:
- Structural role in membranes.

- PC level at shoot apex correlates with flowering time; may bind to Flowering Locus T (FT).

- NPCs (non-specific PLCs) hydrolyse PC to DAG – important under phosphate deprivation.

- PC-Derived PA (via PLD) is a key signalling lipid.

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
text:
- PC is present in ~10% of bacterial species.

- Crucial for symbiotic and pathogenic microbe–host interactions.

- Required for full virulence in pathogens (e.g., Brucella abortus, Legionella pneumophila, Agrobacterium tumefaciens).

- Important for beneficial symbiosis (e.g., Bradyrhizobium japonicum forms root nodules).

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
section: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES › F. KEY POINTS
text:
- PC is the most abundant phospholipid in animals and plants.

- Forms bilayers and is crucial for membrane structure and function.

- Essential for lipoprotein metabolism, lipid droplet stability and bile secretion.

- Acts in signalling and is a precursor of many bioactive lipids.

- Alterations in PC metabolism are linked to many diseases and cancers.

- Important in plant stress responses and microbe–host interactions.

title: 5. PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – FUNCTIONS IN TISSUES
text: Phosphatidylcholine is a fundamental lipid in all living systems. It provides structural stability to membranes, enables specialised functions in surfactant and nuclei, participates in lipid transport and metabolism, acts in signalling, and serves as a precursor of bioactive lipids. Its metabolism is tightly linked to health and disease.

title: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE (PC) – STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE
text: Phosphatidylcholine or 1,2-diacyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine is a neutral (zwitterionic) phospholipid over a wide pH range. It is usually the most abundant glycerophospholipid in animals and plants, often ~50% of total phospholipids. In nucleated cells it is concentrated (80–90%) in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane and is the major phospholipid in plasma lipoproteins (especially HDL).

text:
- Abundant in animals and plants (~50% of phospholipids).

- Key structural lipid of membranes; major in plasma lipoproteins.

- Less common in bacteria (~10% of species); absent in E. coli and B. subtilis.

- Functions partially overlap with sphingomyelin, but PC has many unique roles.

- Lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC): one fatty acyl chain.

- Platelet-activating factor (PAF): ether analogue with potent bioactivity.

- Lysophosphatidylcholine and related lipids have signalling and other biological roles (see below).

- Found in trace amounts in animal tissues.

- Most abundant in plasma (10–50 µM, ~1% of total serum phospholipids).

- Formed mainly by hydrolysis of phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) by phospholipase A2 (PLA2).

title: 4. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE (LPE)
section: 4. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE (LPE) › Neuronal and bone cell functions
text:
- Involved in differentiation and migration.

- Oleoyl-LPE in brain stimulates neurite outgrowth and protects against glutamate toxicity.

- Greatly reduced levels of 22:6-LPE observed in Alzheimer’s disease brains (post-mortem).

- May act as an agonist for the LPA receptor LPAR1 (G-protein–coupled receptor).

title: 4. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE (LPE)
text:
- Administration of LPE to aging rats improves diastolic dysfunction.

- Alleviates mitochondrial injury.

title: 4. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE (LPE)

- Alkenyl (18:1) LPE acts as a signalling molecule.

- Induced by inflammatory stimuli; transcriptional regulation of nuclear receptor RORγt (retinoic-related orphan receptor gamma).

text:
- Reported to influence proliferation, migration and invasion of various cancer cells.

title: 4. LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE (LPE)

- Influences cell proliferation, survival and motility.

- May act via LPA receptor LPAR1.

Lysophosphatidylethanolamine inhibits phospholipase D (PLD), a key enzyme in the early stages of plant senescence.

- Extends shelf-life of fruit and vase life of cut flowers.

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
text: Phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) is a major membrane phospholipid with unique physical properties and diverse biological functions. It plays essential roles in membrane organization, protein interactions, organelle function, lipid metabolism and cellular homeostasis.

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
section: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION › 1. Structure and shape
text:
PE has a small head group (phosphoethanolamine) → cone shape

Diagram labels: Choline (PC); Ethanolamine (PE)

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
text:
- Does not form bilayers by itself; favors inverted hexagonal (HII) phases.

- In bilayers, PE exerts lateral pressure that promotes curvature.

- Stabilizes membrane proteins in their optimal conformations.

- Forms hydrogen bonds: – To adjacent lipid acyl chains – To proteins via head group (phosphate interacts with Lys, Arg or Tyr side chains)

Diagram labels: Cone shape → negative curvature; Inverted hexagonal (HII) phase

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
text:
- Enriched in the inner leaflet of plasma membrane (with PS).

- Present in both leaflets of mitochondrial membranes; highly enriched in inner mitochondrial membrane.

Diagram labels: Plasma membrane; Outer leaflet (PC, SM); Inner leaflet (PE, PS, PI); Mitochondrial membranes; Outer membrane (PE present); Inner membrane (high PE); PC; PE; PS; PI; SM; Cholesterol; Hydrogen bond; Electrostatic interaction

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
section: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION › 1. Positive-inside rule and charge balance
text:
- Positively charged residues are more abundant on cytosolic side of membrane proteins.

- PE helps balance charge density at the cytosolic surface.

- PE can inhibit location of negative residues on cytosolic side, but can allow them when required for function.

Diagram labels: Outer (non-cytosolic) side; Cytosolic (inner) side

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
section: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION › 2. Protein binding to PE
text: Diagram labels: Lys (NH3+); Arg (NH2+); Tyr (OH); Hydrogen bond; Electrostatic interaction

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
section: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION › 3. Specific protein targets and roles
text:
Mitochondrial proteins Essential for oxidative phosphorylation (e.g., cytochrome bc1 complex, complex III). PE binds a conserved site in the bc1 complex subunit.

PE-binding proteins (PEBPs) Superfamily (>400 members from bacteria to humans) Functions: lipid binding, neuronal development, serine protease inhibition, signalling regulation. PEBP4 is highly expressed in many cancers → increases therapy resistance. BLTP2 (Vps13-like) transport protein also implicated in cancer resistance.

Ca2+-ATPase One PE molecule binds in cavity between two transmembrane helices → acts as a wedge. Displaced when Ca2+ binds.

Other PE-binding proteins Rhodopsin, aquaporins, Annexin V (binds PE when translocated to outer leaflet and can inhibit blood coagulation by competing with PS).

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
text:
- PE content is high in nascent VLDL and in apo B-containing particles in the Golgi lumen.

- Participates in VLDL assembly and/or secretion.

- Rapidly and efficiently removed from circulating VLDL.

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
section: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION › 2. Lipid droplet dynamics
text:
- PE promotes coalescence of small lipid droplets into larger ones.

- PE synthesis increases in brown adipocytes (and liver) during cold exposure.

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
section: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION › 3. Membrane fusion and fission
text:
- PE promotes negative membrane curvature.

- Facilitates membrane fusion, vesicle trafficking, and fission events.

- Important in exocytosis and endocytosis.

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
section: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION › 4. Membrane contact sites (ER–mitochondria)
text:

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
text:
- PE is the primary lipid factor required in brain for propagation and infectivity of mammalian prions.

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION

- PE enriched in bacterial inner (cytoplasmic) leaflet.

- Contributes to antimicrobial activity.

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
text:
- PE is essential for the expansion and closure of autophagosome membranes.

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
section: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION › 4. Membrane fluidity and rigidity
text: - Like cholesterol, PE increases membrane rigidity in eukaryotic cells (e.g., insects) to maintain optimal fluidity.

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
section: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION › 5. Stress and disease
text:
- PE composition and distribution change in stress, ischemia, and many diseases.

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
section: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION › E. SUMMARY OF KEY FUNCTIONS
text: Diagram labels: PE; Structural role: Major component of membranes; regulates curvature and fluidity; Organelle function: Critical for mitochondria, autophagy, and ER–mitochondria contact site integrity; Protein interactions: Binds many proteins; essential for mitochondrial protein function; Cell signalling: Modulates Ca2+ signalling, membrane proteins, and signal transduction; Lipid metabolism: Required for VLDL assembly, lipid droplet dynamics, and membrane trafficking; Host defence & disease: Important in antimicrobial activity, prion propagation, and disease responses

title: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION
section: 3. PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE – BIOLOGICAL FUNCTION › Key take-home messages
text:
- PE has unique physical properties that influence membrane structure and protein function.

- It is indispensable for mitochondrial efficiency and membrane trafficking.

- It interacts with a wide range of proteins, including PE-binding proteins with roles in health and disease.

- It is crucial for lipid metabolism, autophagy, immunity, and cellular homeostasis.

- Alterations in PE metabolism and distribution are linked to many human diseases.

title: PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE (PE) – BIOSYNTHESIS
text:
- Two major pathways: CDP-ethanolamine (de novo) in ER/Golgi and PS decarboxylation in mitochondria.

- PE is synthesized in different cellular locations and released to distinct membrane pools.

- Pathways produce PE with different fatty acid patterns (ER pathway: mainly mono/di-unsaturated; PSD pathway: PUFA at sn-2).

- Remodelling by the Lands’ cycle fine-tunes molecular species.

- All routes are tightly regulated; disturbances cause serious developmental and metabolic consequences.

title: PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE (PE)
text: Phosphatidylethanolamine or 1,2-diacyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine (once given the trivial name ‘cephalin’) is usually the second most abundant phospholipid in animals and plants after phosphatidylcholine, and it is often the main lipid component of microbial membranes. It can amount to 20% of liver phospholipids and as much as 45% of those of brain; higher proportions are found in mitochondria than in other organelles. As such, it is obviously a key building block of membrane bilayers, where it is present exclusively in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane in animal cells. It is a neutral or zwitterionic phospholipid (at least in the pH range 2 to 7).

title: PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE (PE)
text:
- Phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) is a major phospholipid in all domains of life.

- It is especially abundant in mitochondria and the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (in animals).

- PE species are diverse: diacyl, alkylacyl, and alkenylacyl (plasmalogen).

- Fatty acid distribution is conserved: saturated at sn-1; polyunsaturated (especially 20:4, 22:6) at sn-2.

- PE is essential for membrane structure, function, and as a precursor for lipid metabolism and signalling.

- Essential for cell growth, signalling and survival

title: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
section: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP) › C. OCCURRENCE
text:
- Ubiquitous in animal tissues (~1–2% of total phospholipids).

- Highly enriched in lysosomal membranes: 15–70% of lysosomal phospholipids depending on tissue/cell type (e.g., ~11% of total in macrophage/microglial cell lines).

- Trace levels in plasma: ~40% in lipoprotein fractions and ~60% in lipoprotein-deficient compartment.

- Not found in plants.

- Reported in some bacteria (e.g., Agrobacterium tumefaciens, some alkalophilic Bacillus sp.), but stereochemistry uncertain.

title: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
section: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP) › Key message
text: Bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate (BMP) is a unique animal phospholipid with distinctive stereochemistry and fatty acid compositions, highly enriched in lysosomal and late endosomal membranes. It promotes membrane curvature, vesicle formation and enzyme function, and may serve as a signalling lipid when hydrolysed to LPA.

title: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
section: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP) › B. PHYSICAL AND CHEMICAL PROPERTIES
text:
Molecular shape and membrane behaviour

- Cone-shaped molecule with a small hydrated, negatively charged head group.

- Strongly non-bilayer forming → promotes membrane curvature, fusion and inward budding (invagination).

- Enriched in late endosomes and lysosomes → aids formation of intraluminal vesicles and multi-vesicular bodies.

Diagram labels: Bilayer membrane; + BMP; Inward budding / vesicle formation

title: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
section: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP) › Enzymatic stability
text:
- Unique stereochemistry → resistant to most phospholipases.

- Protects lysosomal membranes from self-digestion.

- Fatty acyl chains can turn over by transacylation, but glycerophosphate backbone is stable.

- Putative catabolism under acidic conditions via PLA2-like enzymes (identity and regulation not fully established).

- Stereochemistry may help evade immunorecognition by antibodies.

title: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
section: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP) › Parameters favouring BMP function in lysosomes
text:
- Acidic pH (4.6–5.0)

- High content of unsaturated long-chain fatty acids

- Association with positively charged lysosomal proteins (hydrolases, coactivators, etc.)

Together these factors promote membrane dynamics, enzyme function and vesicle formation in the endo-lysosomal system.

title: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
section: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP) › Comparative stability
text:
- S,S-(2,2′-diacyl)-BMP is more tightly packed but less thermodynamically stable than S,S-(3,3′-diacyl)-BMP.

- 3,3′-BMP is more rapidly degraded by lipases than 2,2′-BMP.

title: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
section: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP) › Functions (established and proposed)
text:
- Structural lipid of lysosomal and late endosomal membranes.

- Essential for development of intraluminal vesicles and multi-vesicular bodies.

- Modulates activity and localization of lysosomal enzymes.

- Involved in lipid trafficking, membrane repair and exosome biogenesis.

- May act as a signalling lipid after hydrolysis to lysophosphatidic acid.

title: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
section: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP) › Exosomes
text:
BMP is enriched in exosomal membranes.

- Released by most cells.

- Small vesicles (<200 nm) that mediate cell–cell communication.

- Carry lipids, proteins, nucleic acids and bioactive molecules.

title: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
section: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP) › D. BIOLOGICAL SIGNIFICANCE
text:
Membrane dynamics and trafficking

- Promotes curvature, budding and fusion events.

- Essential for endosome maturation and intra-luminal vesicle formation.

Enzyme function

- Enhances optimal activity and fusion of lysosomal hydrolases.

- May influence enzyme localization and cofactor binding in acidic lumen.

Exosome biogenesis and secretion

- Enriched in exosomal membranes.

- Important for vesicle formation and cargo sorting.

Signalling potential

- Hydrolysis → lysophosphatidic acid (LPA), a bioactive signalling lipid.

- Potential roles in cell communication and inflammation.

Diagram labels: PLA2; LPA; P; O

title: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
section: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP) › E. KEY POINTS
text:
- BMP is a unique stereochemical phospholipid of animals.

- Main structural lipid of lysosomes and late endosomes.

- Highly enriched in these membranes.

- Forms non-bilayer structures that enable vesicle budding and membrane fusion.

- Resistant to most phospholipases → protects lysosomal membranes.

- Involved in lipid trafficking, enzyme function and exosome biogenesis.

- Distinct fatty acid compositions are tissue- and organelle-specific.

- New therapeutic potential is emerging in lysosomal storage and inflammatory diseases.

title: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
section: 2. BIOCHEMISTRY AND FUNCTION OF BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP) › Outlook
text: Understanding BMP biosynthesis and function may lead to new interventions for lysosomal storage disorders, neurodegeneration and inflammatory diseases.

title: BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
text:
A unique lysosomal phospholipid of animals

Bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate (BMP) is a minor but ubiquitous phospholipid of animal cells, highly enriched in lysosomal and late endosomal membranes and in exosomes. It has a unique stereochemistry in which the phosphodiester links only the sn-1 and sn-1′ positions of glycerol.

title: BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
text:
Stereochemical configuration: The phosphodiester moiety is linked to sn-1 and sn-1′ of glycerol, not to sn-3 and sn-3′ as in other glycerophospholipids.

Structural comparison of bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate (BMP) and phosphatidylglycerol (PG)

- BMP is highly enriched in lysosomal and late endosomal membranes.

- Up to 15% of lysosomal phospholipids (70% in some macrophage/microglial cell lines; ~11% of total cellular PLs).

- Marker lipid of lysosomes.

- Absent from plants.

- Reported in some bacteria, but stereochemistry uncertain.

title: BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
text: Found at trace levels; ~40% associated with lipoprotein fractions and ~60% in the lipoprotein-deficient compartment.

title: BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
text:
- Ubiquitous in animal tissues (~1–2% of total phospholipids).

- Distinct fatty acid compositions depending on tissue, cell type or organelle.

- Enriched in exosomes.

- Only lipid (of >1200 studied) that accumulated in tissues of mice and humans during aging.

title: BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
text:
- Structural component of lysosomal/late endosomal membranes; influences membrane curvature and dynamics.

- May regulate lysosomal enzyme function and intraluminal vesicle (ILV) formation.

- Involved in lipid trafficking and exosome biogenesis.

- Potential signalling roles (BMP can be hydrolysed to lysophosphatidic acid).

title: BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
text:
- Unique geometry gives BMP distinct packing in membranes.

- S,S-(2,2′-diacyl)-BMP is more tightly packed but less thermodynamically stable than S,S-(3,3′-diacyl)-BMP.

- High content of unsaturated long-chain fatty acids confers high fluidity and curvature-favouring properties.

title: BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
text:
- Derived from lysophosphatidic acid (LPA): acylation → monoacylglycerol-3-phosphate (MG3P) → condensation of two MG3P molecules → BMP + H2O + Pi.

- Enzyme(s) and exact fatty acid positions (sn-2/2′ vs sn-3/3′) remain to be established.

title: BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
text:
- Hydrolysed by specific phospholipase A1-like enzyme → lysophosphatidic acid (LPA).

- Turnover is slow; enriched in long-lived membranes such as lysosomes.

title: BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
text:
- Biomarker of lysosomes and indicator of endo-lysosomal function.

- Alterations may be involved in lysosomal storage disorders, neurodegeneration and inflammatory diseases (under study).

title: BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
text:
- Agrobacterium tumefaciens can convert lyso-phosphatidylglycerol to two isoforms of BMP.

- Reported in some alkalophilic Bacillus spp.

- Whether bacterial BMPs have the unique animal stereochemistry remains unproven.

title: BIS(MONOACYLGLYCERO)PHOSPHATE (BMP)
text:
- BMP is a unique stereochemical phospholipid of animals, concentrated in lysosomes and exosomes.

- Distinct compositions suggest specialized membrane roles and functions.

- Key aspects of its biosynthesis and function are active areas of research.

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL PHOSPHATES (POLYPHOSPHOINOSITIDES) IN ANIMALS
section: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL PHOSPHATES (POLYPHOSPHOINOSITIDES) IN ANIMALS › A. STRUCTURE AND OCCURRENCE
text:
- Discovered by Mable and Lowell Hokin in the 1950s. PI is phosphorylated on the inositol ring at the 3-, 4- and/or 5-positions by specific kinases to give seven phosphoinositides with vital signalling and metabolic roles.

- Present at low levels (~0.5–1% of total lipids) in the inner leaflet of eukaryotic membranes; very low in prokaryotes.

- Turnover is very rapid.

- PI is synthesised on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), especially at mitochondria-associated membranes (MAM).

- PIS can catalyse the reverse reaction; net synthesis depends on concentrations.

- PI is transported to other membranes by vesicles, tubular carriers and by lipid transfer proteins (PITPs) and 'Nir2' family transporters.

Subcellular (general rules)

- Most mono-phosphorylations occur in endomembranes (Golgi, endosomes).

- Di- and tri-phosphorylations occur primarily at the plasma membrane.

- Distinct PIP composition in each compartment supports specific functions.

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL PHOSPHATES (POLYPHOSPHOINOSITIDES) IN ANIMALS
section: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL PHOSPHATES (POLYPHOSPHOINOSITIDES) IN ANIMALS › F. KEY POINTS
text:
- PI is the precursor of seven phosphoinositides (PIPs).

- PIPs are produced and interconverted by specific kinases, phosphatases, and phospholipase C.

- They are concentrated in the inner leaflet and in specific intracellular membranes.

- PIPs act as second messengers, recruit proteins, and regulate trafficking, cytoskeleton, and gene expression.

- Dysregulation of the PI cycle is implicated in many human diseases.

title: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL PHOSPHATES (POLYPHOSPHOINOSITIDES) IN ANIMALS
section: 2. PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL PHOSPHATES (POLYPHOSPHOINOSITIDES) IN ANIMALS › KEY MESSAGE
text: Phosphatidylinositol phosphates are dynamic, low-abundance lipids that orchestrate diverse cellular processes through highly regulated cycles of phosphorylation and dephosphorylation. Spatial and temporal control of these lipids is central to cell signalling and homeostasis.

title: 1. PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL (PI)
text: Phosphatidylinositol is an anionic phospholipid that is both a membrane constituent and a crucial participant in metabolic and signalling processes. It is concentrated in the inner leaflet of eukaryotic membranes and is the precursor of many important inositol phospholipids and second messengers.

title: 1. PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL (PI)
text:
- Present in all tissues, cell types and membranes of eukaryotes at relatively low levels.

- Abundant in brain (~10% of phospholipids).

- Entirely in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane of nucleated cells and of the erythrocyte membrane.

- Not found in most prokaryotes (exceptions: some Mycobacteria, Actinomycetales; thermo-philic Rhodothermus marinus has dialkylether forms).

- In humans, kidney synthesises ~2 g/day from glucose.

title: 1. PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL (PI)
text: Although a minor membrane component, phosphatidylinositol is at the heart of cell signalling and metabolic regulation in all eukaryotes.

title: 5. THE PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL CYCLE
text: Phosphatidylinositol (PI) is at the centre of a dynamic cycle of inter-converting lipids that drives cell signalling and membrane homeostasis. Enzymes in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and plasma membrane (PM) work together, and phosphoinositides are shuttled between membranes by phosphatidylinositol transfer proteins (PITPs) to complete the cycle.

title: 5. THE PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL CYCLE
section: 5. THE PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL CYCLE › ENERGY REQUIREMENT PER TURN OF THE CYCLE
text: Diagram labels: 3 ATP (for PI4K, PI4P5K, DGK); CTP; myo-Inositol; Energetic diphosphate (PPi); Pyrophosphatase; 2 Pi (inorganic phosphate)

title: 5. THE PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL CYCLE
text:
- PLC and PI4P5K are in the plasma membrane; CDS2 and PI synthase are in the ER.

- PITPs shuttle phosphoinositides between membranes to maintain the cycle.

- Each turn consumes 3 ATP, CTP and inositol; hydrolysis of PPi drives the cycle forward.

- DAG can be converted to PA, which returns to the ER for reuse in PI synthesis.

- Numerous branches link to other lipid pathways and signalling cascades.

title: 5. THE PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL CYCLE
section: 5. THE PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL CYCLE › MAJOR BRANCHES AND OUTPUTS
text:
- DAG → activates PKC; precursor of TAG.

- IP3 → releases Ca2+ from ER stores.

- PA → precursor of PC, PE, PS.

- Arachidonic acid release → eicosanoids.

title: 5. THE PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL CYCLE
text: The phosphatidylinositol cycle integrates membrane trafficking, lipid remodelling, second messenger production and cross-talk with other lipid pathways to sustain signalling and membrane composition.

title: 5. THE PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL CYCLE
section: 6. LYSO-PHOSPHOINOSITIDES AND OTHER RELEVANT LIPIDS › A. Lysophosphatidylinositols (LPI)
text:
Diagram labels: sn-1; sn-2; sn-3

- Intermediates in remodelling by PLA1 or PLA2 (e.g., cPLA2α).

- sn-2-Arachidonoyl-LPI is an endogenous ligand for GPR55. → activates kinases → promotes cancer cell proliferation, migration and metastasis.

- Biomarker for poor prognosis in cancer (↑ in ascites).

- Present in brain, intestine, pancreatic islets (may trigger insulin release); involved in inflammation and obesity.

- Hydrolysed by glycerophosphodiesterase 3 (lysophospholipase C) → 2-arachidonoylglycerol (endocannabinoid).

- LPI induces insulin release from pancreatic β-cells.

LPI species with phosphates (e.g., LPI(4)P, LPI(3,4,5)P3) may also act as signalling molecules.

title: 5. THE PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL CYCLE
section: 6. LYSO-PHOSPHOINOSITIDES AND OTHER RELEVANT LIPIDS › B. Glycerophosphoinositol (GPI)
text:
- Formed by removal of both acyl chains from PI by PLA2IVα.

- Can be dephosphorylated to inositol 1-phosphate.

- Possesses anti-inflammatory activity.

- Inhibits inflammatory and thrombotic responses to bacterial lipopolysaccharides (endotoxins).

- 1,2-Diol backbone has same stereochemistry as sn-glycerol-3-phosphate.

text: Lysophosphoinositides, glycerophosphoinositol and related lipids are not merely by-products of PI metabolism. They act as signalling molecules, modulators of inflammation and metabolism, and structural anchors that influence cell communication, growth and host–pathogen interactions.

title: 3. WATER-SOLUBLE INOSITOL PHOSPHATES (AND DIACYLGLYCEROLS)
section: 3. WATER-SOLUBLE INOSITOL PHOSPHATES (AND DIACYLGLYCEROLS) › A. PHOSPHOLIPASE C AND DIACYLGLYCEROL (DAG) GENERATION
text:
- Phosphoinositide-specific phospholipase C (PLC) hydrolyses PI phosphates.

- Six PLC families (≥13 isoenzymes): β, γ, δ, ε, η, ζ.

- PLCs possess pleckstrin homology (PH) domains (~120 aa) that bind phosphoinositides in membranes.

- Activated by GPCRs, RTKs, Ras-like GTPases and Ca2+ → translocate from cytosol to plasma membrane.

- PLCβ is most widely implicated; PLCγ1 in cancer; PLCγ2 in neurodegeneration; PLCε in cardiovascular system.

Diagram labels: Plasma membrane (inner leaflet); PLC (activated); sn-1; sn-2; sn-1,2-Diacylglycerol (DAG); Plus; Inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3)

- DAG remains in membrane → activates protein kinase C (PKC) isoforms.

- IP3 diffuses in cytosol → releases Ca2+ from ER stores.

title: 3. WATER-SOLUBLE INOSITOL PHOSPHATES (AND DIACYLGLYCEROLS)
section: 3. WATER-SOLUBLE INOSITOL PHOSPHATES (AND DIACYLGLYCEROLS) › B. INOSITOL PHOSPHATES (IPs)
text:
- Up to ~60 inositol phosphates possible; ≥37 identified in nature.

- Generated by PLC and by specific kinases and phosphatases.

- Act as second messengers and regulators of many cellular processes.

- Produced in specific membrane/nuclear domains → act locally and transiently.

Diagram labels: Common inositol phosphates; Inositol 1-phosphate (IP1); Inositol 1,4-bisphosphate (IP2); Inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3); Inositol 1,3,4,5-tetrakisphosphate (IP4); Inositol 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexakisphosphate (IP6, phytic acid)

title: 3. WATER-SOLUBLE INOSITOL PHOSPHATES (AND DIACYLGLYCEROLS)
section: 3. WATER-SOLUBLE INOSITOL PHOSPHATES (AND DIACYLGLYCEROLS) › C. IP3–Ca2+–DAG SIGNALING AT ER–PLASMA MEMBRANE CONTACT SITES
text:
1. Agonist binds GPCR/RTK → activates PLC.

2. PLC hydrolyzes PI(4,5)P2 → DAG + IP3.

3. IP3 diffuses to ER and binds IP3 receptor (IP3R).

4. IP3R opens Ca2+ channel → Ca2+ released from ER lumen.

5. Ca2+ rise + DAG → activate PKC and other Ca2+-dependent targets.

Diagram labels: Extracellular agonist; GPCR; PLC; DAG; PKC; PI(4,5)P2; IP3; IP3R; Downstream effects; ER (Ca2+ store); Ca2+

Contact sites couple the plasma membrane and ER to control Ca2+ dynamics and cell responses.

title: 3. WATER-SOLUBLE INOSITOL PHOSPHATES (AND DIACYLGLYCEROLS)
section: 3. WATER-SOLUBLE INOSITOL PHOSPHATES (AND DIACYLGLYCEROLS) › D. MAJOR FUNCTIONS OF INOSITOL PHOSPHATES
text:
- Regulate intracellular Ca2+, ion fluxes and cell secretion.

- Control actin cytoskeleton dynamics and cell shape.

- Mediate vesicle trafficking and membrane fusion/fission.

- Modulate gene transcription, RNA processing and nuclear export.

- Scaffolding/cofactor role in protein–protein interactions.

- Act as 'molecular switches' via specific phosphorylation patterns.

Examples of functions

- IP: IP3; Function: Releases Ca2+ from ER via IP3 receptors.

- IP: IP4 (Ins(1,4,5,6)P4); Function: Regulates Cl− secretion in intestinal epithelial cells; Ca2+-independent roles.

- IP: IP5; Function: Modulates transporter activity and vesicle trafficking.

- IP: IP6 (phytic acid); Function: Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, lowers serum cholesterol; binds metals and proteins.

text:
- IP: Pyrophosphates (InsP7, InsP8); Function: High-energy signals; regulate kinase/phosphatase activities and chromatin structure.

Sites of action: Plasma membrane, endosomes, Golgi, nucleus, mitochondria, cytoskeleton, and enzyme complexes.

section: 3. WATER-SOLUBLE INOSITOL PHOSPHATES (AND DIACYLGLYCEROLS) › H. KEY POINTS
text:
- PLC-generated IPs and DAGs are central second messengers.

- IPs act rapidly and locally to control Ca2+, enzymes, trafficking and gene expression.

- DAG activates PKC and multiple signalling proteins.

- Phosphoinositide metabolism forms a tightly regulated, compartmentalized cycle essential for cell function and health.

text: Sphingomyelin (SM) is synthesised by transfer of phosphorylcholine (P-Cho) from phosphatidylcholine (PC) to ceramide by sphingomyelin synthases (SMS). It is enriched in the trans Golgi and outer leaflet of the plasma membrane.

text:

- Reversible reaction. In absence of ceramide, SMS1 and SMS2 show phospholipase C activity → PC + DAG.
