title: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN › REGULATION BY LIPIDS AND PROTEINS
text:
- DAG activates protein kinase D (PKD). PKD phosphorylates CERT → conformational change → reduced ceramide transfer.

- Phosphoinositides and OSBP1 (oxysterol-binding protein 1, cholesterol transfer protein) also inhibit CERT → repress SM synthesis.

- Molecular species of SM differ from ceramide precursors → SMS enzymes show substrate specificity.

title: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN › FUNCTIONAL ROLES OF ISOFORMS
text:
- SMS1 (Golgi): requires CERT-delivered ceramide.

- SMS2 (plasma membrane): not CERT-dependent; recycles ceramide (e.g., from SMase action) back to SM → protective mechanism.

- SMS2 present in nuclear membranes (rat liver).

- Some synthesis occurs in hepatic lipid droplets.

title: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN › ALTERNATIVE PATHWAY (in ER)
text: Ceramide + Phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) → Ceramide phosphoethanolamine (CPE) → stepwise methylation → Sphingomyelin (SM)

title: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN › B. ENZYMES INVOLVED
text:
- Enzyme: SMS1; Gene: SGMS1; Location: Trans Golgi (luminal side); Topology: 6 transmembrane domains; N- and C-termini face cytosol; Notes: Requires CERT for ceramide delivery.

- Enzyme: SMS2; Gene: SGMS2; Location: Plasma membrane (outer leaflet); Nucleus; Trans Golgi; Topology: 6 transmembrane domains; N- and C-termini face cytosol; Notes: Does not require CERT; recycles ceramide to SM.

- Enzyme: CERT; Gene: CERT; Location: ER cytosolic surface → trans Golgi; Topology: Soluble cytosolic protein; Notes: Transfers ceramide in ATP-dependent, non-vesicular manner.

title: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN › KEY POINTS (BIOSYNTHESIS)
text:
- SM is made by transfer of phosphorylcholine from PC to ceramide.

- SMS1 acts in the trans Golgi (requires CERT); SMS2 acts in the plasma membrane (does not require CERT).

- Reaction is reversible; SM can be hydrolysed to generate ceramide for signalling.

- Diacylglycerol (DAG) from the reaction participates in negative feedback regulation via PKD.

title: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN › Structural features that confer unique properties
text:
- Amide bond at position 2 and hydroxyl at position 3 → extensive hydrogen bonding.

- Trans double bond (4E) in sphingoid base → promotes tight packing and intermolecular interactions.

- Sphingoid motif (C1–C5 region) interacts with lipids and proteins via H-bonding, charge-pairing, hydrophobic and van der Waals forces.

- Zwitterionic head group (P-Cho) like PC, but packing and H-bonding are very different.

title: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN › Physical behaviour
text:
- Cylindrical shape → geometric stability of bilayers.

- High melting temperature (Tm usually >37 °C) due to long saturated/monoenoic chains → remains in gel (ordered) phase at 37 °C.

- Increases membrane order and rigidity.

- Less permeable to small molecules and O2.

title: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN › Differences from phosphatidylcholine (PC)
text:
- PC has two ester carbonyls (H-bond acceptors only); SM has amide + hydroxyl (donor & acceptor).

- Different acyl chain composition (SM more saturated/very-long-chain).

- Pack in very different ways → different biophysical behaviour.

title: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN › Lipid raft (microdomain) organisation
text:
- SM has strong affinity for cholesterol and certain proteins → forms lipid rafts (ordered nano-domains).

- Initially thought SM + cholesterol always form liquid-ordered phase; current view: cholesterol important but not sole determinant in vivo.

- SM and cholesterol metabolism are closely linked (reciprocal regulation).

- Ceramide generated by SM hydrolysis displaces cholesterol from SM-rich domains (ceramide has higher affinity).

Diagram labels: Bulk disordered membrane; Clustering; Lipid raft (ordered domain); Sphingomyelin; Phosphatidylcholine; Cholesterol; Protein; Unsaturated acyl chain

title: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN › Functional consequences
text:
- Rafts concentrate receptors and signalling proteins (e.g., GPCRs, RTKs, Src-family kinases).

- Facilitate signal initiation and amplification.

- Important in endocytosis, cell adhesion, immune responses, myelin stability and viral entry.

- Contribute to membrane mechanical stability, especially under stress.

title: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN › Chain-length dependence
text:
- Very-long-chain SMs (20–24 carbons) → strongest ordering and raft association.

- Short-chain SMs (≤16 carbons) → less ordered, less raft-promoting.

- Tissue- and species-specific molecular species determine membrane behaviour.

title: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 2. BIOSYNTHESIS AND MEMBRANE PROPERTIES OF SPHINGOMYELIN › KEY TAKEAWAY MESSAGE
text: Sphingomyelin is synthesized by SMS enzymes using PC as the phosphorylcholine donor. It is enriched in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane and trans Golgi. Its unique structure enables tight packing, strong interactions with cholesterol and proteins, and the formation of ordered lipid rafts critical for signalling and membrane stability.

title: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › A. INTESTINAL DIGESTION OF DIETARY SPHINGOMYELIN
text:
- Most dietary SM is hydrolysed at the intestinal brush border.

- Alkaline SMase (optimum pH 8.5–9) → ceramide.

- Neutral ceramidase → free fatty acid + sphingosine.

- Enzymes are also secreted in bile from liver.

- Bile salts aid hydrolysis of SM and other phospholipids.

Diagram labels: Dietary sphingomyelin (SM); ceramide; Ceramide; Phosphocholine (P-Cho); Neutral ceramidase (pH ~7); Sphingosine; Fatty acid (R-COOH); Intestinal brush border (lumenal side)

Absorption and fate:

- Sphingosine is absorbed into enterocytes.

- Partly re-N-acylated → ceramide → complex sphingolipids.

- Remainder → sphingosine-1-phosphate → palmitic acid (major product) → esterified into TAG of chylomicrons.

- Some intermediates act as anti-inflammatory signalling mediators.

title: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › Ectoenzyme alkaline SMase
text:
- Member of NPP family (ecto-nucleotidepyrophosphatase–phosphodiesterase).

- Crosses plasma membrane via N- or C-terminal domain; mainly extracellular.

- Also acts as phospholipase C on PAF and lysophosphatidylcholine → anti-inflammatory effects.

title: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › B. CATABOLISM IN OTHER TISSUES – SPHINGOMYELINASES
text:
- Enzyme (type): Acid SMase (lysosomal); Optimum pH: ~5; Location: Endo-lysosomes (→ plasma membrane upon stimulation); Key features and roles: Zn2+-dependent; contains built-in N-terminal saposin domain. House-keeping enzyme: membrane turnover, lipoprotein remodelling. Stimulated → traffics to plasma membrane; generates ceramide for signalling (apoptosis, stress responses, cilia formation). Broad phospholipase C activity in vitro (e.g., ceramide-1-phosphate, glyco-, glycerophospholipids, BMP).

- Enzyme (type): Secreted acid SMase; Optimum pH: ~5–7; Location: Extracellular (plasma membrane outer leaflet; e.g., endothelial cells); Key features and roles: Same gene as lysosomal form; different glycosylation. Zn2+-dependent; participates in signalling and SM turnover.

title: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › B. CATABOLISM IN OTHER TISSUES – SPHINGOMYELINASES
text:
- Enzyme (type): Neutral SMases (NSM 1–4); Optimum pH: ~7.4; Location: NSM-1: ER, nucleus; NSM-2: Golgi, plasma membrane; NSM-3: Plasma membrane (bone, cartilage); MA-NSM (NSM-4): Mitochondria; Key features and roles: NSM-1: Broad substrate specificity; signalling role appears limited. NSM-2: Activated by phosphatidylserine. Major driver of ceramide regulation in plasma membrane. Critical for ceramide homeostasis and signalling (esp. brain). NSM-3: Essential for mineralization; also in striated & cardiac muscle. MA-NSM: Generates ceramide; precise function less well understood.

- Enzyme (type): Bacterial SMases; Optimum pH: Varies; Location: Extracellular; Key features and roles: Many lyse host RBCs. Pseudomonas aeruginosa SMase can act as a SM synthase in vitro.

title: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › Clinical significance
text: Targeting SMases (inhibitors or activators) is being explored for cancer therapy, inflammatory diseases, neurodegenerative and viral infections. Lifestyle factors and diet can influence sphingolipid metabolism and disease risk.

title: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › C. OVERALL HYDROLYSIS OF SPHINGOMYELIN
text:
Diagram labels: Sphingomyelinases (phosphodiesterases); Sphingomyelin; H2O; Sphingomyelinase (asmase / nSMase); Ceramide; Phosphocholine (P-Cho)

Phosphocholine is a valuable nutrient source in cells.

title: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › Major functions of sphingomyelinases
text:
- Generate ceramides → powerful lipid second messengers.

- Ceramides → sphingosine → sphingosine-1-phosphate: regulates proliferation, apoptosis, inflammation, metabolism, etc.

- Enzyme location determines site and nature of signalling.

title: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › D. ACID SPHINGOMYELINASE AND DISEASE
text:
Deficiency of acid sphingomyelinase → Niemann–Pick disease.

- Type: A; Cause: Severe deficiency (infants); Major features: Massive accumulation of SM in lysosomes → foam cells, organomegaly, neurodegeneration, early death.

- Type: B; Cause: Partial deficiency (children/adults); Major features: Hepatosplenomegaly, pulmonary disease, neurological symptoms.

- Type: C; Cause: Defects in NPC1 or NPC2 proteins; Major features: Impaired cholesterol transport; SM accumulation; variable phenotypes.

↑ SM → ↑ cholesterol; lack of ceramide may contribute to pathology. SM degradation is important for cholesterol homeostasis.

title: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › E. REGULATORS AND ACTIVATORS
text:
Mediators that activate SMases / induce ceramide production

- Chemotherapeutic agents

- Tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α)

- 1,25-dihydroxy-vitamin D3

- Endotoxin (LPS)

- Gamma-interferon (IFN-γ)

- Interleukins (ILs)

- Nerve growth factor (NGF)

- Oxidative stress

- Ionizing irradiation

- Other cellular stress conditions

Consequences: apoptosis, growth arrest, differentiation, inflammation, immune responses, autophagy, membrane remodelling, etc.

title: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › E. REGULATION OF BIOSYNTHESIS AND TURNOVER
text:
Regulation of synthesis

- CERT transfers ceramide from ER → trans Golgi (ATP-dependent, non-vesicular).

- DAG produced by SMS activates PKD → phosphorylates CERT → reduces ceramide flux to Golgi.

- Phosphoinositides and OSBP1 (oxysterol-binding protein 1) also inhibit CERT → repress SM synthesis.

- SMS1 (Golgi) and SMS2 (plasma membrane) have phospholipase C activity in absence of ceramide → regulate PC and DAG levels.

Regulation of hydrolysis

- SMases are stimulated by stress signals (listed below).

- Acid SMase translocation to plasma membrane is tightly controlled.

- SM hydrolysis is balanced by use of ceramide in glycosphingolipid synthesis and by SMS2 (plasma membrane), which reconverts ceramide to SM.

title: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › F. PHYSIOLOGICAL AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGICAL ROLES
text:
- Maintain membrane integrity, rigidity and barrier function.

- Essential for myelin sheath formation and neuronal function.

- Organise lipid rafts with cholesterol and proteins → signalling platforms.

- Participate in lipoprotein structure and cholesterol transport.

- Dysregulation linked to cancer, inflammatory diseases, atherosclerosis, Niemann–Pick disease, metabolic disorders, neurodegeneration, viral and bacterial infections.

title: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › G. KEY POINTS SUMMARY
text:
- Dietary SM is hydrolysed by alkaline SMase at intestinal brush border.

- In tissues, SMases hydrolyse SM → ceramide + phosphocholine.

- Acid SMase (lysosomal / secreted) and neutral SMases act in different compartments with distinct roles.

- Ceramide generation is central to signalling: apoptosis, stress responses, inflammation, metabolism and more.

- SMases also regulate membrane composition and cholesterol homeostasis.

- Alterations in SM metabolism are associated with many human diseases.

title: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
section: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM › H. KEY ENZYME FAMILIES
text:
- Acid sphingomyelinase: Zn2+-dependent hydrolase; has built-in saposin domain.

- Secreted acid SMase: extracellular Zn2+-dependent; operates at neutral pH.

- Neutral SMases (1–4): Mg2+-dependent phosphodiesterases in ER, Golgi, plasma membrane and mitochondria.

- Alkaline SMase (intestinal): member of NPP family (ectoenzyme).

title: 3. SPHINGOMYELIN HYDROLYSIS AND CATABOLISM
text: SM: sphingomyelin SMS: sphingomyelin synthase SMS1/2: sphingomyelin synthase 1/2 SMase: sphingomyelinase (phosphodiesterase) nsSMase: neutral sphingomyelinase asmase: acid sphingomyelinase CERT: ceramide transport protein PC: phosphatidylcholine P-Cho: phosphocholine DAG: 1,2-diacyl-sn-glycerol PKD: protein kinase D OSBP1: oxysterol-binding protein 1

title: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN › A. OTHER FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN
text:
- Inhibits phospholipase A2α → ↓ eicosanoid biosynthesis.

- Required for transferrin internalization → iron uptake.

- Essential for many membrane proteins: ion channels, receptors, transporters.

- Most abundant sphingolipid in the nucleus → involved in chromatin assembly, dynamics and nuclear matrix.

- C18-acyl sphingomyelin binds coat protein p24 → formation of membrane vesicles.

- Acts as receptor for actinoporins (pore-forming toxins from sea anemones).

- Accumulates during brown adipocyte differentiation → regulates UCP1-mediated non-shivering thermogenesis.

- Amyloid β (Aβ) binds SM → promotes Aβ aggregation (implicated in Alzheimer's disease).

- Ganglioside GM1 may protect against Aβ aggregation.

title: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN › B. THE SPHINGOMYELIN (OR CERAMIDE) CYCLE
text:
Diagram labels: SPHINGOMYELIN (SM); Ceramide synthases (reverse reaction); SMS (1/2) (uses PC) Golgi / Plasma membrane; Sphingomyelinases (acid, neutral, alkaline); CERAMIDE (Cer); PHOSPHORYLCHOLINE (P-Cho); Phosphodiesterases (reverse reaction); LONG-CHAIN BASES (sphingosine, sphinganine); CERAMIDE-1-PHOSPHATE (Cer-1-P); SPHINGOSINE-1-PHOSPHATE (S1P)

- Precursors of S1P and other lipids.

- Potent lipid second messenger.

Key points

- SM is a central hub → source of ceramide and other signalling sphingolipids.

- Reactions are reversible and compartment-specific (Golgi, plasma membrane, endosomes/lysosomes, nucleus).

- Ceramides generated form distinct membrane domains and trigger diverse cellular responses.

title: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN › C. BIOLOGICAL CONSEQUENCES OF SM HYDROLYSIS
text:
Diagram labels: SM-rich membrane (ordered domain); After SM hydrolysis → ceramide generation; Sphingomyelin; Sphingomyelinase; Ceramide; Cholesterol; Other phospholipids; Protein

- Ceramide-rich domains exclude cholesterol.

- Recruits/excludes specific proteins → alters membrane signalling platforms.

- Triggers: apoptosis, cell cycle arrest, stress responses, differentiation.

- Influences cancer, neurodegeneration, inflammation and more.

title: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN › D. SM AND DIACYLGLYCEROL (DAG) CROSS-TALK
text:
SM synthesis reaction Ceramide + Phosphatidylcholine → (SMS) Sphingomyelin + DAG

Roles of DAG

- Activates protein kinase D (PKD).

- Pro-survival and mitogenic mediator.

- Competitor to ceramide-induced apoptosis.

- Links glycerolipid and sphingolipid signalling pathways.

DAG provides feedback regulation of SM synthesis and participates in many metabolic and signalling pathways.

title: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN › E. SPHINGOMYELINASES – TYPES, LOCATION AND ROLES
text:
- Enzyme (type): Alkaline SMase (intestinal); Optimum pH: 8.5–9.0; Location: Intestinal brush border (luminal side). Also in bile (liver secretion); Key features: Member of NPP family (ectoenzyme). Crosses membrane via N- or C-terminus. Acts as phospholipase C.; Major roles / Notes: Hydrolyses dietary SM → ceramide. Limits cholesterol uptake. Anti-inflammatory effects.

- Enzyme (type): Acid SMase (lysosomal); Optimum pH: ~5.0; Location: Endo-lysosomes. Stored intracellularly; translocates to plasma membrane upon stimulation; Key features: Zinc-dependent; built-in saposin domain. Broad substrate specificity (SM, PC, Cer-1-P, BMP, etc.).; Major roles / Notes: Membrane turnover and remodelling. Generates ceramide for signalling (apoptosis, stress responses). Implicated in Niemann–Pick A/B disease.

title: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN › E. SPHINGOMYELINASES – TYPES, LOCATION AND ROLES
text:
- Enzyme (type): Secreted acid SMase; Optimum pH: 5–7 (works at neutral pH); Location: Extracellular space; outer leaflet of cell membrane; Key features: Derived from SMPD1 gene; different glycosylation. Zn2+-dependent.; Major roles / Notes: Cellular signalling; endothelial function. Involved in inflammatory and metabolic processes.

- Enzyme (type): Neutral SMases (NSM-1 to -4); Optimum pH: ~7.4; Location: ER, Golgi, plasma membrane; one in mitochondria; Key features: Mg2+-dependent. Distinct isoforms with diverse roles.; Major roles / Notes: NSM-1 (ER/nucleus): limited signalling role. NSM-2 (Golgi/PM): key in ceramide synthesis; hormones secretion; brain. NSM-3 (plasma membrane): bone/cartilage mineralization. MA-NSM (mitochondria): precise role less understood.

title: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN › E. SPHINGOMYELINASES – TYPES, LOCATION AND ROLES
text:
- Enzyme (type): Bacterial SMases; Optimum pH: Varies; Location: Extracellular; Key features: Lyse host RBCs (many pathogens). Some (e.g., P. aeruginosa) act as SM synthase in vitro.; Major roles / Notes: Virulence factor; hijack host lipids.

Phosphocholine (P-Cho) released from SM hydrolysis is an important nutrient and signalling molecule.

title: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN › F. SM IN HEALTH AND DISEASE
text:
- Disease / condition: Cancer; Role of sphingomyelin / metabolite: High plasma SM (esp. 16:0-SM) → poor prognosis. Source of ceramide → apoptosis; SM synthase supports pro-survival signalling.

- Disease / condition: Cardiovascular disease; Role of sphingomyelin / metabolite: High plasma SM associated with atherosclerosis. May retain cholesterol in arterial wall; impairs reverse cholesterol transport.

- Disease / condition: Neurodegenerative diseases; Role of sphingomyelin / metabolite: Aβ–SM interaction promotes aggregation (Alzheimer's). Acid SMase activation → SM depletion → disrupted lipid–protein interactions and signalling.

- Disease / condition: Lysosomal storage disorders; Role of sphingomyelin / metabolite: Niemann–Pick A/B: acid SMase deficiency → SM accumulation, foam cells. Niemann–Pick C: NPC1/2 defects.

title: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN › F. SM IN HEALTH AND DISEASE
text:
- Disease / condition: Inflammation & immune disorders; Role of sphingomyelin / metabolite: SMases modulate inflammatory signalling pathways. Dysregulation linked to IBD, sepsis, etc.

- Disease / condition: Infectious diseases; Role of sphingomyelin / metabolite: Chlamydiae acquire SM from host (essential for growth). Bacteria (P. aeruginosa, N. gonorrhoeae) hijack SM metabolism. Viruses (HIV, HCV) exploit host SM.

Altered sphingomyelin levels or species composition are being explored as biomarkers for many diseases.

title: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN › G. NUTRITIONAL ASPECTS
text:
- Dietary sources: egg, meat, dairy foods.

- Estimated intake (USA): 0.3–0.4 g/day per capita.

- Infants: present in milk; may support myelin formation and brain development (evidence from animal studies).

- Poorly absorbed intact; hydrolysed and catabolized.

- Dietary sphingolipids can:

- Reduce intestinal absorption of cholesterol and other lipids.

- Lower serum lipid concentrations.

- Inhibit colon carcinogenesis; may alleviate IBD symptoms.

title: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN
section: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN › H. KEY TAKEAWAY MESSAGE
text: Sphingomyelin is far more than a structural membrane lipid. It is a central metabolic hub connecting membrane organisation, lipid signalling, stress responses and disease. Through the actions of sphingomyelinases and biosynthetic enzymes, it regulates the balance between pro-survival and pro-apoptotic pathways and influences metabolism, immunity, infection and many chronic diseases.

title: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN
text: SM, sphingomyelin; PC, phosphatidylcholine; P-Cho, phosphorylcholine; SMS, sphingomyelin synthase; CERT, ceramide transport protein; DAG, 1,2-diacyl-sn-glycerol; SMase, sphingomyelinase; NSM, neutral sphingomyelinase; SMPD1, sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 1; PKD, protein kinase D; ER, endoplasmic reticulum; Golgi, Golgi apparatus; PM, plasma membrane; S1P, sphingosine-1-phosphate; Cer, ceramide; BMP, bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate; UCP1, uncoupling protein 1.

title: 4. METABOLIC FUNCTIONS OF SPHINGOMYELIN
text: Sphingomyelin metabolism integrates membrane structure, lipid signalling and metabolic regulation. Its enzymes and metabolites are crucial determinants of health and disease.

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
text: Diagram labels: Sphingosine phosphocholine (SPC, lyso-sphingomyelin)

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
text:
- Trace levels in tissues.

- Plasma concentration: ~50–130 nM, associated with HDL.

- Released from activated platelets.

- In skin from sphingomyelin deacylase; implicated in atopic dermatitis.

- Rapidly metabolized in tissues.

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
text:
- Multi-functional lipid produced under many physiological and pathological conditions.

- Acts via GPCRs (S1P1–5, GPR12 – low affinity) or as a second messenger → intracellular Ca2+ release.

- Promotes cell proliferation, differentiation and cancer progression (e.g., breast cancer invasion).

- Can be converted to S1P by autotaxin.

- Anti-inflammatory: reduces organ dysfunction from LPS toxins in vivo.

- Elevated in Niemann–Pick disease type C (biomarker).

- Increased in metabolic syndrome; possible pro-inflammatory roles.

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
text: Diagram labels: Sphingosine phosphocholine; Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P); Autotaxin (LPAAT); Ecto-phosphodiesterase (choline-specific)

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
text:
- Pathogens (e.g., P. aeruginosa) hydrolyse SPC to alter host sphingolipidome → promote infection.

- Involved in cardiovascular regulation.

- Biomarker for Niemann–Pick disease type C and metabolic syndrome.

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
section: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN) › Related lipid in Niemann–Pick disease type C
text:
Occurs together with an unusual lipid, now known to be N-palmitoyl-O-phosphocholineserine (lysoSM-509 in older literature).

Diagram labels: N-palmitoyl-O-phosphocholineserine (not a sphingolipid; a lipoamino acid)

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
text:
- SPC (lyso-sphingomyelin) is a potent signalling lipid with diverse roles.

- Can act externally via receptors or internally as a second messenger.

- Converted to S1P by autotaxin; rapidly degraded by phosphodiesterases.

- Anti-inflammatory in some models; pro-cancer effects reported.

- Elevated in Niemann–Pick disease type C and metabolic syndrome.

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
text:
- Formed by deacylation of sphingomyelin via sphingomyelin deacylase.

- Found in skin, heart, vessels, brain, immune cells.

- Released on platelet activation.

- Present in HDL; influences the cardiovascular system.

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
text: SPC → (phosphodiesterase) sphingosine + phosphocholine Sphingosine → S1P → palmitic acid + ethanolamine (▶ lipid metabolism)

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
text: Sphingosine phosphocholine is a bioactive lysosphingolipid present in plasma (mainly HDL) and tissues at low levels. It influences cardiovascular function, inflammation and cancer, and is a biomarker for certain metabolic and lysosomal storage disorders.

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
section: 6. OTHER SPHINGOLIPIDS CLOSELY RELATED TO SPHINGOMYELIN › A. 3-O-ACYL-D-ERYTHRO-SPHINGOMYELIN
text:
Present in newborn pig and human infants (not in adults); disappears after ~4 weeks.

An additional fatty acid (C16 or C18) is esterified to the 3-hydroxyl of sphingosine (alkali-labile ester).

- R1 = fatty acid (amide-linked, usually 16:0 or 18:0)

- R2 = fatty acid (ester-linked, usually 16:0 or 18:0)

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
section: 6. OTHER SPHINGOLIPIDS CLOSELY RELATED TO SPHINGOMYELIN › B. STRUCTURE OF 3-O-ACYL-SPHINGOMYELIN
text:
- R1: amide-linked fatty acyl chain

- R2: ester-linked fatty acyl chain (at C-3 OH)

- Extra acyl chain is alkali-labile (ester).

- Not detected beyond infancy.

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
section: 6. OTHER SPHINGOLIPIDS CLOSELY RELATED TO SPHINGOMYELIN › Other unusual finds
text:
- Cyanobacterium Scytonema julianum: SM with acetyl group esterified to ω-1 hydroxyl of long-chain FA.

- Brown spider venom phospholipase D converts SM to cyclic phosphate (intramolecular transphosphatidylation) → disrupts membranes.

- Earthworms and C. elegans: phosphorylcholine linked to carbohydrate moiety of glycosphingolipids rather than directly to ceramide.

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
section: 6. OTHER SPHINGOLIPIDS CLOSELY RELATED TO SPHINGOMYELIN › C. OTHER RELATED SPHINGOLIPIDS
text:
- Bacterial sphingomyelinases (e.g., P. aeruginosa) can act as SM synthases in vitro.

- Pathogens and toxins exploit host sphingolipid metabolism.

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
section: 7. CERAMIDE PHOSPHOETHANOLAMINE AND OTHER SPHINGOPHOSPHOLIPIDS › A. CERAMIDE PHOSPHOETHANOLAMINE (CPE)
text:
Diagram labels: Sphingolipid analogue of phosphatidylethanolamine

- Occurs in insects, some freshwater invertebrates and certain Bacteroides (gut microbiota).

- Trace levels in most mammalian cells (300–1,500-fold below SM).

- N-methylated by PE N-methyltransferase → sphingomyelin.

- Synthesized in ER (low levels) by SMS1 and SMS2 (bifunctional).

- Major sphingolipid in Drosophila melanogaster (d14:1; d16:1 bases).

- Replaces galactosylceramide in insect "myelin-like" membranes.

- In insects synthesized using CDP-ethanolamine (Kennedy pathway).

- Modulates circadian rhythm via neural–glial coupling in Drosophila.

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
section: 7. CERAMIDE PHOSPHOETHANOLAMINE AND OTHER SPHINGOPHOSPHOLIPIDS › Key features of CPE
text:
- Structurally similar to PE but with ceramide backbone.

- Negatively charged head group (zwitterionic at physiological pH).

- High phase transition temperature; does not form rafts with cholesterol.

- Important for membrane organization in insects and some microbes.

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
section: 7. CERAMIDE PHOSPHOETHANOLAMINE AND OTHER SPHINGOPHOSPHOLIPIDS › B. OTHER SPHINGOPHOSPHOLIPIDS
text:
1. Ceramide Phosphoglycerol (CPG) Diagram labels: (n = 12–16)

- Anaerobic Bacteroides spp.; also in P. gingivalis (oral pathogen).

- In P. gingivalis: R1 = 3-hydroxy-iso-methylhexadecanoic acid (amide-linked); esterified to iso-methyltetradecanoic acid (estolide linkage).

- Other relatives: dihydroceramide phosphoglycerol; ceramide phosphoethanolamine.

2. Ceramide Phosphorylmannose (CPMan) Diagram labels: (n = 12–18)

- Found in Sphingobacterium spiritovorum (iso-branched base and FA). Stimulates murine macrophages via Toll-like receptor.

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
section: 7. CERAMIDE PHOSPHOETHANOLAMINE AND OTHER SPHINGOPHOSPHOLIPIDS › Other sphingophospholipids reported
text:
Ceramide phosphoinositol (CPI), ceramide-1-phosphate (Cer-1-P), diphosphoglycerate derivatives, phosphonolipid analogues in some marine invertebrates, protozoa (e.g., Trypanosoma brucei makes SM, CPI, CPE).

Second type: glycosphingolipids further phosphorylated on carbohydrate (earthworms, C. elegans).

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
section: 7. CERAMIDE PHOSPHOETHANOLAMINE AND OTHER SPHINGOPHOSPHOLIPIDS › Abbreviations
text: SPC: sphingosine phosphocholine; S1P: sphingosine-1-phosphate; GPCR: G protein-coupled receptor; HDL: high-density lipoprotein; LPAAT: lysophospholipase D (autotaxin); LPS: lipopolysaccharide; SPC: sphingosine phosphocholine.

title: 5. SPHINGOSINE PHOSPHOCHOLINE (LYSO-SPHINGOMYELIN)
section: 7. CERAMIDE PHOSPHOETHANOLAMINE AND OTHER SPHINGOPHOSPHOLIPIDS › Take-home message
text: A diverse family of sphingophospholipids related to sphingomyelin exist in animals, microbes and lower eukaryotes. They have unique structures and roles in membranes, signalling and host–pathogen interactions.

title: SPHINGOMYELIN
text: Sphingomyelin (SM) or ceramide 1-phosphocholine is the sphingolipid analogue of phosphatidylcholine. It is zwitterionic and the most abundant sphingolipid in animal cells. It serves as a reservoir for signalling molecules upon stimulation.

title: SPHINGOMYELIN
text:
Diagram labels: Ceramide; Representative molecular species d18:1/16:0 (Lipid Maps: SM(1) 18:1(4E):3OH/16:0); Sphingoid base (d18:1); Fatty acid (16:0); Phosphorylcholine (head group)

- Zwitterionic at physiological pH: positively charged choline head group and negatively charged phosphate.

- Most stable sphingolipid in membranes; precursor for important signalling molecules.

title: SPHINGOMYELIN
section: SPHINGOMYELIN › 1. OCCURRENCE AND COMPOSITION OF SPHINGOMYELIN
text:
- Can comprise up to 50% or more of total lipids in some tissues.

- ~10% of brain lipids (major myelin constituent); ~70% of phospholipids in human lens.

- Highest in plasma membrane, lysosomes, trans Golgi network and nucleus.

- All SM in erythrocytes is in the outer leaflet; ~90% in nucleated cell plasma membranes.

- Present in all lipoprotein fractions; higher in VLDL/LDL.

- Composed of sphingoid bases (mainly sphingosine, sphinganine, C20 homologues) linked to very-long-chain fatty acids.

- ~100 molecular species identified in human plasma.

- Polyunsaturated fatty acids are rare (exception: testes, spermatozoa).

Table 1. Fatty acid composition of sphingomyelin (wt % of total)

- Egg; 16:0: 66; 18:0: 10; 18:1: 1; 20:0: 4; 22:0: 6; 22:1: 1; 23:0: 2; 23:1: –; 24:0: 5; 24:1: 3

title: SPHINGOMYELIN
section: SPHINGOMYELIN › 1. OCCURRENCE AND COMPOSITION OF SPHINGOMYELIN

title: SPHINGOMYELIN
text:
- Palmitic acid (16:0) most common in peripheral tissues.

- Stearic acid (18:0) abundant in neural tissue.

- Brain (grey matter): ~60% 18:0.

- Brain (white matter): 60% 24:0 + 24:1; increases during first 2 years of life as 18:0 decreases (82% → 33%).

- Testes and spermatozoa: very-long-chain polyunsaturated FAs (up to C34), mainly 28:4(n-6) and 30:5(n-6); some 2-hydroxy FAs.

title: SPHINGOMYELIN
text:
- Sphingosine (d18:1) usually most abundant.

- Sphinganine (d18:0) major base in human lens (mainly 16:0).

- Bases range from C16 to C26.

- Ruminants: contain unusual bases (e.g., d17:1, d17:1-methyl).

- Nematode C. elegans: iso-methyl branched bases with long/very-long-chain saturated FAs (often methyl-branched).

title: SPHINGOMYELIN
text:
Diagram labels: Ceramide; Sphingomyelin synthase (SMS); CDP-choline; CMP; Sphingomyelin (SM); SMases (sphingomyelinases); H2O; Ceramide + Phosphorylcholine

SMases hydrolyse sphingomyelin → ceramide + phosphorylcholine. Ceramide is further metabolized to sphingosine, ceramide-1-phosphate, sphingosine-1-phosphate, etc.

title: SPHINGOMYELIN
text:
- Major structural lipid of cell membranes. Contributes to membrane stability, integrity and mechanical resilience.

- Forms lipid rafts with cholesterol; organizes membrane microdomains for signalling.

- Important for myelin sheath formation and nuclear chromatin structure.

- Reservoir for signalling molecules (ceramide, sphingosine, S1P) upon stress or stimulation.

title: SPHINGOMYELIN
text:
- Plasma membrane (10–20% of lipids)

- Lysosomes / endocytic recycling (high)

- Trans Golgi network (high)

- Nucleus (chromatin) (main phospholipid)

- Endoplasmic reticulum (low, 2–4%)

- Mitochondria (very low)

title: SPHINGOMYELIN
text:
- Ubiquitous in animals (mammals, birds, fish, nematodes, and some protozoa).

- Not synthesized in plants, fungi or bacteria.

- Many bacteria and viruses utilize sphingomyelin or its metabolites from animal hosts.

- In ruminant erythrocytes, SM replaces phosphatidylcholine almost entirely.

- Evolutionary advantage: confers membrane stability and specialized signalling.

title: SPHINGOMYELIN
text:
- Tight packing with cholesterol.

- Reduces permeability to water and solutes.

- Essential for mechanical strength of membranes.

title: SPHINGOMYELIN
text:
- Major lipid of myelin sheath.

- Important for nerve conduction and protection.

title: SPHINGOMYELIN
section: SPHINGOMYELIN › Lipid raft organization and signalling
text:
- Forms rafts with cholesterol.

- Organizes receptors and signalling proteins.

title: SPHINGOMYELIN
text:
- Source of ceramide, sphingosine, C1P, S1P after stimulation.

- Involved in apoptosis, inflammation, stress responses.

title: SPHINGOMYELIN
text:
- Synthesized de novo (ER, Golgi).

- Interconverts with ceramide.

- Transported in lipoproteins.

title: SPHINGOMYELIN
text: Sphingomyelin is a ubiquitous, zwitterionic sphingophospholipid that is essential for membrane integrity, myelin formation, and signalling. It acts as both a structural lipid and a metabolic reservoir whose composition is highly regulated and tissue– and species-specific.

title: SPHINGOMYELIN
text: SM: sphingomyelin SMase: sphingomyelinase ER: endoplasmic reticulum FA: fatty acid LPA/LDL: very-low/low-density lipoprotein TG: triacylglycerol C1P: ceramide-1-phosphate S1P: sphingosine-1-phosphate CDP: cytidine diphosphate CMP: cytidine monophosphate Raft: lipid raft (microdomain) VLDL: very-low-density lipoprotein

title: SPHINGOMYELIN
text:
- Altered SM metabolism linked to neurodegeneration (e.g., Niemann–Pick disease), cardiovascular disease, infection, cancer, and metabolic disorders.

- Target of therapeutic strategies (SMase inhibitors, etc.).

title: Fundamentals_of_Inflammation_----_(Part_I._The_Inflammatory_Response_%E2%80%93_an_Overview)
text: Introduction Venule Lumen of Endothelial Venule wall PMNs venule PMNs cells wall The inflammatory response consists of an innate system of cellular and humoral responses following injury (such as after heat or cold exposure, ischemia/ reperfusion, blunt trauma, etc.), in which the body attempts to restore the tissue to its preinjury state. In the acute inflammatory response, there is a complex orchestration of events involving leakage of water, salt, and proteins from the vascular compartment; activa- tion of endothelial cells; adhesive interactions between leukocytes and the vascular endothelium; recruitment of leukocytes; activation of tissue macrophages; acti- vation of platelets and their aggregation; activation of the complement; clotting and fibrinolytic systems; and release of proteases and oxidants from phagocytic cells, all of which may assist in coping with the state of injury. Whether due to physical or chemical causes, infectious organisms, or any number of other reasons that damage tissues, the earliest in vivo hallmark of the acute inflammatory response is the adhesion of neutrophils (polymorphonuclear leukocytes, PMNs) to the vascular endothelium (“margination”) (Figure 1.1). The chronic inflammatory response is defined accord- ing to the nature of the inflammatory cells appearing in tissues.

When tissue injury occurs in various organs, the resolution of the inflammatory response may, to an extent, involve regeneration in which an organ can rapidly replace damaged or destroyed cells with an architectural outcome that resembles the orig- inal uninjured tissue. A good example of this is acute injury (chemical, viral, etc.) in the liver in which the inflammatory response resolves via regeneration of liver cells (hepatocytes, Kupffer cells, endothelial cells, etc.), reconstituting the damaged or destroyed liver, with the end result being tissue that is virtually identi- cal to that before injury. In other situations, such as in the myocardium, ischemic destruction of cardiomyo- cytes results in an intense acute inflammatory response with a heavy build-up of PMNs (Figure 1.4). The regen- erative abilities of the myocardium are extremely lim- ited, if at all, and the destroyed myocardium must be quickly replaced with a fibrous (collagenous) scar. If scar formation is insufficient, the clinical outcome may be fatal due to cardiac rupture and a filling of the pericardial cavity with blood ­(hemopericardium).

title: Fundamentals_of_Inflammation_----_(Part_I._The_Inflammatory_Response_%E2%80%93_an_Overview)
text: Once the acute inflammatory response has been trig- gered in tissues, it is important to understand the con- sequences. Initially, the acute inflammatory response can be triggered by the presence of infectious agents such as bacteria. The rapid build-up of plasma constitu- ents in the lung alveolar space results in accumulation of antibodies, complement proteins, clotting factors, and other factors that may assist in containment of microorganisms. Traumatic injury triggers an acute inflammatory response in a locale, although in spite of the localized nature of this response, there are often systemic symptoms such as fever, increased numbers of circulating neutrophils (neutrophilia), increased heart rate (tachycardia), and sometimes a feeling of anxiety and apprehension. The local consequences of traumatic injury are well known. The common situ- ation of a sprained ankle results in increased blood flow to the local area which is characterized by red- ness and increased local temperature. Soon, extensive edema develops, causing soft tissue swelling and pain in the joint area which prevents a full range of motion. Induration (increased thickness of soft tissue) is due to the accumulation of leukocytes and edema fluid. Occasionally, hemorrhage may develop.

Granulomatosis Inflammation Granuloma formation is a special type of inflam- matory response, consisting of globular (granular) accumulations of inflammatory and fibrotic nodules, together with chronic inflammatory cells (lympho- cytes, macrophages) and giant cells. Chronic Inflammation Chronic inflammation is defined not as the persistence of acute inflammation but is defined morphologically by the presence of lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells in tissues (Figure 1.15). In many cases, the chronic inflammatory response may persist for long periods (months to years). It is considered to be caused by persistent engagement of innate and acquired immune responses, such as in rheumatoid arthritis, in chronic allograft rejection, in beryl- liosis, and in granulomatous inflammation, to list a few examples. There is evidence that macrophages in these lesions produce a series of proinflammatory mediators that activate fibroblasts to lay down colla- gen and activate other macrophages and lymphocytes

One of the objectives of resolution is for inflamed tissues to resolve with limited tissue injury and to reacquire the physiologi- cal state it enjoyed before injury. To emphasize this, we need to appreciate that naive tissue have a complement of innate immune cells that control the severity of inflamma- tory responses. The peritoneal or pleural cavities, for instance, have a defined popula- tion of innate-type lymphocytes which control the severity of acute responses as well as tissue-resident macrophages, in a state of immune suppression. Once inflammation ensues, these protective cells transiently disappear and remain absent for the duration of the response only to repopulate tissue postinflammation/resolution. The objective therefore is to achieve the state the tissue enjoyed before injury to restore homeostasis and immune function.

text: Figure 3.1. Innate immune regulation of T-cell activation. DC presentation of peptides on MHC molecules to T-cell receptors (TCRs) on naive T cells (“signal 1”) is necessary, but not sufficient, for T-cell activation, clonal expansion and the generation of effector and memory cells. In the absence of costimulation, the provision of signals (“signal 2”) through cell surface–expressed molecules on the APC (e.g., CD80 and CD86, CD40) to cognate receptors on the T cell (CD28, CD40L), the result of antigen presentation is deletion or suppression. “Effective” antigen presentation to T cells is the result of DC maturation: upregulating antigen processing, MHC class I and II expression and loading, and costimulatory molecule expression. DC maturation is a result of PAMP and DAMP signaling through innate immune PRRs (e.g., TLRs, NLRs, RLRs) on DCs. Maturation can also occur through interactions with other innate immune cells. IFN-γ secretion by NK cells (pictured; activated through widely expressed PRRs such as TLRs, or through NK activating receptors such as NKp46) or other innate lymphocyte populations can drive DC maturation; as can TNFα and type I IFN secretion by macrophages activated through PRRs. MΦ, macrophage; MHC, major histocompatibility complex; NLR, NOD-like receptor; RLR, RIG-I-like helicase receptor; TCR, T-cell receptor.

text: Figure 3.3. Regulation of CD4+ T-cell polarization by the innate immune systems. Specification of the effector (or regulatory) class of immune responses by CD4+ T cells is largely the result of functional polarization of naive CD4+ T cells in the periphery into differentiated populations that produce unique patterns of cytokines and have distinctive biological properties. Such polarized CD4+ T-cell populations include Th1 cells, Th2 cells, Th3 cells, Th17 cells, and induced regulatory T cells (Treg; N.B., natural Treg are already differentiated upon leaving the thy- mus). Control of the functional polarization of CD4+ (and CD8+) T cells is under the instructive guidance of cytok- ines (“signal 3”), largely derived from DCs, as well as other innate (as well as adaptive) immune cells. The relevant “signal 3,” its sources, and the transcription factors (the latter in white, in the cells) critical for the differentiation of these polarized populations, along with their signature cytokine profiles and biological activities, is schematized here. It appears that the more polarized a T cell, the more likely it is to express IL-10 and have counter-regulatory properties. Baso, basophils; I. Drawing firm conclusions from these studies is lim- ited by the potentially confounding effects of patho- logical conditions in human donors (allergic diseases, mastocytosis, malignancy), medications donors take to treat these diseases, and the lack of details and vari- ation in culture conditions (cytokines, growth factors, and conditioned media) among studies. The possibility that there may be two or more basophil subpopula- tions, one more closely related to mast cells, another more akin to eosinophils, has not been explored, but would resolve the apparently conflicting data and would suggest that basophils resemble dendritic cells in their developmental heterogeneity. An alterna- tive reconciling hypothesis is that basophils and/or eosinophils may, in some contexts, (de)differentiate into hybrid cells, but definitive studies documenting this are presently lacking. The current dogma posits that basophils exit the bone marrow as fully differentiated cells, as they are identified in peripheral blood relatively easily, and once isolated are functional for mediator release.

text: Figure 9.1. T-cell and B-cell development. T and B cells derive from a common stem cell in the bone marrow. The precursors of T cells leave the bone marrow and mature in the thymus. Here, they express different mol- ecules which aid the maturation process. Some of these are shown in the figure. Pro B cells express VLA-4 which binds VCAM-1 on bone marrow stromal cells. This interaction induces the expression of CD117 (also known as Kit) on the B cell, which is the receptor for stem cell growth factor (SCF). In the bone marrow, BCR rearrangement occurs. This process is mirrored in the thymus where pro T cells begin by expressing Kit and rearrange their TCR to produce a highly diverse population. In the thymus, γδ T cells diverge from the αβ T-cell lineage. Once the TCR and BCR have been selected, T and B cells migrate from the thymus and bone marrow to the periphery. Now the cells have reached maturity but are naive. They then circulate in the body until they encounter specific antigen, become activated and differentiate further. The different subsets of mature T cells are shown on the right along with internal transcription factors and other internal molecules used to identify them.

title: Fundamentals_of_Inflammation_----_(Part_II._Individual_Cell_Types)
text: Figure 9.2. MHC processing and presentation. MHC class I molecules typically present peptides derived from intracel- lular sources whereas MHC class II molecules present those from extracellular sources. During viral replication, some proteins are released from the proteosome (1) and are taken into the endoplasmic reticulum (2). Here, they encounter the membrane-associated transporter protein TAP which loads the peptide onto the MHC class I binding domain. The peptide-loaded MHC I molecule then leaves the ER in a vesicle (3) and is transported to the cell surface where it displays the peptide to passing CD8+ T cells (4). Innate APCs can ingest proteins from the extracellular space (5). These are internalized and degraded in endosomes. Though MHC class II molecules are processed in the ER (6), they leave this compartment in vesicles before being loaded with peptide. The peptide-binding site of MHC II is protected by the CLIP fragment of the invariant chain which is only completely removed once the MHC-containing endosome has fused with the antigen-containing endosome (7). CLIP is removed by a related MHC class II protein (HLA-DM or HLA-DO), allowing the foreign peptide to bind, and the peptide:MHC complex is then transported to the cell surface where it can present antigen to CD4+ T helper cells (8).

title: Fundamentals_of_Inflammation_----_(Part_II._Individual_Cell_Types)
text: On rare occasions, externally derived peptides can be presented by MHC class I in a process known as cross- ­presentation (9).

text: Figure 9.3. TCR signaling. A T cell is activated when its TCR binds to antigenic peptide presented by an antigen-presenting cell (APC). This peptide is bound to MHC, and a co-receptor (CD4 or CD8) stabilizes the interaction by binding to nonpolymorphic regions of the MHC molecule. Protein tyrosine kinases, such as Lck, quickly act to phosphorylate the immunoreceptor tyrosine–based activation motifs (ITAMs) located on the intracellular portions of CD3 and the ζ chains of the TCR. The ζ chain– associated protein ZAP 70 then binds and phosphorylates the membrane-bound adapter proteins, linker of activated T cells (LAT), and SH2 domain-containing leukocyte protein of 76 kDa (SLP-76). LAT, SLP-76 and another kinase, ITK, then activate phospholipase C (PLC)γ1 and recruit guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) to continue the signaling cascade.

text: Figure 9.7. The role of T helper cell responses in pathogen clearance and immunopa- thology. Th1 and Th2 responses are important for pathogen clearance. However, both responses can exacerbate autoimmunity and in some diseases, the type of Th response generated can determine the outcome of infection as in the case of leprosy. The Th1/ Th2 paradigm has been at the forefront of research for many years but it is now clear that Th17 cells take part in many Th1-based responses and that these cells are also involved in many autoimmune diseases. Similarly, regulatory T cells can influence T cell responses, play a role in foetal tolerance and can inhibit tumor immunity.

text: Figure 9.11. BCR signaling. Like the T cell, the B cell needs a signal through its BCR to become activated. However, unlike the T cell, the B cell does not need an APC to pres- ent processed peptides. B cells can recognize and respond to native foreign antigens. Like the TCR, the BCR lacks any significant intracellular signaling domains and must associate with accessory molecules in order to signal. In this case, signals are trans- mitted by CD79, the α and β chains of which associate with the BCR and also contain ITAMs. When the BCR encounters antigen, Src family kinases, such as Lyn, quickly act to phosphorylate the ITAMs located on the intracellular portions of CD79. Another kinase, Syk, is then able to bind and becomes activated going on to phosphorylate the B cell linker (Blnk) and recruiting Tec kinases and guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) to continue the signaling cascade.

Figure 9.12. Opsonization of pathogens by antibody. Another major role of antibody is to 'opsonize' foreign par- ticles. The variable chains of antibodies can bind specific foreign peptides on the surface of pathogens. Once the variable regions have bound, the constant regions of the antibodies are recognized by Fc receptors on phagocytes, which engulf the antibodies along with the pathogen to which they have bound. The antibody/pathogen complex is then degraded in a phagolysosome within the phagocyte.

text:
Figure 9.16. NK cell killing. NK cells have evolved to recognize MHC class I molecules. When a NK cell interacts with a healthy cell, it receives signals through both killer activating receptors (KARs) and killer inhibitory receptors (KIRs). The balance of these signals suppresses the killing response and the healthy cell is released. If, however, the cell is infected with a virus or becomes cancerous, it loses MHC class I from its surface. The NK cell no longer receives an inhibitory signal through its KIRs so the KAR signal promotes the release of cytotoxic granules from the NK cell which induces apoptosis in the infected cell.

text: Figure 10.3. Regulation of inflammatory responses by the stroma. Evolution of an inflammatory response is char- acterized by recruitment of immune system cells via production of inflammatory chemokines. Recruited cells may undergo proliferation and/or differentiation. As an inflammatory process reaches its conclusion, the resolution of inflammatory leukocyte infiltrates within a microenvironment is governed by a number of dynamic factors including the balance between cell recruitment and emigration and the balance between cell death and proliferation. Recent evidence suggests that tissue stromal cells are able to determine the type and duration of leukocyte infiltrates in an inflammatory response. At the resolution of such responses, stromal cells contribute to the withdrawal of survival sig- nals and normalization of chemokine gradients, allowing infiltrating cells to undergo apoptosis or leave via draining lymphatics.

title: Fundamentals_of_Inflammation_----_(Part_II._Individual_Cell_Types)
text: Figure 10.4. Fibroblast roles in inflammation. Fibroblasts may be subjected to various inflammatory stimuli. Bacterial cell products activate toll receptors, proinflammatory cytokines, such as TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 are most abundantly secreted by infiltrating macrophages and neutrophils. Infiltrating T lymphocytes may activate macrophages by direct contact to produce further inflammatory cytokines, and also activate fibroblasts by CD40Ligand–CD40 interactions. In response, fibroblasts break down and elaborate new extracellular matrix (ECM) by means of metalloproteinases and prostaglandin E2 (PGE2). A wide range of cytokines including IL-6 and GM-CSF and a broad range of chemokines may be elaborated. In conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, interaction with bone metabolism is important: RANKLigand promotes osteoclast differentiation and activation, while DKK-1 (Dickkopf) inhibits osteoblast activation. Alternatively, bone formation may be stimulated by bone morphogenic proteins (BMP) and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), which also has a primary role in promoting vasculogenesis. Fibroblasts are a rich source of other growth factors which modulate stromal cell survival such as platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) and epidermal and fibroblast growth factors (EGF, FGF).

text: Figure 10.5. Inappropriate survival and retention of T lymphocytes mediated by synovial fibro- blasts. Interferon-β, produced by synovial fibroblasts, has been identified as one of the principal factors responsible for prolonged T-cell survival in the rheumatoid joint. Similar mechanisms exist for stromal-induced survival of B cells. It is likely that these mechanisms of stromal cell–induced leukocyte survival occur in many chronic inflammatory conditions in which lymphocytes accumulate. In addition, aberrant ectopic expression of constitutive chemokines such as CXCL12 by synovial stromal cells contributes to the retention of T cells within the RA synovium. CXCL12 (SDF-1) and its receptor CXCR4 plays an important role, both in the constitutive traffic of lymphocytes and in the recruitment and retention of hemopoietic cells within the bone marrow. In the rheumatoid joint, fibroblast-derived TGF-β induces high levels of CXCR4 receptors in T cells, leading to retention of cells. CXCL12 is highly expressed on endothelial cells and fibroblasts at sites of T-cell accumula- tion. Positive feedback loops enhance CXCL12 production by fibroblasts via CD40–CD40 ligand interactions.

text: Figure 10.8. Three cell model of recruitment to the inflamed rheumatoid synovium. A multicellular coculture model of RA synovium was used to reconstruct the persistently inflamed RA microenvironment in vitro, by coculturing RA synovial fibroblasts or skin fibro- blasts with human endothelial cells (EC). After a period of conditioning, fibroblasts and EC were isolated and screened using microarray analysis. Recapitulating the RA environment upregulated message for several CXC chemokines in ECs and RASFs, an effect that was absent in cocultures of ECs and skin fibroblasts. Flow adhesion assays demonstrated that only CXCL5 was functional on ECs cocultured with RASFs and recruited flowing neutro- phils. EC expression of DARC was induced by coculture with RASFs, and antibody-blocking CXCL5 interactions with DARC or small interfering RNA (siRNA) targeting DARC expression abolished neutrophil recruitment. Thus, DARC edits the leukocyte recruitment code in a chemokine-specific manner in a model of human inflammatory disease, demonstrating the impact of inflammatory “cross-talk” between cells of the stromal microenvironment.

The cyclooxygenase pathways produce prostaglandins, prostacyclin, and thromboxane. The lipoxygenase pathways produce leukotrienes and lipoxins. Figure 12.4. Lipoxin biosynthesis. Two main routes lead to biosynthesis of the lipoxins. In each pathway, sequential lipoxygenase reactions are required, followed by hydrolysis. The immediate precursor of the lipoxins is epoxytetraene; hydrolysis of epoxytetra- ene yields the lipoxins. Left pathway: Arachidonic acid is converted to 15-HETE by sequential activity of 15-LOX and peroxidase. 15-HETE is converted by 5-LOX to the chemical intermediate 5-hydroperoxy, 15-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid, and 5-LOX acts on this intermediate to form epoxytetraene. LTA4 route: Arachidonic acid is converted to 5-HPETE by 5-LOX, and 5-HPETE is con- verted to LTA4 by further action of 5-LOX. LTA4 is converted to epoxytetraene by 15-LOX (see text for further details).

In this example, the leukocyte (neutrophil) obtains arachidonic acid (AA) internally via activation of cPLA 2 and also externally from platelets, and uses this AA to bio- synthesize LTA4 and LTB4. LTA4 is transferred from the leukocyte to platelets and endothe- lial cells, which synthesize and secrete LTC4. Platelets also biosynthesize lipoxins (LXA4, LXB4) from LTA4. Note that the eicosanoids biosynthesized within each cell type are deter- mined by the enzymatic repertoire of that cell type: for example, neutrophils biosynthesize primarily LTA4 and LTB4 because they express 5-LOX and LTA4 hydrolase, whereas platelets biosynthesize LTC4 and lipoxins because they express LTC4 synthase and 12-LOX.

Hematopoietic cytokine receptors (class I) have similar extracellular domains, and often form multi- meric structures with one another. For instance, the IL-2 receptor gamma subunit is shared by IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, and IL-15 receptors, and is thus referred to as the common γ chain (γc). A common β chain is shared by the IL-3, IL-5, and GM-CSF receptors. The interferons are also referred to as class II cytokine receptors, and include the receptors for IFN-α and IFN-β, IFN-γ, and the IL-10 receptor. The TNF ligand and receptor family (class III) includes ligands that can be cell associated or soluble. Many members of this family are homotrimers in both the ligand and ligand-bound receptor. Many members of the TNF family are not cytokines, but are membrane-bound signaling molecules important for costimulation of immune responses. In addition, many members of the TNF receptor family have a cytosolic tail that contains a number of death domains, which can activate the caspase cascade, resulting in apoptosis or cell suicide. Cytokine signals from innate immune cells and non- immune cells promote one of several pathways of CD4+ T cells (TH) cell differentiation. IL-12 promotes the generation of IFNγ-producing TH1 cells, important for the clearance of viruses and intracellular bacteria. The immunosuppressive regulatory T-cell lineage (Treg) is promoted by TGF-β and IL-10 and serves to negatively regulate many types of immune responses.

text: Figure 15.3. Agonist-triggered conformational changes in p47phox. In the cytoplasm of resting phagocytes, p47phox exists in a conformational state wherein domains that pos- sess the capacity to support protein–protein and protein–lipid interactions are cryptic and inaccessible. There is a PX domain, which binds to specific phosphoinositides; tan- dem Src homology 3 (SH3) domains, which interact with proline-rich regions (PRR); and a C-terminal PRR. Very importantly, there is a cationic region between the second SH3 domain and the PRR known as the autoinhibitory region that is rich in arginine and ser- ine residues. Stimulation of phagocytes activates several protein kinases that phospho- rylate 8–10 serines in the autoinhibitory region. Consequently, there is a conformational change in p47phox, rendering its interactive domains available for binding. SH3 domains interact with a PRR in p22phox, PX domain binds phosphoinositides on the inner leaflet of the phagocyte membrane, and other interactions between cytosolic elements and flavocytochrome b558 stabilize the assembled complex.

text: Figure 15.5. Potential MPO-based reactions in the phagosome. Concurrent activation of the NADPH oxidase and release of azurophilic granules into the phagosome delivers reac- tive oxygen species and granule products, respectively, in close proximity of the ingested microbe. Among the many interactions that occur among oxidants and granule proteins to produce an environment inhospitable to microbes are those dependent directly or indi- rectly on MPO. MPO and H2O2 combine to form Compound I that in turns supports the two- electron oxidation of Cl – to Cl+ and thereby generate HOCl, or bleach. MPO and H2O2 also directly oxidize tyrosine to generate tyrosyl radicals, a substrate for production of tyrosine peroxide as well as tyrosyl cross-linking of free tyrosines or tyrosyl residues in proteins. HOCl is a very potent oxidant and directly attacks amino acids, especially methionine and cysteine, as well as amide sidechains on peptides and proteins, and other biological sub- strates. HOCl also supports generation of other reactive species, including hydroxyl radical (OH•), singlet oxygen (1O2), and chloramines. The latter products include those that are rela- tively long lived and exert significant antimicrobial activity. Some chloramines decay and release aldehydes, some of which are antimicrobial in their own right.

text: Figure 15.6. Members of the NOX family of NADPH oxidases. The NOX family of NADPH oxidases includes seven proteins (NOX1–5, DUOX1, and DUOX2) that are identified by sequence homology with gp91phox (aka NOX2) and share dependence on NADPH and FAD for activity. Distributed broadly in a nearly all tissues and cell types in both plant and animal kingdoms, the non- phagocyte oxidases serve diverse functions. The organization of the nonphagocyte oxidases differs in several ways from that of the phagocyte oxidase. Only NOX1, 3, and 4 pair with p22phox in the membrane. NOXO1 and NOXA1, homologues of p47phox and p67phox respectively, interact with NOX1, 3, and 4, whereas NOX5 and the DUOX proteins function independently of cytosolic pro- tein cofactors. In contrast to the agonist-dependent assembly and activation seen in the phagocyte oxidase, the nonphagocyte systems function constitutively, with modulation by exposure to various agonists. Both NOX5 and the DUOX proteins possess EF-hands in their cytoplasmic domains and are regulated by changes in intracellular calcium.

(A) Upper panel: JAMs are characterized by two ­immunoglobulin-like domains in the extracellular portion, a single transmembrane segment and a short cytoplasmatic tail with a PDZ-domain-binding motif (Phe-Leu-Val). A dimerization motif Arg- (Val-Leu-Ile)-Glu in the membrane-distal domain is essential for homodimer formation. Bottom panel: Model of JAM homodimerization. (B) JAMs can form homo- and heterodimers, then forming specific cis- or trans- interactions with other CAMs.

Zileuton and 5-lipoxygenase activating protein (FLAP) inhibitors prevent the conversion of arachidonic acid to 5-HPETE and LTA4; zileuton has been used in the chronic management of asthma. Zafirlukast and montelukast are antagonists at CysLT1, the receptor for all cysteinyl leukotrienes (mainly LTC4 and LTD4); these drugs are used in the chronic management of asthma. The cysteinyl leukotrienes also interact with CysLT2 (not shown). BLT1 and BLT2 are LTB4-related G protein-coupled receptors; BLT1 is the major LTB4 receptor. title: Pharmacology of Eicosanoids(Chap42)
text: FIGURE 42-5. Lipoxin biosynthesis. Two main routes lead to biosynthesis of the lipoxins. In each pathway, sequential lipoxygenase reactions are required, followed by hydrolysis. The immediate precursor of the lipoxins is epoxytetraene; hydrolysis of epoxytetraene yields the lipoxins. Left pathway: Arachidonic acid is converted to 15-HETE by sequential activity of 15-lipoxygenase and peroxidase. 15-HETE is converted by 5-lipoxygenase to the chemical intermediate 5-hydroperoxy, AQ1 15-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid, and 5-lipoxygenase acts on this intermediate to form epoxytetraene. Right pathway: Arachidonic acid is converted to 5-HPETE by 5-lipoxygenase, and 5-HPETE is converted to LTA4 by further action of 5-lipoxygenase. LTA4 is converted to epoxytetraene by 15-lipoxygenase. Common pathway: Epoxytetraene is hydrolyzed to the active lipoxins LXA4 and LXB4. The lipoxins have both anti-inflammatory and pro-resolving roles, are counter-regulators of leukotriene action, and regulate many cytokines and growth factors. LXA4 is a highly selective agonist for the G protein-coupled receptor FPR2/ALX. In a transcellular reaction, platelet 12-lipoxygenase can also catalyze the formation of LXA4 from neutrophil-derived LTA4; the detailed mechanism remains to be elucidated (not shown; see also Fig. 42-7).

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text: Preface The 2025 edition of Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS) continues the tradition of being freely accessible as a PDF, with a print version available on Amazon at no additional royalty cost. This edition expands upon the practical and conceptual aspects of mass spectrometry analysis, particularly in its integration with "Activity Metabolomics". The AMMS 2025 edition is a significantly refined version of the original book, featuring comprehensive edits and the inclusion of new content. Notable additions include chapters on “In-Source Fragmentation” and “XCMS-METLIN,” as well as entirely new sections on tandem mass spectrometry across instrument platforms. These updates reflect the evolving capabilities of mass spectrometry and its applications. This book underscores my ongoing commitment to advancing mass spectrometry technologies and the corresponding informatics tools, XCMS and METLIN, for identifying endogenous metabolites. These metabolites, which can modulate phenotypes and address disease, hold immense promise for improving health outcomes.

text:
Chapter 1 A History of Mass Spectrometry and Metabolomics Mass Spectrometry

Mass spectrometry has a special intrigue that comes from its interdisciplinary nature, as it freely crosses the borders of physics, chemistry, and biology. Its history goes back to the early 1900’s, and its development has reached a pinnacle in recent years, being widely applied to a range of problems. Thousands of women and men have contributed to the development of mass spectrometry, and this timeline highlights some key individuals and events. The study of metabolism and lipids has also had an equally interesting trajectory encompassing many different technologies, however it is safe to say that mass spectrometry has been a key technology in its evolution (Figure 1.1).

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text:
1. A History of MS and Metabolomics

Early Mass Spectrometry – The Physical Roots

The history of MS begins with J.J. Thomson (Figure 1.2) of the University of Cambridge. Thomson’s “theoretical and experimental investigations on the conduction of electricity by gases” led to the discovery of the electron in 1897 for which he was awarded the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physics. In the first decade of the 20th century Thomson went on to construct the first mass spectrometer (then called a parabola spectrograph), in which ions were separated by their different parabolic trajectories in electromagnetic fields and detection occurred when the ions struck a fluorescent screen or photographic plate.

Figure 1.2. Thomson’s cathode ray tube J.J. Thomson 1906 Nobel Prize in Physics

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text:
1. A History of MS and Metabolomics

Later, Thomson's protégé, Francis W. Aston (1922 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, Figure 1.3) of the University of Cambridge, designed a mass spectrometer that improved resolving power, allowing Aston to study isotopes. During this same period, A.J. Dempster of the University of Chicago also improved upon resolution with a magnetic analyzer and developed the first electron ionization source, which ionized volatilized molecules with a beam of electrons. Electron ionization ion sources are still very widely used in modern mass spectrometers for small molecule analysis. Thomson, Aston, and Dempster created a strong foundation of MS theory and instrument design that made it possible for those who followed to develop instruments capable of meeting the demands of chemists and biologists.

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text: An important goal, particularly for chemists, was to create an instrument capable of analyzing both the elements and small organic molecules. Eventually this led to mass analyzers of five different forms: magnetic sector double-focusing, time-of-flight, quadrupole, Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance and fourier transform orbitrap mass analyzers. In its time, the most widely used high mass-resolution double-focusing instrument was developed by Professor Alfred O.C. Nier at the University of Minnesota during World War II to perform isotopic analysis and separate uranium-235 from uranium-238. The first nuclear bomb was developed entirely from the uranium separated by this type of mass spectrometer.

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text:
The concept of time-of-flight mass spectrometry (TOF MS) was proposed in 1946 by William E. Stephens of the University of Pennsylvania. In a TOF analyzer, ions are separated by differences in their velocities as they move in a straight path toward a collector. TOF MS allows for rapid analyses (5-20 kHz repetition rates), it is capable of high resolving power and high accuracy, it is applicable to rapid chromatographic detection, and it is now used for the mass determination of large biomolecules because of its virtually limitless mass range.

One type of mass analyzer that proved to be ideal for coupling to gas chromatography and liquid chromatography (in the 1990s) was the quadrupole mass filter. The quadrupole was first reported in the mid-1950s by Wolfgang Paul (Figure 1.4), who

3

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text:
1. A History of MS and Metabolomics

shared the 1989 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on ion trapping. In a quadrupole device, a quadrupolar electrical field (comprising radiofrequency and direct-current components) is used to separate ions. Although quadrupole mass analyzers are not as accurate and precise as double-focusing instruments, they offer excellent dynamic range, are quite stable, and are also readily applied to tandem mass spectrometry experiments – features that make them popular for quantitative analysis and drug discovery applications. Quadrupoles are the most widely used mass analyzers.

Figure 1.4. Paul’s Wolfgang Paul quadrupole and quadrupole 1989 Nobel Prize in ion trap resulted in two of Physics the most used mass analyzers.

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text: Ion cyclotron resonance MS (ICR-MS) and the orbitrap have proven to be a powerful MS solutions for high resolution and high accuracy. ICR was initially described by John A. Hipple of the National Bureau of Standards, Washington, D.C. It operates by subjecting ions to a simultaneous radiofrequency electric field and a uniform magnetic field, causing the ions to follow spiral paths in an analyzer chamber. By scanning the radiofrequency or magnetic field, the ions can be detected sequentially. In 1974, Melvin B. Comisarow and Alan G. Marshall of the University of British Columbia revolutionized ICR by developing Fourier transform ICR mass spectrometry (FTMS). The major advantage of FTMS is that it allows many different ions to be measured at once. Sub-part per million accuracy – such as an error of less than 0.001 Dalton for a 1000 Dalton peptide – is now routinely possible with commercial FTMS instruments. The orbitrap, released by Makarov in 2005, was the first high resolution and

sensitivity trapping type of mass analyzer that employed electrostatic fields which also employs FT data deconvolution.

Ionization Advances allow for Biological Applications

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text:
A variety of mass analyzer and tandem mass spectrometry designs are widely used today and are continually being developed for new applications. Despite advances in mass accuracy, mass range, quantitative analysis, and the ability to couple the instruments to chromatography, MS still lacked efficacy for large and small biomolecule analysis. Significant molecular decomposition or fragmentation during vaporization/ionization and poor sensitivity proved very problematic in biomolecular MS. The development of “soft ionization” – electrospray ionization MS (ESI MS) and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization MS (MALDI MS) – allowed MS to transcend into the realm of biology (Figure 1.5).

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)

1. A History of MS and Metabolomics

In ESI MS, highly charged droplets dispersed from a capillary in an electric field are evaporated, and the resulting ions are drawn into an MS inlet. The technique was first conceived in the 1960s by chemistry professor Malcolm Dole of Northwestern University but was not put into practice for biomolecule analysis until the early 1980s by John B. Fenn of Yale University.

In soft laser desorpton/ionization and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI) MS, analyte molecules are laser-desorbed from a solid or liquid UV-absorbing matrix. The technique was initially reported by Koichi Tanaka and coworkers for proteins at Shimadzu Corp., Kyoto, Japan, and was also developed by Franz Hillenkamp and Michael Karas at the University of Frankfurt, Germany.

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text:
For their work on developing soft ionization techniques suitable for large biomolecule analysis, Fenn and Tanaka shared the 2002 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Their work on ESI-MS and MALDI-MS made MS increasingly useful for sophisticated biological experiments. Applications include protein identification, drug discovery, DNA sequencing, carbohydrate analysis, and biomarker discovery.

Small Molecule and Protein Analysis

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text:
The importance of these MS developments can be seen in research efforts at every major pharmaceutical company and university. Arguably the most important MS application is in small molecule and peptide quantification using triple quadrupoles (QqQ) MS (Figure 1.6), the most widely used mass spectrometer. Endogenous biomolecules, exogenous molecules and peptides are routinely quantified with this technology. Perhaps most compelling is that virtually all newborns in the United States as well as elsewhere are tested with QqQs for over 30 different diseases.

Soft ionization ESI MS methods have made it possible to study increasingly larger structures and their noncovalent interactions. ESI instrumentation designed by Henry Benner at Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory was the first to measure intact viral ions measuring millions of Daltons, and earlier experiments show that viruses maintain their structure and virulence (Figure 1.7).

Metabolomics, Lipidomics, Metabolites, and Lipids

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text:
The 100+ year history of mass spectrometry pales in comparison to the centuries long history of metabolism. The discovery of metabolites and the subsequent field of metabolomics has played a critical role in advancing biochemistry. Hermann Boerhaave, an 18th-century scientist, and author of Elementa Chemiae characterized the first metabolite, urea, which set the stage for identifying the other most abundant metabolites such as amino acids, sugars, and lipids over the next two centuries. However, with the emergence of advanced analytical technologies from the 1930s onwards, finer details of metabolism began to surface. These technologies provided a much clearer and detailed image of biochemistry, uncovering its structural complexity and revealing new metabolic activities.

Figure 1.8. The evolution of metabolic sciences.

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text:
Recent advances (Figure 1.8) have revitalized the importance of metabolism in many biological and therapeutic fields, including cancer, bioengineering, systems biology, the microbiome, and nutrition, among others. The integration of

8

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text:
1. A History of MS and Metabolomics

metabolomics/lipidomics, that includes a suite of technologies that characterize and quantify metabolites and lipids contributing to the structure, function, and dynamics of an organism, has provided an additional tool for classical biochemistry, enabling further advances in biochemical research. Mass spectrometry technology, particularly the Nobel Prize-winning ESI, has made it possible to routinely observe intact molecular ions, a capability previously unachievable for most biomolecules. In addition, ESI has enabled sensitivity several orders of magnitude greater. These breakthroughs have facilitated the discovery of metabolites and lipids that were not previously known to exist in nature, including those found in multicellular organisms such as animals and plants, as well as microorganisms such as bacteria.

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text: Determining the structures of unknown metabolites is a significant technological challenge, but it also presents an exciting opportunity to expand our biochemical knowledge base for both characterized and uncharacterized organisms. The identification of all known and unknown small molecules in an organism, referred to as the metabolome, represents the future of metabolism discoveries. From the 1700s to the 1900s, newly discovered metabolites were identified due to their ubiquitous nature. Their abundance made them easy enough to be isolated and characterized by the analytical techniques available at that time (for example amino acids, monosaccharides, and nucleotides). However, in recent decades, the discovery of new and less ubiquitous metabolites and classes of metabolites has opened new avenues of research and led to a sustained effort to characterize and understand their physiological effects.
