Multi-omics integration for determining activity

In addition to metabolomics, the correlation and integration of multi-omic data present a useful approach to enhance the selection process of metabolites and lipids. By combining candidates with transcriptomic and proteomic data,

279

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text:
12. Activity Metabolomics

researchers can gain deeper insights into selected pathways of interest. This multi-omic integration has been applied across diverse research areas, ranging from cancer metabolism to plant physiology and microbiology, yielding valuable information about distinct metabolite/lipid activities through quantitative modeling. The aim is to enable targeted interventions on specific pathways.

To handle the vast amount of data and reduce complexity, various mathematical approaches can be employed. For instance, metabolite, lipids, and other omics data can be added to curated pathways, or novel pathways and fluxes can be modeled using the data. The field of multi-omics integration is continuously evolving, with multiple approaches being explored.

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text: One common strategy in multi-omics integration involves using gene nomenclature linked to unique metabolite identifiers and combining existing pathway information (e.g., KEGG, Reactome, Biocyc pathways, Recon) with metabolomic/lipidomic set enrichments (available via platforms like MetaboAnalyst) and the newly developed ChemRICH platform. By utilizing this pathway information, researchers can effectively reduce complexity and filter out noise.

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text: However, integrating the metabolome and other omic layers can pose challenges. Complex datasets are often acquired without a preset integration strategy. Addressing data robustness, sample harvest artifacts (batch effects), and distinct features of different omic datasets is crucial. Challenges in multi-omic data integration include noise removal, data prefiltering, matching various identifiers, selecting data dimensionality reduction methods, choosing computational approaches and mathematical models, model validation, and integration into trans-omics network modules. Efficiently advancing these approaches is an area of ongoing development.

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text:
Metabolic networks face major validation challenges due to the overrepresentation of in-source fragmentation in the data sets. Additionally, the full potential of omics data is not always utilized comprehensively, and data sharing strategies need improvement. However, multi-layered omic strategies, once

acquired and integrated, can be highly useful, especially when applied to in vivo metabolism.

The future integration of genome-scale modeling, big data analysis, and machine learning strategies is anticipated to further prioritize metabolite/lipid activity in biological systems. In vivo and in vitro modeling studies have already demonstrated the power of this integrative omics approach, accurately predicting biological behavior based on multi-layered omic data acquisitions and metabolic phenotypes. Predictive pathway analysis within these platforms allows for straightforward and efficient metabolite mapping to background knowledge databases, be they curated reference pathway databases or genome-scale networks.

Ultimately, these integrated approaches aim to generate accurate biological models, allowing the identification of the most promising candidates for activity screening. The multidimensional integrated "omic" landscape offers exciting opportunities and unconventional solutions for predicting metabolites that modulate phenotype.

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text:
12. Activity Metabolomics

Applications of activity metabolomics and lipidomics

Activity metabolomics/lipidomics has a broad range of applications, impacting phenotypes across various organisms, from simple prokaryotes to complex human physiology. Its versatility is exemplified by its ability to enhance biotechnological applications, such as boosting Bordetella pertussis vaccine and protein production in E. coli. Additionally, activity metabolomics/lipidomics plays a significant role in modulating the microbiome, where alterations to the mammalian metabolome can influence microbial communities, with microbiome-derived metabolites impacting immune cells and satiety.

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text: In the emerging field of immunometabolism, specific metabolites like prostaglandin E2 have been found to influence immune responses, promoting certain T cell types while suppressing macrophage and neutrophil activity. At an organ level, metabolites like leukotrienes control pathophysiological reactions, such as in asthma. In complex organisms, nutritional interventions, like omega-3 fatty acid supplementation, have shown multiple benefits without severe side effects.

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text: In pharmacology and toxicology, metabolites and lipids are administered to reduce toxicity, such as using ethanol to counteract methanol poisoning or administering scavenger metabolites to mitigate the effects of certain chemotherapeutics. Drug synergies with endogenous metabolite classes are also utilized for therapeutic purposes. Even simple metabolites like glutamine have proven effective in treating complex diseases like sickle cell disease, as evidenced in phase 3 clinical trials.

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text:
These examples highlight the wide applicability of active metabolites and lipids in modulating biological processes, cellular metabolic states, cell activation, differentiation, proliferation, and complex tissue functions. Notably, the effect of a metabolite is context-dependent, and its induced phenotype can vary significantly based on the biological system it is applied to. The goal of activity metabolomics is to provide a framework to understand and systematically quantify these phenotypic changes.

283

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text:
12. Activity Metabolomics

One such example is α-ketoglutarate (AKG), an active metabolite that alters phenotypes in a context-dependent manner. It regulates glucose metabolism and uptake in bacteria, extends the lifespan in Caenorhabditis elegans through mTOR inhibition, supports regulatory T-cell differentiation from Th1 cells in immune cells, and enhances tissue and muscle regeneration in humans via processes involving ERK and other factors. Its binding to the G-protein-coupled receptor Oxgr1 translates into increased transporter synthesis and hypertension through salt reabsorption in the kidney. An overarching theme in these settings may be the modulation of anabolic cell activity, which could be considered the "common denominator" of AKG's role in the activity metabolome.

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text:
The current challenge in activity metabolomics and lipidomics is to link metabolites systematically and quantitatively to an organism's phenotype ("phenome"). Achieving this goal will necessitate comprehensive metabolomics and phenotypic data, as well as the computational integration of other omic data. Through such efforts, activity metabolomics and lipidomics holds promise in unraveling the intricate connections between metabolites, lipids, and phenotypes, contributing to a deeper understanding of biological systems, and paving the way for innovative therapeutic strategies.

Conclusions

title: Activity Metabolomics and Mass Spectrometry (AMMS)
text:
Increasing attention is being drawn to the idea that metabolites and lipids can act as controllers, not just cogs in a system. Termed "activity metabolomics," this approach employs metabolomics and lipidomics to identify active metabolites and lipids. The central focus is to identify master metabolites/lipids, achieved through computational integration of metabolomics, lipidomics, systems biology, and bioactivity data. This enables the identification of potent naturally occurring molecules that modulate biological processes and cell physiology. Challenges, such as metabolite/lipid identification, have already seen significant progress. Figure 12.1 illustrates the goal: leveraging metabolomics/lipidomics-driven screening methods to identify these master regulators. Activity metabolomics and lipidomics stand to impact multiple scientific disciplines.
